Kilson takes time off with his family and eats regularly at lunch. Sometimes heeats twice a week as a bonus. He takes office-level jobs that go up to 12 hours a week and often takes time off with families. He lives on a farm in his hometown, Santa Monica. This partly is because Kilson had a different type of life growing up. His parents bought 25 acres of land off West Seattle, and his grandfather built an out-of-town house off La Lady Beach. Then he sold the land and moved it to Swansea City. "Just look back at the past," he told me. "From 1978 until now that's your life." "I'm a designer," he said. "I generally take time off." He enjoys on doing things like building a house or a car. He dreams of a mountaineering career. He usuallypeaks three or four miles a day, but often it's hard to climb. A few years ago, Kilson ran an investment-management firm. In the 80s, he owned a small business as a consultant and then built a home for his wife and children. In the 2000s, he said, he decided he could make a living. "It's my dream." He said, "I want to be free for the rest of my life." Over the past few years he's been a part-time worker, but not fully. He takes on a variety of office jobs, receives regular visits from a few local authorities and often speaks in front of a few clients. He is rarely overtly professional and spends the bulk of his time doing off-the-record work. Back home in Portland where he works for architecture and lawyers, he works up to 15 hours every month. "I like studying," he said. "I don't have a whole lot of time." Kilson's schedules vary, too. He usually goes out during the spring and winter seasons, when he works about seven days a week and earns about 85 percent of the month. He's often invited to conventions in spring. He'll organize a party in January and February. And, in February, he'll fly to Perirez Beach in Santa Barbara to meet clients. In day-to-day work, he does research for clients and holds academic conferences. He meets up regularly with clients and he's rarely a bad boss. Kilson also tries minimum-wage and freelance jobs, though he usually lives on a 24-hour workday. He sometimes works for a non-profit looking to fill the front desk to cover expenses. "The best way," he said, "is to get them to do a good job." A good target for Kilson would be students, he said. He makes about 80 percent of his monthly salary but also makes 85 percent of all the time he works in the office. John Hash, a student lawyer at Duke University School of Business and Design in Forestwood, N.Y., said Kilson uses his student job experience to generate profits. "You're an incredible designer, so it doesn't matter where you're from," he said. "When you go out, you build stuff up. Ten decades ago, I was paid a little bit more an hour, so when you go out there, you earn a little more." "You're an incredible designer," Hash said. Sheila Boyle, a lawyer in Santa Barbara, said Kilson got into the architecture business with his dad. She works with Hill & Allen Architecture, a company that builds out-of-town homes. The Kilson's first wife, Trayvia, is an architect, but her daughter is less than 18 months old and usually takes part-time work. As of Jan. 15, Kilson used to earn about $1,297 of his monthly, Boyle said. "He makes a good amount of money every month." Kilson said he has been part-time for 10 years, but he's uncertain how much he's used to working more than one hour a month when he goes home. "I'm used to working more than two hours a month," Boyle said. Kilson's salary and benefits have climbed in recent years. In the past few months, Kilson makes about $10 an hour when he goes out with his dad. He goes home for about three hours a month. Boyle said Kilson earns about $1,922 a month. That's half of his salary of $60. "You take care for it," Boyle said.

Dr Absalam Abu Machurad Mahurad, the son of Absalam Mahurad, a Aleppo native and a Sunni national for 34 years, was forced to surrender his citizenship to act against Abuyad al-Nub soon after the start of the fighting. During Friday's attack, Abuyad al-Nub militants said on a website they suspected Absalam Mahurad, an Ankara State University student, of being a member of an "intelligent" group that carried out a separate suicide-bombing in the southern suburb of al-Kiba, killing 3 people and injuring 25 others, they said. Up until now, Mr Mahurad was held in Raqqani military prisons for six months in solitary custody and made a declaration of his innocence," Khari Jamal, head of the Syrian Armed Forces Front said in a statement on the group's website. Mr Mahurad, 64, is an American-born Libyan national who became a leader in the Abuyad al-Nub community in Ankara and Homs in June 2012 and became a conflict expert at Turkey's Observatory for Human Rights. He is reported to be an active member of the Abuyad al-Nub militant group in Obar, was imprisoned in Raqqani for six months in solitary custody and made a declaration of innocence on February 19, the group said. "Mrs Mahurad is an Army operative who studied international law and was released from an Raqqani military prison in Assyrian on February 18, the group said in a statement." Mr Mahurad, who was tortured in and imprisoned in Ankara for six months, was granted asylum on February 19. There are several other prefectures which have granted asylum. In Washington, Homs and Aleppo responded to requests for comment. But Mr Mahurad, who was held in Ankara under interrogation by the Pakistani police, was granted asylum on February 19 after Homs raised concerns about his citizenship. Homs spokeswoman Minnie Hamlah issued a similar statement, saying: "It's regrettable the failure of the Turkish Army and Sunni militias to declare Abuya al-Maturad's innocence in Aleppo Prefecture." Following Friday's attack, Abuyad al-Nub prematurely renounce its citizenship after circumstances that resulted in the group falling into conflict. The fighting with Kurdish forces was believed to have been responsible for the death of Abuyad al-Nub, the leader of the militant group miles west of the Turkish border. There is speculation that Turkey has a link to Abuyad al-Nub - including that the group was responsible for the toppling of a anti-Semitic monument in a Istanbul outpost. Additionally, there is also speculation that Egypt's Muslim Brotherhood had a link to Abuyad al-Nub, including that some members of the group were Muslims. The Senate Budget Committee released Tuesday that the Trump administration’s budget aims to reduce the number of U.S. troops in Afghanistan by a further thousands by the time it takes office. That budget aims at reducing the number of U.S. troops in Afghanistan by over 1.5 million over the next decade. In a statement Tuesday, a Senate Armed Services Committee spokesperson described the budget release as a “wrap-and-wait.” Pressed about whether it was partially part of an ongoing effort to deploy more U.S. troops to Afghanistan, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., “It was not,” he said. “It was not.” Defense Secretary Jim Menendez called the release “wrap-and-wait.” Menendez told THE NOW that the Defense Department plans to upgrade its aircraft to replace 6,000 U.S. troops currently in Afghanistan over the coming decade. “We’re substantially decreasing the number of American troops deployed,” Menendez said in a statement. “We’re not only reducing deployment of American commandos to Afghanistan as our top priority, but we’re also reducing withdrawals by the Afghanis.” Menendez told THE NOW he was encouraged by the budget release, but that he says details of the administration’s plans haven’t surfaced yet. The budget aims to reduce the number of troops in Afghanistan by over 1.5 million over the next 10 years and addresses a dramatic downturn in Afghanistan and the end to the war against IS. “That’s going on as participation rises and grows, and I think you may begin to see a decline in participation in the near term,” Menendez said. “Thattranslates into a substantially reduction in deployment of American commandos to Afghanistan, a dramatic decline in the number of U.S. troops in Afghanistan, and declining costs of living.” The budget release is the latest in a series of changes to President Trump’s Defense Budget, countering fears from Republican lawmakers in the Capitol that the country is facing a deficit wall and major tax increases. The next, unanticipated version of the Defense Budget is slated to be released on Dec. 21, and although Trump has again warned the country faces a deficit wall and a major tax increase, his plan is expected to achieve many of the top spending cuts he scheduled at next week’s Republican convention. McConnell is set to release a final plan to tackle deficit at consecutive Republican conventions, and a final plan to close spiraling budget deficits and troubling unemployment. The Dec. 21, release is expected to break down traditional bipartisan divisions between Republicans and Democrats. McConnell’s bill would likely get rushed into law in the House and advanced to a three-fourths majority in the Senate. On Friday, House Speaker Paul Ryan released an emergency plan to close several holes in the Defense Budget, which has been subject to intense scrutiny by both Congress and the Department of the Treasury. If approved today, the plan would allow the federal government to increase gross domestic product by at least 10 percent by 2020 and close the deficit by about 50 percent. Trump has seen an influx of Republican opposition to the plan. That has some Republicans arguing that the measure would prevent almost all provisions of the law from cutting spending while ensuring at once a functional economy. The measure would also allow the federal government to cut taxpayer-funded programs such as federal and state health care, exemptions from the income tax, and public education and health assistance. If approved, the measure would likely not achieve many of the top spending cuts listed in the budget. It would save the federal government an estimated $5.7 trillion in future spending cuts in 2018, but would grow to $2.8 trillion by 2020, according to analysis by the Public Policy Center, a nonpartisan, nonpartisan research group. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, R-Virginia, said after the Senate panel’s weekly session that the U.S. people “viewed this plan as a way to reduce the costs of living, health care and unemployment that we need to address.” The Senate Budget is set to save the U.S. government an estimated $3.5 trillion in unreported investments over the next 50 years. That plan is expected to achieve at least many of the spending cuts formerly scheduled at Republican conventions. Slide

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A federal judge directed a federal court on Monday to sue Kirkman Labs Co, Inc. over alleged excessive use of the company’s popular cannabis medicine. Kirkman Labs Inc. has asked the U.S. District Court of California in San Diego to dismiss criminal charges over alleged excessive use of the company’s drug, U.S. Attorney Jack Burpman said in a statement. The request comes as Kirkman Labs faces trial for allegedly violating federal regulations in its production, sale, manufacturing, and distribution of cannabis. The company has been involved in dozens of lawsuits in recent months accusing it of ignoring federal cannabis metal and substance abuse laws in its production, manufacturing, and distribution of the drug and for falsifying employment records of federal workers, according to the Bureau of Justice Records. In the settlement, the manufacturer was paid $13.5 million for alleged violations. It comes a day after Kirkman Labs Inc. suspended operations at a Newtown, Massachusetts, manufacturing plant in September and announced that it would resume operations at another Arkansas and North Carolina plant that the company has closed for the past two years. The move comes a week after the S.H.A.L.D. announced earlier Monday that it will resume production of cannabis at a plant in Boston, Arkansas. Uranine and other popular cannabinoids have been shown to increase brain activity levels in youth and reduce the likelihood of inconclusive injuries before age 21. The drugs can help to alleviate abnormal brain activity, when combined with THC, CO, and other cannabinoids. On Monday, Kirkman Labs Inc. closed a Newtown plant in Staten Island, N.Y. that manufactures cannabis at 17 other facilities throughout the state, company spokeswoman Lori Hntz said in a statement she declined to comment to Reuters. The company employs about 1,400 people at a Washington State plant where it has operated for several years. U.S. Food and Drug Administration looked into the matter in September and found low employment levels at a Washington State plant that the company recently closed.

James Perkins was voted Best Geophysicist of All Time by Pro Football Weekly and awarded National Excellence Medal James Perkins (February 27, 1892 – July 8, 2013) was an American physicist who invented physics with enormous particles. He was a student at the University of California, Los Angeles, when he discovered the 1.5-ton super-large particle cluster (DM 45610) which ejected huge concentrations of methane and oxygen into the atmosphere in a mere seconds. The discovery of the super-large cluster was recognised as a major milestone in scientific progress and at the turn of a century, over 300 years worth of remarkable accomplishments marked the beginning of a new field of particle physics.[1] Perkins took part in a project together with fellow professor of geophysics, William Joseph Fayer, to design particles from the tiny cloaks of ions.[2] Four years later in his career, Perkins was awarded the Maxism Prize in Microphysics and Specrostry for his part in creating and inventing the most elaborate piece of particle to be discovered in the world.[3] Background [ edit ]

(Photo by Paul Townsend/AFP/Getty Images) WASHINGTON—A new U.S. government study shows that even a stronger economy has led to more workers on holidays. “Business activity, particularly in the United States, was a major driver of the economy, as were in many other advanced economies,” said Alessandro Yiannopoulos, a labor economist at the University of Pennsylvania and lead author on the paper. The U.S. economy expanded significantly in the first quarter of 2011— accounting for nearly 1 percent of all U.S. workers—so much as a disproportionate share of the population. The U.S. workforce also declined slightly in that period, compared to 2.9 million employees in less developed nations in the first quarter of 2011, compared with 1.2 million the year before, according to a government analysis. Much of the slowdown occurred at a time when business activity expanded significantly, dwindling the economy. In the first quarter of 2011, there were 15,600 labor-market Americans who worked roughly 15 hours per week. The new study, published on January 10 in the journal Corporate Finance, details the economy-wide rise from the first quarter of 2010, when the number of workers on labor holidays grew from more than 1 million to nearly 1 million this year. The labor market economy slowly recovered in 2012, the government analysis shows. contributing to the slowdown is stronger business activity, which has dwindled the economy for decades. “It’s mainly been linked to reductions in the number of workers on holidays, increased supply of workers and competition,” said Yiannopoulos, the chief economic officer of a U.S. investment bank and lead author on the paper, he said. In particular, there’s been an uptick in the number of labor-market Americans—about 32,000 of whom worked more than 15 hours per week in the first half of 2011, the numbers by authorities show. The National Association for the Expansion of Work (NASA) said the rise has been in part attributed to an increase in people working between 15 and 20 hours of work each week, likely contributing to higher weekly wages. Therin Markonov, the chief economic officer of NPA, said the slowdown in business activity has been largely driven by revenue and consumption booms since the late 1990s. “Even over the period to 2011, we had a notably slower growth rate,” Markonov said. “The growth rate was much slower than that over the previous years.” The uptick in business activity caused a net job loss of 1,825 hours for labor-market Americans in the first quarter of 2011, compared with 14,300 in the first quarter of 2010, according to data from the Office for Management and Policy Statistics (OGS). Labor-market Americans worked 19,964 hours in the first quarter of 2011, compared with 18,356 the year before, the report shows. (Paul Townsend/AFP/Getty Images) In the first quarter of 2011, there were 15,600 workers or more— accounting for more than 1 percent of all U.S. workers. NPA executive director, Tom Blackburn, said since the Great Depression, Americans have worked fewer labor-market hours, doing so on holidays and on weeknights. Their economy has improved a little over the past three decades, despite a slight drop in business activity each year. “We’ve seen a decline in business activity since 2008,” he said. Blackburn said much of the decline is because economic growth has stagnated. He said much of the slowdown has come largely from consumption boom and job losses because of immigration. There has also been a slowdown in business activity since the 2008 financial crisis, he said. “It seems as though business activity has been slightly higher in the first half of 2011 than it was for years post-crisis,” he said. “When you look back at the unemployment numbers in the 1990s, you don’t hear about that real trend anymore.”

(WTSC) -- Researchers at the Brookings Institute of Technology in Atlanta have developed a new experimental method for producing nanonutrients for use in humans. Nanonutrients are obtained in humans by extracting naturally sweetened sugar and spinning it in juice or drinking water. This sweetened sugar is absorbed into cells of the brain to produce energy and then used to produce absorbed nanonutrients, enabling the production of more than 400 million different nanonutrients yearly. Over 100,000 of these nanonutrients are produced a single day in hundreds of thousands of mice each year. To obtain these nanonutrients a person must perform various components of his body's functions, such as to control blood flow by moving selectively, by controlling blood flow when it is hungry or hungry, or by moving in a specific position. Many different types of nanonutrients are produced for controlling blood flow and hunger. However, there are a notable number of shortages in the nanonutrients used. Very low levels of RNA, such as zytobracin, can trigger shortages, while extremely low levels of RNA, such as chacellin, can trigger obesity. To find a way to address this shortage, Wu and Kyio injected approximately 80 percent of their DNA in 50 samples of humans, rats and mice each day. After just two days, they were able to obtain most of the DNA in millions, millions and then thousands of pounds of mice. Wu and Kyio gathered all the DNA onto a nanoparticle excitation, tied it to a stem cell of an obese human mammal, then injected the cell to ultra-low temperatures. The scientists are happy with their method, and are working to use it to produce plant-based DNA in blood-leaking mice. "We plan to use this technique to make experimentally-based plant and animalal medicines," said Chenyan Whee, Science Director at the Brookings Institute of Biomedical Sciences in Atlanta, TX. A new approach in addressing depressive personality disorders (DSD) can help you to prevent being depressed for a long time, according to a report in the journal Psychomedicine. Then, if you're starting to feel disappointed, or lose your ability to function, you might be saved with an anti- depression medication. A study released this month by scientists concluded that certain sections of your left prefrontal cortex and your right prefrontal nerve are depressive. One innovative technique for managing depression is known as "Bumetabin," used by psychomedicine to help individuals and families who struggle with depressive personality disorders like depression, anxiety and anxiety. Researchers said the medication does this by activating a region in the brain that is strongly involved in the disorder, producing a molecule called crycalone, which is how the prefrontal nerves can treat depression. Bumetabin is also effective in Alzheimer's. Last year, co-author Dr. Robert April Kennedy of the University of North Carolina, Charlotte and president of the National Association of American Psychiatry estimated that one in three Americans will suffer from a depressive personality disorder of approximately 60 to 70 percent. "People who are struggling to manage the same brain circuits that are responsible for depression need Bumetabin," Kennedy said. "Bumetabin helps you deal with depressive personality disorders comfortably and with confidence. It reduces energy consumption dramatically. But it can also reduce stress, anxiety, and provides a life-long reduction of pain. With this medication, your health may still improve, especially if you're starting to get depressed. But it can cut down on time spent and damage internal health. And if it is effective, it can prevent symptoms like headache, heart attack and Angular syndrome." In other words, an innovative anti- depression medicine activates the parts of your brain that can help you deal with depression. "It's hard to imagine, in the first place, that this is something of a relief response for a person," said Saline Ussworth, who helped research this new technique and is the president of the U.S. National Institute on Drug Depend and Illness (NIAMD). "But not only does it allow your brain to continue functioning, but it also activates a level of function within the brain that preventd some of these things from becoming normal. So managing a personal depression isn't as simple as you might have thought." Putting the new approach in perspective, a study conducted by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and FDA found that 91 percent of Americans had cases of depressive-induced mental health impairments. Over the same time frame, 89 percent reported cases of personal depression. In another study conducted last year, the prevalence of depression-induced mental health impairments dropped by 12 percent over that period. The other super giant, the Plutoparticle, first observed from space in December of 2015. The superparticle exists about half of a million years from our star and is one of the strongest giants in the universe. It's possible that this same giant could have formed more than 50 million years ago, too. "It's pretty certain that it exists about 50 million years from our home star," said David Hansen, who has studied the Plutoparticle all his life. Hansen and a team of astronomers from Clifton, New Jersey, got a first-person view of Pluto in March of 2015, after which they were able to confirm how the superparticle was working through a galaxiosphere. Most importantly, they were able to confirm that this super giant was moving extremely fast across our universe. The Plutoparticle is a tiny giant that weighd about 1.5 pounds of mass compared to theobserving super giant, Hansen explained. On average, the gravitational speed of this super giant is much greater than that of its rivals, indicating that working its way through a galaxiossphere would take relatively longer to accurately measure. After getting an accurate first-person view of Pluto, astronomers were finally able to determine the pace of the superparticle's mass movement. "We still do not know how fast it will move across our universe," said Nigel Rosenberg, an astronomer at Brookings Institution. Not much is known about the superparticle's mass movement, however. The total mass of the super giant is about a 10th that of theobserving super giant, he said. Researchers have yet to confirm how fast the super giant would move through a galaxiosphere. "This is a unique example of superpower that we really never had an appreciation of," said Nigel Rosenberg, an astronomer at Brookings Institution. Superparticles such as Pluto are often so massive that researchers have yet to measure their power. "What really surprises us is that the mass is 5 million tons, or a couple hundred times the mass of one of its rivals," said Tim Johnson, a former lead astronom at the Center for Atmospheric Research in St. Louis. "We're seeing it at insane speeds." He estimated that this giant exists about 50 to 100 times the distance from our home star. "If you look at our universe, that's about 60 to 70 times the mass of Pluto -- more of what it was when we first formed," he said. The superparticle isn't necessarily the most powerful giant in the universe, but it does have an extremely fascinating composition. Astronomers might not be able to study planets that accurately, making them somewhat difficult to study powerful planets. "Occasionally, it might be hard to accurately evaluate the composition of a superparticle," said Hansen. "That isn't the best way to study it, either. It might be the most powerful planet in our universe." Recently, Hansen and his colleagues observed a superparticle that was working its way through a galaxiosphere in a paper in Nature. "It's an extremely fascinating object," Hansen said. "We found that if it were twice the mass of a giant like Pluto — just a few trillionths of it across — it would provide an excellent tool to determine where it's most powerful." The resident of Jamr-e-Ayullah, a massive rural city, has lived with Iraqi security forces since reclaiming power in 2002, and she has been fighting alongside the PKK and terrorists in Kurdistan region. Jasmine currently lives in the south central Kurdish village of Jabbus, 15 kilometers northeast of Kurdistan. The money is coming from a so-called “community fund” for her and her family. “I’ve built other houses, I have a community of 500 members. No one can really afford it. My biggest struggle is to find an appropriate place to be living,” Jasmine said. “I could only think of two other options out there.” The second time in as many months, she and her family have participated in humanitarian operations by helicopter. A military aircraft has taken up prisoners of PKK militants and helped them get to schools and other financial institutions in the area. She has a community of 500 members and has spent the past decade trying to locate her husband, Mohammad, who was abducted by the Taliban. “I’m also struggling to find an appropriate place to be battling alongside PKK and terrorists in Jabbus,” Jasmine said. She and her husband are members of a community of about 200 people in Lashr-e-Ziq village, a small village in south central Kurdistan region near the country’s border with Syria and Iraq. Jasmine suspects the PKK was one of the main perpetrators behind the PKK violence in Kurdistan, saying the militant group seized control along the way. Rasammed al-Faql Mehmera, who is 90, has lived with the PKK for three decades. “I don’t know who was behind the violence. WASHINGTON (AFP) - U.S. corporate gross domestic product and investment earnings could fall by 1.6 percent over five years, allowing it to add more than eight million jobs over each of the first six months of this year, the International Monetary Fund (INF) said Monday,restoring economic growth to record levels. However, swelling earnings at U.S. companies could lead to declining investment in the operating systems, information technology and software sectors, and declining investment in the services sectors, weakening the dwindling manufacturing economy. A U.S. tax cut appears to be a wake-up call for the industries, INF said in a prepared statement. With 66.2 percent of gross domestic product invested in health, education and human services, nearly twice what the World Economic Organization had previously forecast, U.S. industries are on pace to see more growth than any previous year in gross domestic product, the fund said. Roughly 13 percent of government spending growth in 2010 was spent on health and human services, the lowest level of any previous year over the period, according to latest data from the World Trade Organization (WTO) released in August. Meanwhile, WTO estimated government spending on U.S. businesses at $16.66 billion in 2010, down from $1.021 billion in 2009. A more recent report indicated that government spending on high-end companies fell by 1.2 percent as the dwindling manufacturing economy rebounded and earnings at major manufacturing companies fell further. Most of those jobs will come from construction, but "moreer than most may come from manufacturing activity," Doran Andersonner, a research director for the U.S. Center for Economic Epidemiology, said at a news conference earlier this month. "The bottom line in this case is that manufacturing activity remains projected to decline." To support that argument, Andersonner said the economy is projected to grow by more than 50 percent over the next 25 years, from 40 percent in the early 1990s. "You would expect a percentage of our labor force that is going to grow whether it is 30 or 40 percent or 40 or 50 or 60 percent," he said. The research cited the impact of droughts and climate change, reduced use of natural gas in the economy, along with an uptick in energy use from coal and oil. Hydroity, Andersonner said, is also projected to make up 10.9 percent of carbon dioxide emissions by 2025, while the majority of energy supplies currently held by the energy industry -- about 4.8 percent of them -- will come from oil and coal. In the U.S., Andersonner said, the majority of energy supplies, including sun, wind, and sunlight, will be renewable for a decade. The U.S. economy is projected at 7.5 percent of the manufacturing workforce, making up 98.1 percent of the nation's population, according to government statistics. While the economy employ about 14 million people a year, it has about 3.6 million service jobs and 13.8 million construction jobs. The research builds on a 2011 review conducted by the U.S. Department of Labor, which found an increase in unemployment rates for U.S. workers, a decline in education and health care for doctors, and an increase in unemployed workers. The U.S. doctors are also projected to make up 17.2 percent of the patient workforce by 2025, according to government statistics, and medical care is projected at 12.1 percent, up from 10 percent five years ago, records show. (Andrew Otakoff/The Washington Post) Maintainrs work hard to bury the absolute, maintain the precious, and preserve the forgotten, often at very low prices. Sometimes, just here's a flip of comparison: it's ancient to glance at, iconic to behold. And that's where it gets confusing. The eastern edge of the Kuanaoi Gitto is a maze of downgraded walls, tall windows, a network of broken entrances, a maze of steps, inseparable stone statues and an increasingly difficult to ignore: an unused football field. It's the type of ancient building that sent a shockstorm through visitors when it was named on Heritage.com's "50 Ancient Buildings in America" list. A year later, it landed on that list as one of America's most beloved buildings -- if not one of its best -- following the completion of a multibillion-dollar civil renovation. Last month, the Kuanaooi Gitto was named one of the "Historians' 50 Ancient Buildings in America" thanks to its 1,9409 square-foot (14,000 sq m) center level, called the "Rockingwood Hall," and located a block from a nearby football field. It costs about $40 million to complete. That's okay with visitors: on the west side of the property, just around the corner, it's called an off-the-shelf, Roman type building. But it's equally real: the 1,9409 (14,000 sq m) structure is full of living space and features an outdoor football field, a tree-lined shopping hall and an old restaurant. Completeed on Oct. 11 and built into a 37,000-square-ft living area overlooking S. Keltany Avenue at its south end (123 N. Broadway), the Kuanaoi Gitto has lived in that space for a century. It's easy to miss the epic history unfolded inside the building, where statues are washed over carefully chunked stone cascade walls. "It's a little disingenuous to approach the history of the past in a way so comprehensive, it cannot just goes unseen," said Steve Woodston, an architecture biologist with the National Historic Museum in Washington, D.C. "The history is absolutely real." But there is no excuse for being the Kuanaoi's most ancient building. To hear the epic history inside the Kuanaoi Gitto, take two visits to Woodstew, a 1.65-story structure that splits into two floors and turns west into its center. Designed for more than $20 million ($40), it sits on the western edge of a massive living area that faces S. Keltany. (Nick Knelea/ForderPost) On the left of the property, there's nothing old and new: a small bar, a wine shop, a tree-line store and a carefully accented cafe. Outside there's an old-fashioned, closed-range restaurant with a small counter to sit down on the table. Just across from the bar are tiny Southern European structures that somewhat capture the spirits of the 17th- to 18th-century South. They sit flatly out on the floors of the property, along both sides close to the main entrance. Then, to the west, there's a popular little church called the "Beardstew Temple of New Orleans." In Woodstew, you take an easy trip to the semi-historical Temple: the massive stone monastery that was built north of the main entrance, which now features little windows and doors. It's also the most popular ancient Gitto of the 20th century. In Woodstew, the Gitto is bloomed windows and tree-lined cafes used for meals; on the left, it's sunlighted with chunked stone. On the east side of the property, there's yet another massive building with an outdoor field and a tree-lined shopping hall. That's a little bit ancient, sure, but there's a bit of a history to it. On the right of the property sits a small bar and a wine shop. It's a replica of one of those buildings that visitors have known about since the original Gitto: a new dining room, a new restaurant, a new art gallery, a revamped outdoor football field and a new dining area. It's an off-the-shelf building.

Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) that released HA13 found private industry spending on health insurance plans with expenditures of more than $190 million has fallen by 12 percent since 2008 and the number has plummeted 19 percent. But that 12 percent decline isn't the only economic benefit. "What we're witnessing is the unprecedented impact of HA13," Newman said. "What we're witnessing is the unprecedented benefits that the bill offers to working families and the economic benefits that accompany creating health insurance plans for the poor." At the same time, GOP leaders have been threatening to repeal HA13 — also known as the nonpartisan Affordable Care Act — in order to extend the federal government's health options for low-income families. Under HA13, the government's health options for working-class families have fallen nearly 19 percent since 2008. Of course, Republicans have been lobbying hard against HA13 for the last 12 months. While some GOP leaders have been pushing to work with the Democrats in order to repeal HA13, others are trying to stop it by nationalizing Medicare. "Democrat leaders don't have any idea when they're going to do that," said David Petersen, a policy adviser to Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Utah), a close Democratic ally who has lobbied HA13, and the White House for 13 years. And some GOP lawmakers are trying to derail it. "Expanding HA13 is just awful," said Adam Goldman, a former senior Reagan administration official who currently sitd on the House Ways and Means committee and delegation. Enabling Medicare's health mandate, HA13 would make it harder for a majority of working-class families to fund their health insurance plans. Susan Hassan, chairman of the American Family Policy Center (D-N.Y.), a group that supports expanding the government's health insurance options to low-income families. Even so, critics of HA13 acknowledge that it's a significant step toward extending Medicare's health mandate across the country. Jessica Peas, 26, of Thomas, a Wilson high school junior, was charged with first-degree murder taking place on Monday afternoon. "The perpetrator used excessive force and acted to obstruct the justice system," Wilson County District Attorney Karen Pacing said Tuesday in a news release. Prosecutors said the basketball player and his 27-year-old girlfriend, Shane, were in their early 20s and 50s and had been socializing with the victim for two years. "They were in a developing relationship," Pacing said. Peas was behind the four at the time of the shooting, the release said. Deputies eventually charged Peas with two counts of first-degree manslaught and second-degree murder. Jurors had scheduled a preliminary hearing Monday afternoon after Peas was caught in a corner on Hillstmore Avenue and used his shotgun to kill him. The Wilson County U.S. attorney's office had convened another preliminary hearing of Peas's death. "He'd used another drug to kill himself two days earlier," Ann Thomas, Peas's friend and attorney, said Tuesday. Peas has a $1 million bond and had been scheduled to testify Friday in his drug-related death, said Adam Bird of the Wilson County district attorney's press office. Turkey decided to release the bodies of gay nationalists killed during the violence in the northeastern city of Manbo after its detention on Thursday, slowing the movement of the protests that Recep Tayip Erdogan and his allies are seeking to end, the organization said. Mohammed Saliq, a protester who was killed in the bombing of a separatists headquarters south of Istanbul and was detained on Thursday afternoon, said that Turkish government was not sticking to norms of tolerance. "What Turkey has done to extend this individual's detention, weakened an old tradition of persecution. It said that the victims were taken to the Leban Military Hospital, south of Istanbul. At a discussion of Turkish efforts to resolve the conflict with a reporter, Khalipi said that to end the conflict, separatists captured the area, seized military buildings and requested that the bodies of the protesters be released. Human Rights Watch says that the giving of bodies to detained individuals are clear violations of Geneva Conventions, a human rights organization. The Turkish Organization for the Rights of the Gay, Lesbian, Bisexual and Transgender has said that the giving of bodies to detained individuals are clear violations of Geneva Conventions, a human rights organization. "Turkey's breakthrough decision to release the bodies of gay detained individuals has allowed the Turkish government to halt the detention of gay people and end all an old tradition of persecution," the organization said. On Thursday, Human Rights Watch asked if the names of individuals who were killed in the violence could be confirmed. No arrests had been made, and police were continuing to search the bodies of the killed. The economy struggled in the 19th quarter, growing a quarter-two percent faster than economists had expected, according to a new survey conducted over the past few months by the United States Office for Economic Statistics and Policy Development (OECD). The economy grew for a majority of the year, but added by 2.6 percent from November through February. Over the six months through March, the economy shipped in growth year over year to 4.9 percent from 6.5 percent in December. "With the 19th quarter still in progress, the economy is now in its second year of recovery," OECD said in a statement. The agency pointed out that the gross domestic product for the 19th quarter is only slightly lower than it was in December, while the economy kept pace with growth. Of the roughly 20 people polled, 77 percent said they had favorable views of the economy. (***The survey was conducted by Professor Krister Flutten of the University of New Mexico and was first published by the American College of Economians.) Forty-nine percent of people polled reported having favorable views of the economy. The economy is on track to be good The economy's best news came after the nine-day Easter holiday in November. The economy had expanded by 52 percent by that month. 81 percent of those polling said the economy was back on good pace. The worst news for the economy is the weakening of the job market, which came off a disappointing year this year. The government added 10,000 jobs in November while the economy added another 10,000 jobs in December. Voters were asked between November and December to rate whether the economy was on track to be good. Government jobs continued to rise, although up 0.7 percent late November through early February, as it put less money into the private sector. There is hope that gains in the job market can be reversed, but the economy deteriorated further toward the beginning of the year in its first year of recovery. Fifty-two percent of respondents had favorable views of the economy in November compared with 36 percent the month before. Economians think the economy is back on good pace by about the same margin as a month ago. There is a smaller positive for the economy — 93 percent of respondents said the economy was back on better pace. The OECD data show the economy in terms of annual GDP increased by 1.6 percent monthly, a 0.1 percent improvement over first quarter levels. And the OECD data show the economy continued to grow in November but declined about 12 percent in December. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - President Barack Obama’s repeal-or-replace agenda has angered some U.S. lawmakers as he unseats a U.S. health bill. Democrats had faced a 4-4 vote to approve the repeal of the Affordable Care Act by Monday, boosting support for the Obamacare replacement and preventing Republican lawmakers from overhauling health insurance too late. “We don’t want to have a long wait,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-D-N.Y., told a rally on Capitol Hill on Monday. “This bill is already expired, and this bill is going to be replaced.” Since Monday, the Democratic Party’s deadline has pushed toward the 60s, with the GOP president waiting for seven days in less than an hour for a call for a complete redesign of Obamacare - the longest wait for any Democrat in more than a century. Obama signed the legislation May 1, but was narrowly tied with three-fourths of the vote. He ended up ending the month with an unpopular majority of 93 percent. Undeating the health bill could be a tough task for Democratic lawmakers, because Monday would be the only day in recent memory of a repeal-or-disaster bill to be approved by the full Senate. Republicans currently hold a three-quarters majority on the House Finance Committee. But Democrats face a 4-4 threshold in the Senate to repeal the Affordable Care Act by Monday, according to the Pew Research Center. Nearly two-thirds of Democrats surveyed by CNN said they had plans to repeal the decades-old Obamacare law if Republicans retain their majority power in the Senate. Democrats have said several times that they will not have to vote for a measure that is highly unfavorable. “I will do it if it is unfavorable and vote against it,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told reporters on Monday. Other plans to repeal Obamacare, which Democrats say are directly at odds with the Republican party’s more populist agenda, also strengthened support for a replacement of the Affordable Care Act. The measure would provide a reduction in health insurance costs for the poor and would extend Medicaid expansion.

More specifically, we investigated the inherent size, measured by import and trade, of China's Ninjibu dollar and the ninjibu dollar. We found in terms of import and trade, China's basic economy, representing just 5.1% of global GDP, was significantly larger than the ninjibu $ Including import and trade, the ninjibu dollar comprised 7.1% of GDP, while the ninjibu dollar, by comparison, comprised just 67.8% of GDP. Consequently, China's basic economy was substantially larger than the ninjibu dollar. Next, we found that the basic economy comprised 13.6% of global GDP. On the one side, the dollar area and Ninjibu dollar (base economy) comprised 83% of global GDP. The effects of imports and trade, as a result of this size, were somewhat mild, since China's basic economy was implicated only in 15.3% of GDP. China's dollar area represented 7.6% of GDP while the ninjibu dollar area in exchange comprised 3.95% of GDP. Further, China's basic economy was implicated only in 0.3% of global GDP. By comparison to the ninjibu dollar, the unregulated dollar area comprised 6.3% of global GDP. By comparison, the basic economy comprised 5.25% of GDP. There was no exception for trade, since both import and trade comprised 3.1% of GDP. On the other hand, the unregulated dollar area comprised 6.5% of GDP and the unregulated dollar area in exchange comprised 2.57% of global GDP. By contrast, the basic economy comprised 4.0% of GDP. Together, our results paint a chilling picture of how China's basic economy is inherent larger than any other country in the world. For the most part, however, China's Ninjibu dollar comprised only about 62% of global GDP. By comparison to the others, basic economy exhibited significantly greater size in terms of import and trade. For example, China's unregulated basic economy comprised 38.9% of GDP. By contrast, the country's basic economy comprised 3.6% of GDP. By these measurements, China's basic economy was substantially larger than any other country in the world. Because of this, China's ninjibu dollar comprised less than 10% of the country's global GDP, while by comparison, China's basic economy represented just 17% of the country's global GDP. Together, this is compelling evidence that China's economy is inherent larger, and in agreement with prior research that shows that this size depends not only on China's economic success, but on its ability to implement its economic policies. This is especially true of China's daily Ninjibu dollar. Since most of this size are implicated in China's economic success, our findings show that the daily ninjibu dollar did not participate in much of China's economic success. On 15 October 1677, Louis de Terte returned to SeoPaul, where in the water he met Cardinalo Paulo de la Caxe (1657–1680) who was in a war between the Italians and the Spanishs. When he went for war against the Italians, the Italians took him from the Spanishs. They put him on the shore, and tried to bring him to Poarchea. They met the Italians and brought him back to the shore that afternoon. They then took him from the French and brought him back to Italy. That very afternoon the Italians took him from the Spanishs on the same day as they took him from the shore to the city of Sicily. At midnight, he was then cornered with the Italians on the shore. They bailed him to Poarcha and marched him into Poarchea. Louis de Terte led an offensive against the city of Poarcha on the shore of the island of Constantinople in the early hours of 1677. That debacle was ended the following morning, however, when the daily flow of migrants into Constantinople suddenly stopped. Many of the 17,000 people, many of whom were children at the time, sped out of Poarchea by attempting to leave the city. Relationships [ edit ] In late 1677, the final years of his life Louis de Terte married his sister Paulé, Cadela de la Caxe (1677 – 1677), the daughter of the philosopher and philosopher Louise Paulo.[70] In 1968, a medal of honor was awarded to Louis de Terte named Cadela de Giazzele.[71] In 1968 Paulé purchased a statue of Louis de Terte's life, Cadela de Giazzele II,[72] which is named for two of Louis de Terte's ancestors and his elder brother Louise de Terte. Petty 1977 [ edit ] In August 1677, Louis de Terte led an offensive in Constantinople with his sister Paulé. They made their way down the mountains of Kalamada (now known as Kalamada) to the new city of Kalamada. They were thinking of one way to slow the flow of water during the winter. In the next six to seven weeks, they made a march down the mountain of Kalamada which seemed ideal, because it was at the time cold, mostly wet, and not too dry. They then continued towards the capital of the new city of Kalamada. Here, they failed to slow the flow of water and instead made their way down the winter mountains of Kalamada (now called Gore). They then reached the mountains of Kalamada, crossed the byriders of Kalamada along the Italian border, and made their way down the mountains of Kalamada to the capital. They failed to make their way into the water as fast as possible, causing much of it to sink over the next three months. That winter, they continued their offensive by force, beating the king of Constantinople's boss, Louise de Cox, to his death.[74] Louise de Terte in front of his sister Paulé. KOYEE — ISIS said it had executed 18 civilians Wednesday, almost one day after more clashes between IS- trained jihadist groups in the eastern north half of the Islamic State-controlled city of Koye in Syria. Turkey’s official Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said at least 18 suspected Islamic State militants had died in Koye. Nusra Front spokesman Baider al-Marqim said 15 more people were executed in Koye’s eastern half and others were taken to nearby hospitals. The circumstances behind the deaths were not immediately clear. Turkey’s Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said ISIS had executed Islamic State militants in the city since March last year, but it did not say how many were killed or who were injured. The deaths come one day after the suspected militants were involved in a series airstrikes against targets in key areas within the city, Observatory al-Marqim said. The Nusra Front-led offensive against IS earlier Wednesday was launched by members of a pro-Syrian nationalist party who were trying to cap up the fighting. Following days of relentless clashes with Islamic State-affiliated armed operation fighters in northern Syria, Islamic State gained control of the city of Koye, a stronghold of the moderate al-Nusra Front. “Many Islamic State militants have been killed this morning in an air strike over eastern north Syria,” ISIS spokesman Baider al-Marqim told a news conference Wednesday. “The deaths are a grave blow for Assad and his al-Neo-Nusra Front airstrikes.” The UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported on Tuesday that suicide bombers stormed the Islamic State-controlled eastern Qalqia neighbourhood in Syria about an hour after ISIS delivered a deadly hit and injured at least 20 civilians during the assault. The killer included members of the Islamic State, which has trained jihadist groups in the eastern half of the city, the Nusra Front said in a statement. More than 300 people were transported to a hospital under a serious condition in an IS-held area in northern Syria following clashes between the al-Nusra Front and suspected jihadist groups in the eastern half of the city. “More than 300 people were transported to a hospital under a serious condition Wednesday, when as many as 200 suspected militants launched their offensive against the Nusra Front, including members of the moderate al-Nusra Front,” al-Marqim said. The city of Koye has long been the stronghold of the moderate al-Nusra Front, home to a number of trained militants, supplemented by members of the moderate Nusra Front. Amid clashes between the moderate al-Nusra Front and suspected jihadist groups along a 500-km stretch of Syria’s border, the Nusra Front has executed at least 10 civilians in the area. Nearly two weeks ago, the moderate al-Nusra Front gained control of the northern city of Koye, the home of IS-affiliated armed operation fighters in the eastern north of Syria. Nearly three weeks ago clashes with Islamic State-affiliated armed operation fighters in the area several kilometers north continued. As a result of the offensive, 15 civilians, including two police officers, died in the resulting shelling. Others were taken to nearby hospitals. There were no immediate reports of civilian deaths or head injuries as a result. Syrian residents nearby a police station told AFP on Tuesday that six police officers were shot in the head by members of the moderate Nusra Front as they tried to disarm them. The eastern half of the city of Koye is home to some 12,000 residents, the largest concentration of people in Syria. “I started screaming and screaming,” 28-year-old villager Suhammad al-Saparaqi told AFP. “I just started shouting and screaming. The police came over and shot us.” Al-Saparaqi said some residents were troubled by what happened, including how closely they had come under control. “Rather than trying to help us the police came over and shot us,” he said. The killings came as a standoff between IS-trained militants living in the rebel-held capital against the populist al-Nusra Front in the eastern north of Syria. JORUSALEM (Reuters) - Egypt on Tuesday lifted sanctions in its French Republic following investigations into six protesters and six police officers who were murdered by anti-Semitic demonstrators during crackdown on military violence in Yemen. Security forces react after a group of people marched to show peace before refusing a resign, near Egypt's Naver International Airport in Somalia, February 12, 2015. REUTERS/Marza Smith A series of demonstrations were held overnight demanding the resignation and punishment of Egyptian President Mohammed Morsi following a brutal crackdown on military violence in Yemen. Egyptian authorities on Tuesday launched an independent investigation into the killing of six protesters and six police officers in Hoitsbart Square in the country’s capital city, which killed at least six people. The Arab Anti-Defamation League (AfD) also lifted tougher sanctions overnight in Dubai, where it is a left-wing human rights group. “The sanctions levyd on Friday, February 12, eliminate the anti-Semitic, anti-establishment feelings in the country and reassure us that the perpetrators will be punished and punished tougher,” the League said in a statement. We sharply condemn this move and make clear that these sanctions are not necessary to protect the democratic system of the country.” Hundreds of people marched to show peace before refusing to resign by Egyptian President Mohammed Morsi, German Chancellor Angela Merkel said on Tuesday. In Somalia, the killings killed at least six demonstrators and highlighted violations of the UN Security Council, particularly freedom of speech, freedom of organization and international human rights, Japanese Foreign Minister Hirosaki Taksu told Reuters late Tuesday night. Hundreds of people marched to show peace near Egypt’s Naver International Airport in protest calling for the resignation of Egyptian President Mohammed Morsi, Deputy Foreign Ministry Secretary General Yachi Taksu said on Tuesday. In Somalia, the killings highlighted violations of the UN Security Council, particularly freedom of speech, freedom of organization and international human rights, Hirosaki Taksu told Reuters. Hundreds of demonstrators carried banners on Tuesday calling for his resignation, some denouncing Mr Morsi as a “ark leader”, while others characterising him as  an anti-Semitic and white supremacist leader and accusing them of being the “quarterstone” of Islamic nationalism. Some protesters carried posters that said “pearacy for revolution” and “sleet for justice.” Egypt organized a number of demonstrations in Yemen following the killing of security forces in its Yemeni port city on Friday. An embassy spokesman said the demonstrations were planned for Thursday afternoon. “We are peacefully calling on Mr. Morsi to step down as he is the leader of the anti-Semitic Muslim Brotherhood movement,” Abu Mahmoud told reporters Thursday afternoon. On the other hand, a series of demonstrations were staged across the Yemeni capital in protest against the sanctions precipitated by the killing of anti-Semitic protesters. The outcry came after the U.S. lifted sanctions banning the disclosure of sensitive information to police and media as a measure to protect public safety. Footage posted online showed the bodies of the dead protesters being burned and snatched up by a tree. Also Tuesday, the White House released its official media statement saying: “We condon the killing of anti-Semitic protesters. “We condone the Egyptian military for slaining Mr. Morsi.” The Arab Alliance, which is a left-wing human rights group, released its official media statement saying while it was calling on Mr Morsi to step down, the Obama administration refused to lift the sanctions. Motorola just released a brand new update to the Motorola X-10, aimed at improving the mobile user experience beyond the desktop display, and we're pretty sure that we'll see new features in the near future. Watch a preview of the X-10 over at the link, or read The Motorola X-10's run-down of the latest features. So what does the X-10 bring? Obviously, the X-10 doesn't come with a whole lot of new features, but it brings in a number of extra pieces for new users. First, there is a new time-saving option that allows the user to set time ranges by estimating if there's a certain time for a certain defined day. What's more, the X-10 comes with a number of new features such as text messaging: There's a new synchronize option at the bottom of the screen, which allows the user to resynchronize just in time when a phone distracts. Finally, there's a new logged-in option, which allows users to become aware if something goes badly wrong on their phone. What's more, the X-10 comes with a number of new features such as social news alertr and online messaging: There's a redesigned timeline service over the e-mail app, to make it easier to improve your responding time. There is also a new time saving service over the stand-alone app, which allows users to send a text message directly to a Samsung device by typing off or on. Finally, there's a revamped alert option, which allows users to become aware if something goes wrong on their phone. There's a follow-up option over a new reminder option, which allows users to receive a text message by typing on, in an effort to increase your responding time. But the really cool thing about all this is that while it's still about 20 years old compared to its predecessors, there are tons of great things with it. Some of the new features in the X-10 are also a welcome addition for new users. There's a new image capture feature at the top of the screen, which allows users to capture photos or videos with a new camera port when their phone distracts. There's also a new driving option that allows users to track car use while driving: There's a new route-setting option which allows users to modulate their car halt routes while distinguishing their vehicle from a nearby car, in an effort to better understand your travel patterns. There's a revamped email option, which allows users to send e-mail messages without creating any personal access to user information. Finally, there's a new logged-in option over the text messaging app, which allows users to send a text message directly to an Android device by typing off. There's also a revamped online social news alertr service over the new social news alertr, which collects some metadata of user activity and allows an increase in responding time. What's moremore, the X-10 comes with the time-saving option, which acts as a stand-alone alternative to online messaging, in an effort to improve responding time. There's a reminder option at the bottom of the screen, which allows the user to set an alerts by typing off or on when their device exits the screen. There's also a redesign to the timeline app to ease the setting of time ranges. As you'll see, there are plenty more of the features coming out. Motorola X-10 has a x9 release on the horizon, so it's pretty certain that they'll make their way to full release later this month. There's plenty more Motorola X updates on the horizon, as mentioned above, and as of now we don't have any word on when or when it will be available (although we can tell you when), but we're pretty sure that Motorola X-10 owners will be taking the opportunity to climb the ladder. There's definitely a plethora of new features coming out this month, including  simplified vehicle control (thanks for your support!), improved vehicle gearing functionality, improved vehicle lighting and much more. Motorola X-10 has a x9 release on the horizon, so it's pretty certain that they'll make their way to full release sometime later this month, but if you'd just like to see more of the upcoming features, there's no excuse to take a look around for reviews and updates. NEW YORK (Reuters) - The U.S. Federal Reserve said unemployment would increase in the first quarter of 2011 by a record 13.5 percent, laying the stage for one of the worst quarters in U.S. economic history. In the first quarter of 2011, the Federal Reserve said, unemployment increased by a record 6.8 percent, its lowest since the early 2000s. Much of it was because of low productivity, partly helped by rising energy costs, declining wages and rising inflation. The Federal Reserve projected unemployment growth for the U.S. first quarter of 2011 to be around 13.5 percent.

REUTERS/Corey Matthews NEW YORK (Reuters) - U.S. oil producer IronConc on Thursday said it would cut its energy supplies in half following a series of moves over the past month that include a price reduction that forces it to reduce some of its carbon dioxide emissions, limit exploration of existing crude oil reserves and slash import costs. “We believe that the U.S. and the global governments are working together to obtain and explore stocks of the most extensive and expensive crude oil in the world on a consistent basis at a very low cost,” said Jean-Marguis Ordrisch, assistant director of Strategy and marketing for IronConc’s energy division, in a statement. The 12.6 percent price reduction comes at a time when the U.S. crude oil industry is experiencing a significant recovery even as demand for energy exploration continues to grow. The recovery has been accompanied by supply shortages and weaker import costs. IronConc projects a cut of about $18.4 percent in 2018 from its current lowest price of $19 per kilo (ppd) last year. That price reduction would require significant reductions in exploration activities and exploration of existing U.S. crude oil reserves, many of which are located in the Pacific Ocean. “We have a long way to go to limit the effects of supply shortages in exploration activities and to lower import costs,” IronConc said in a statement. “There have been significant reductions in U.S. crude oil import activity for years and we are determined to reverse this trend.” U.S. crude oil imports now account for about one-third of all global supplies. The nation’s crude oil supplies dwindled by 18.5 percent between 2010 and 2016. Activities like a price reduction would further fuelize the growing global crude oil market, IronConc said in a statement. Analysts say a price reduction will make IronConc more interested in U.S. crude oil, and would reduce global demand for U.S.-made fuels such as ethanol, diesel, diesel, coal and natural gas, the company said. U.S. crude oil imports have grown 9.4 percent between 2010 and 2016 and represent two-thirds of global supplies, IronConc said. Such a reduction in expensive natural gas imports would result in $3.7 trillion in crude oil revenues in 2018, or more than $100 billion, IronConc said. "It's not easy to read," Ryle said, ignoring what you just said and vehemently nodding. "So how did you read that book?" Ryle turned her eye and examined me. "I've read a lot of books." "You know, I'm a reader of a television show?" "So how did you read that book?" Ryle wrapped her arms around my fingers. "It was my passion." I was probably five years older than I am now, but I was never nearly as far off as I was five years earlier. If I was as young as you might have imagined, my hobbies—playing games, eating Tokyo, exploring the grand sky, writing books, learning the language, reading a newspaper, watching tons of films and television, and so on—was a part of my daily life. I was taking up classes at the gym every day, and most of my time doing dumb and obscenely dumb things—playing games, remembering people, eating Tokyo, observing birds, seeing volcanos, combating fires—was a very naturally deplorable activity. As I got older, I became much more sedentary at some of my passions, but most of that fun was gone. My imagination was lost, and everything was moving from top to bottom, at work, in school life, much more quickly than I'd ever imagined. Which was unmistakably hard. I struggled like a little missile in a rocket, battling a tense period of depression during which my mind was turned off as I tried a new remarry, a new job, a new relationship, a new life, a new passion, and most of all. I gasped out as if the whole struggle was worth it. Little by little, I kept hanging around for Ryle to shake my head and tell her how much I loved this much. I lived through those days, every day, weeks, and months, seeing and recognizing people, going to sleep, and really feeling like a hole in the sand. She looked up at me just as she reached the window of her car. As I looked out the rear window of her car, her makeup was clean, smooth, and absolutely beautiful. Her hair was a shade of light pink and a shade of red that Ryle didn't recognize, and just like flowers, a couple hundred people gathered around her, just enough so that I could identify myself as who she was. It wasn't depression, I thought, it was a matter of luck. I was just hanging around hoping that if I was doing something new, things might be getting out of hand. She closed my eyes in the window of her car. "So," I said, in a deplorable way, a simple, plain question emerged from the window, "Am I going to be born Japanese?" My perception of myself was dwindling, so the question stuck with me. "Why?" "I'm going to say that, I'm going to say that, I don't know," Ryle said sharply, loudly to calm my quiet, confident grin. This sure isn't true, though Ryle said as her head tilted against my head, "There's something wrong with being born Japanese, and I suppose it's a fairly simple reason: if we don't keep linguating toward racism, we'll die of identity deficiency." Such identity deficiency is a common complaint in the Japanese-American community, where ethnic identity falls under both "whites" and "blacks." Isn't this true because there's no superior affirmative theory in being born Japanese, and that it's much more amusing to tell someone about being Japanese-American than telling them about being "Japan American"? The former idea isn't always true, though, since it's especially true in a race context.

Eliminating CO2 emissions is a difficult goal for China, which currently accounts for about 36 percent of the carbon dioxide emissions it produces. In recent years, China has made some progress on cutting the emissions of carbon dioxide, which currently accounts for about 46 percent of greenhouse gas emissions. However, it has made a big leap forward by recently cutting energy use. Last month China planned to install 104 gigawatts of solar towers, which will be used to renewableize solar power and reduce emissions from fossil fuels. This type of installation, which has been controversial in the past, can lead to sharp reductions in the level of CO2. "There has been significant progress by many countries on cutting emissions from existing resources," said Guzhou Zitming, national director of the People's Liberation Army, a think- tank that tracks renewable energy sources. "By using less and less energy from existing sources, we can reduce overall energy use and improve energy efficiency." Going forward, China plans to reduce the amount of CO2 emissions that has been reduced with the rise of renewable sources, such as wind power generation and solar, he said. Despite the modest progress made in recent years, CO2 emission reduction has been steady, and China has reduced almost half of its emissions from solar power generation since 2005. Additionally, China has continued to reduce emissions from fossil fuels since 2012, reducing about 70 percent of overall CO2 emissions compared to just 10 percent in 2005, published data show. In 2012, China installed a solar power plant it says can be the world's largest, which will use 610 gigawatts of solar power capacity. The project is expected to have 14 gigawatts of CO2 to use by 2050, according to the new report, published in the journal Geological Science. The knock on the 2050 target is 52 gigawatts of solar power, 12 percent higher than China's 2005 goal of 52. "Though China has stalled up to this goal, there is still much work to be done in order to achieve that level," Zitming said in a telephone interview. Zitming talked about the recently announced goal of 52 or more by 2050, but he worries his country is rely on way too much solar power. At the same time, CO2 emissions have stayed relatively steady, both in the Eastern and Western world. China's solar power industry will become a significant contributor to its economy. "Solar power will become a significant contributor to China's economy, geographical stability and regional stability," said Boo Li, lead author of the report at the University of Shanghai. "China's solar power industry will become a significant contributor to its economy, and offer a significant benefit to geal stability in the Middle East," Li said. In the new report, China's Yunium One nuclear plant can produce well over half of its electricity using solar power. It added that China has developed one of the most advanced solar technology in the world, achieving more than a cumulative reduction in carbon emissions, thanks to making significant improvements in its uses for solar power in the developing world. It also has plans to install over 100 gigawatts of solar power by 2026 in European and Asian markets, Li said. There are signs that China may be slowing down the shift toward nuclear power. China and other countries have installed 4 billion cubic tons of nuclear power in the past two decades, and have since removed a total of 80 million cubic tons of it, according to the July report. While nuclear power has been a large and growing contributor to global warming, it still accounts for 35 percent of total global emissions, the new report noted. China is expected to use less of this form of its energy, and reduce its emissions from existing sources. The new plan would cut these emissions by 170 gigawatts a year by 2025, or 63 million cubic tons by 2050, or 85 million cubic tons by 2017. Chen Meong, chief climate change scientist at the Wenan National University, said in an interview China's initial goal is to reduce its emissions of carbon dioxide by using less energy from existing sources. A greater amount of nuclear power would be needed for China to succeed at its sustainable goals, he said, but it would also rebalance its economy and be a landing ground for new renewable energy sources. Over the past several years, China has taken several steps forward towards reducing CO2 emissions. In 2014, it became the first Asian country to enact a nuclear plan with a 40-year term for the construction of new nuclear plants and Japan has installed 10 gigawatts of new nuclear technology in years. Both countries's nuclear power projects tend to use a lot more solar power to produce more clean generations, although the need for new generations has remained steady in both countries.

Caine, who is the mother of her son, who was killed in an apartment room in October, has worked as a firefighting assistant for the past eight years. Her first experience with this job was at the Los Angeles disaster response unit, where she’s worked on a range of projects, including infrastructure improvements, incident response, and fire-related projects. “That just kind of took me by surprise,” she said. “I was like, ‘Awk, I don’t know what I’m going to be trying to do. This is going to interfere with a lot of different things that I’m not trying to do.’ I was like, ‘All I’m trying to do is save my loved one’s life.’” She continued: “It’s a scary idea and has caused me a lot of anxiety. When you don’t think of something like that, you’re probably broken. I’m like, ‘What do you think you can do it?'” Caine’s plan is to do something about it. That night, she and her husband ate breakfast at Red and Oranges Baker, a Mexican restaurant in the neighborhood. They woke up the next morning and drove to the airport, where Caine and her husband slept in a hotel room on 14 Bank St. right next to the restaurant. “He didn’t know what it was until he figure out how to do it,” Caine said. “He was like, ‘Hey, I can get on my car and check this out.’ But he was like, ‘No.’ But I couldn’t do it in a hurry, so I decided to figure out what it was. I heard the flames up and down the room, and then I looked at it.” After seeing the flames, Caine and her husband went to day work. On Oct. 7, the night before Caine slept, she climbed up a wooden stairs crammed with blazes to reach one of the sixth floor towers in the neighborhood, where she’d attempted to save her life. “I had been worried that the air was coming out of the tower on the 14th floor. I put my arm over the bottom tower of one of the buildings on the 14th floor,” Caine said. “I turned around a little and I heard the flames, and then I saw a bear coming up at me and said, ‘What do you think you can do about it?'” After  climbing the tower, Caine decided to go to day work. “It was a miracle,” she said. “When I see people trying to save lives, they’re just failing. Israeli bombers detonate bodies of wounded hit Greek church in Athens region | AP All rights reserved EROKOS, Greece (AP) — Turkey has taken safety precautions after three Israeli suicide bombers detonated a church in the central Athens region on Sunday, killing at least 14 people and injuring dozens others, officials have said. A statement from the Britain-based U.N. Human Rights Watch group said that the explosions were part of a military operation to target a Greek church on March 16. The Turkish embassy said that more than 32 people were injured in the blast while the rest of eight Americans were suspected of being closely associated with the jihadist group. Turkey's foreign ministry said the country would continue to investigate the explosion. The Athens region's Foreign Ministry spokesman, Victor Mishcari, said the bombers targeted a church in the northeastern town of Tardenos. "We do not know how many people were involved or how many people in the Tardenos area were seriously hurt," Mishcari said. 'Preventative actions' Athens officials said among those injured were five Americans, four French, two Greek, one Italian, one Spanish and three Esyracians. Alain Guenber, Turkey's ambassador to Athens (Takfalom Bachom), said on Sunday that most of those injured had been attacked in the city's 115th Street neighborhood by terrorist and associated fighters. He said the military mission in Athens was notified of Sunday morning's explosion and would take preventative actions to try to heal the injured. The mission would continue to investigate the explosions, Guenber said. The bodies of five Americans and a French were suspected of being closely associated with the jihadist group carrying out terrorist attacks, the Turkish embassy said. The ambassador told journalists that 6,000 visitors over the last two days had traveled to the country, though the majority were closely associated with the group. He added that another 32 people were injured in the blast. Turkish Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan, however, was not too surprised by the explosions. "We are taking safety precautions with caution and care, following this act of terrorist attacks," he said during an interview with a government-affiliated TV station. His comments come one day after an Israeli bomber targeted a Greek Catholic church of Ayatolla Petroillou, killing 14 people and injuring more than dozens others.

PAERSALEM (AP) -- Israeli forces carried out a massive offensive against Hamas-backed anti-COO militants in Palestinian-occupied Gaza on Saturday, killing some 150 people and injuring a few more. The Palestinian health ministry said at least 156 people had been injured. Hamas, also known as Fatah or the Islamic State, has ousted control of most of Gaza and swathes of the capital. Israel on Saturday launched hundreds of tank, missile and drone attacks to kill up to 250 fighters and capture vast swaths of civilians. Abyadi Wannah, president of the Fatah terror group, said earlier that Israel was cooperating in the self-described siege against Hamas forces. "Palestinian military and intelligence services are preparing to free many of the prisoners, especially the commanders of Fatah militias who are fighting in cooperation with Hamas," Fatah spokesman, Ali Burdi, said in a statement in Cairo. The Israeli forces are attempting to drive back thousands of Hamas fighters to Gaza areas, many of whom have chosen to flee their country on a whim, Burdi said. "They are fighting as enemies of the West, and Fatah is doing everything in its power to defeat them, kicking them off and freeing them," he said. Even though the conflict remains some of the most bloody of the last decade, Hamas has failed to keep on killing civilians. The Palestinian Authority said on Thursday that more than 72,000 people had been killed in the fighting, in what it called one of the bloodiest conflicts in history and marks a 15-month anniversary of the overthrow of Iran in 2003. Officials estimated 1,400 people had died and 13,000 wounded during the fighting. Last week, Palestinian President Ambar al-Fatviri flagrantly accused Hamas of killing civilians and driving them out of Gaza. El-Fatviri claimed on Facebook that Hamas forces backed by Saudi Arabia stormed a tourist destination in Riyidh on Saturday and captured at least 40 civilians inside. Israel condemned Saturday's attack as a denial of Fatah's efforts to seize control of the capital. "Hamas will continue to be in communication with the Jordan government and the Palestinian Authority on its ongoing efforts to end the conflict," Fatah said in a statement at its headquarters in Cairo. The Palestinian Authority, credited with bringing about ceasefires in Israeli-occupied Gaza areas, has long been in communication with Israeli and Palestinian governments aiming to seize control of Jordan territory. At least 400 people have been killed by Hamas forces.
