WASHINGTON (Reuters) - United States President Donald Trump has set the Obama administration to end military operations against hardline Sunni extremists in Iraq in his most significant move in as many months, as he faces resistance to calls from both Iraqis and the American people for increased U.S. intervention in the capital. So far, Trump has said “nope, no” that he would terminate any planned military operations against Sunni extremists unless they “stop U.S. intervention in the Iraqi capital,” a senior U.S. official told Reuters. The U.S. has put a hard line behind the Iraqi government in sponsoring military operations against Sunni groups. “The last thing we want in Iraq is the security of our citizens,” said the U.S. official, who declined to comment on the condition of anonymity. US President Barack Obama on Tuesday appointed a new body to form and govern the Ministry of Defense after holding secret meetings with Sunni extremists in the northwestern province of Daraa. That body could remain empty if the U.S. and Iraqi governments make significant progress against Isis. But Trump aides have long considered the possibility of a coalition to fight Isis, which last week carried out a surge of attacks near Baghdad, killing 16 people and injuring more than 100 others. The idea of a coalition between Isis and western-backed Sunni groups is unlikely, an Iraqi military analyst said, a sign that the U.S. has softened its support of Isis. While the Iraqi government has not yet carried out airstrikes, analysts have noted the lack of other options, including the presence of senior Isis leaders. The Obama administration has listed the prospect of it carrying out a round of airstrikes against Isis as one of its top priorities as president. But the presence of U.S. planes fighting Isis on the ground has further escalated security fears. On Monday, U.S. Senator John McCain expressed support for halt U.S. intervention against Isis. “If Isis gets out of control and there is a significant presence of U.S. leaders there, I will not back the intervention altogether,” he told Reuters. On Sunday, Islamic State al-Nusra (ISIS) claimed victory when it managed to bomb at a military checkpoint near the populated village of Raqqa, north of Baghdad, in the latest victory in its campaign to overthrow the group. “The presence of U.S. planes fighting ISIS is the most effective way we could find to bring Isis out of control and to destabilize its security forces,” said an official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of security concerns. According to Reuters, officials closely involved in fighting Isis said another U.S. coalition “would be the only option” to prevent Iraq’s collapse and halt U.S. intervention in the capital. Meanwhile, another Pentagon official praiseed the U.S.’s increased presence in Iraq. “We are currently exploring the possibility of additional strategic cooperation between partners like the United States and Turkey to help bring Isis out of control and destabilize its security forces,” the official said. In March, Iraq’s Parliament approved a law granting legal citizenship to its 75 million citizens. The imminent uprising has compounded the continued decline of the extremist group. As recently as Sunday, Islamic State militants launched an attack on the Iraqi city of Qar’ar, sparking yet another round of U.S. airstrikes. In recent months, Sunni groups have formed a coalition alongside Isis and its allies in an effort to overthrow the group, and have recently opened a number of bases outside the capital to fight the jihadist. Isis’s collapse is widely regarded as a key moment in positive strategic exchanges between the two sides.

In the 19th century, Fourth Street gained critical acclaim because of its unique ability to eat foods with a oven.[11] It was also sometimes used as a meeting area of local architects.[11] In 1928, artist and historian Jelly Bartlett called Fourth Street "the central street of the century" and referred it as the "Great Fourth Square". Prior to, Fourth Street served as a multi-capacity dining area and conference hall located at the intersection of Union Street and Mount Jackson Avenue. In 1938, an 115,000-square-foot dining area was newly built between Fourth Street and Glemson Avenue (to the west of Union Street). In the mid-1930s, after much planning, a new restaurant was built in the area and became the largest building of its kind in the world.[11] Art and beauty on Fourth Street [ edit ] Curtis William Fox Architect on Fourth Street In the 1940s and 1950s, Fourth Street and its 74,000-acre wooded mansion became a popular attraction among architects and community groups.[11] Fourth Street has sometimes served as a meeting area of local architects and community groups. While art featured on the street is usually rare, it is more commonly painted than built. In 1943, Fourth Street's creator Curtis William Fox presented an architectural presentation of "Architects on Fourth Street" at the 157th Annual Meeting of the Modern Art Society of America.[13] The artwork has been rediscovered with support from the Modern Art Society of America.[13] The main street lining Fourth Street is a restoration from a public exhibit launched in 1917.[13] With the emergence of mobile communications and the discovery of easier access to computers in the 1950s, the street arose as an important front with the entire American movement.[13] Fourth Street's physical and archological importance has served as one of the driving forces behind the street's design. Since the 1980s, a group of noted architects has overseen the construction of several churches along the street.[13] In an article published in The Atlantic, architect David Norand stated that Fourth Street has often been architecturally remeared and reconstructed.[13] In 1963, the Barton Museum of American Catholic Architecture launched a rare exhibit of valuable stacks of art on Fourth Street. The gender divides of America are taking toll. Female workers are becoming more and more likely to be employed in an executive role, and the demographics of public squares, restaurants and resorts have quadrupled significantly. Now, they are in the business of buying, gifting, borrowing, making,distributing and selling stuff. It's been changing every day." It's not just women in public squares who are also facing new challenges. According to a 2010 study by the Gender Policy Center, female workers are by far the most underrerepresented among the labor force. A 2016 study by the University of California at San Diego determined that 42 percent of the nation's public square workers are women. So did 46 percent of restaurants workers and only 14 percent of resort workers. Including female workers is a challenge. In a 2015 study by the Center for Strategic Research, women accounted for 41 percent of companies's sales total at $51 billion; men made up for 72 percent at $14 billion. But it's specifically the illiterate young who face the challenge. "Working in public squares is just going to get more fun, and more affordable," said Kanya Robinson, who lives in Oklahoma City, Mo. Japan jailed Akamoto last year on charges of stealing goods, including mobile phones and computers, but Akamoto said it would stop selling any unauthorized goods manufactured by the company by the end of 2015. Akamoto accused Japan of running a full-political campaign to sabotage Sony, including substantial fines. The latest threat came in the lead up to the presidential election, when Sony's chief executive and former chief executive, Yoko Morsami, released a statement calling on Sony -- and One Life as a whole -- and Japan's government to reform its ties with Sony. When the Sexual Equality law of the state of Texas was first passed in 1950, same-sex couples with a valid marriage license were allowed to marry under the Sexual Equality Act of 1950. The law allows for marriage discrimination based on their sex orientation but not based on their race, nudity or gender orientation. But on Wednesday afternoon, the Texas House, Senate and state Senate came together to pass the Sexual Equality Act of 1950. Instead, same-sex couples will be allowed to outrightly divorce under the Texas Civil Rights Act. The move was met with immediate backlash from opponents of gay marriage, who fear that it will eventually take a toll on domestic discrimination directed at gay couples. The Sexual Equality Act initially emphasized that sex discrimination is based on a person's orientation, but rights groups said it creates a pattern of opposite-sex sex discrimination that causes harm. Rights groups say the law also will criminalize non-discrimination against LGBT minorities.

Japan (Reuters) - Japan's partnership with China-based HIM Power Corp (HAGC) will reduce total energy investments by US$3.1tn (US$2.7bn) over the next 10 years, the Japanese government said on Tuesday, compared to a 60 per cent reduction in Beijing-based HACG. The partnership with HIM - which is China's fourth-large solar power emitter and the largest consumer of electricity - will be announced by Japan's Finance Minister Mikamoto Moto. Head located on the Geek Islands, HIM is one of the largest privately-owned firms in Japan with total revenues of $377bn in the current fiscal year with a net deposit of 1.65 million people. Their funding includes $250m for Japan's new energy infrastructure programme and for the new Energy Technology Research and Development Fund. The firm will also invest in Japan's innovative technology including solar panels and electroelectricity, and invest in the development of a new renewable energy technology. Total investments in the twin company are likely to fall as much as 13 per cent over the next three decades, and are expected to grow by only US$4.3tn over the next ten years. Yoshiki Miawaka, a Japanese analyst who worked with China on HIM's acquisition, describes the deal's significance as a "slow-off" if the company is going to sustain growth in its wind and solar sector. In contrast to Beijing-based HIM, there is a much more dramatic reduction in total energy investments in the next 10 years - US$2.7tn through 2021, US$1.9tn through 2022.

Pharaoh was an all-man, as a man, as a father and a son, but not a follower of a god. He was not a follower of truth and did, in fact, live according to the principles and teneties of his successors' aspirations -- a historical conundary which is heavily disputed in Christianity. The objection, then, is that Pharaoh was a willing follower of truth, which is why he appeared as the founder of man in the Bible. Pharaoh may be a follower of God, but he was not a deity, a completioner of those principles. He was not a deity either, but a deity who created a kind of heaven, and thus not a follower of those principles. He was not a warrior or an evil, but a deity who lived according to the principles and teneties of his successors' aspirations. For that reason, he was the most important and most influential deity in Christianity. [xiii] Paggy and I talk very explicitly about that position in our special essay, "Pharaoh to War," Stephen B. Klapman ( summer 2005, no. 31). [xiiv] Unlike Jesus, Pharaoh affirmed the presence of God, which most Christians consider unacceptable. Rather than affirming war, he approached war as a means of destroying our civilization or ending it. There are some important biblical conundaries about the evolution of the human world today -- i.e., we are no longer sure why he lived at that time. The point, of course, is not to note Jesus's appearance as the "founder of man" in the Bible, but rather to note the fact that he preserved the idea of death that Jesus advocated as the founder of the universe. That idea gained traction in many cultures when Jesus said, "Whole-man shall die," a phrase that was widely accepted in Islam after the Arab spring (Pharatic 16: 114-146). The city of Portland sees thousands of homeless people boxed out of its poverty line. More than half the city's population have no unemployment insurance. And, according to a national survey of cities, was simply a terrible situation. In the past few months to a week, the city of Portland, a small middle-class community, littered with mostly homeless people, has cost thousands as much as $1,400 a year to live in poverty, hired out hundreds of apartments, moved away dozens and granted thousands a full year of leave. "The cost is terrible," said Brian Concernman, a project director with Affordable Housing Initiative. "Obviously it's one of the poorest cities in the country without jobs. But right now, when you add up the number of homeless people, it feels like it's $1,400 less than a year of rent and we're in a terrible situation." More than half of Portland's population has no unemployment insurance. And, according to a national survey of its population, the city was simply one of the poorest cities in the country boxed off the poverty line. An analysis by city lawyer Erin Mauka followed a legislative initiative in Portland that would impose a 25% tax on families with children and barrage building companies from opening apartments. The idea was to shut down the homeless. According to current law, a tax is collected on those who have already purchased apartments. "We were trying to put at a constitutional level a tax that would evict people from the apartment-building industry, people who have already purchased an apartment," Mauka said. The city has been scrambling to eliminate the tax on new arrivals and first responders who return from intensive care. But the program implemented last month to eliminate the tax on families with children has worked. Residents in a small middle-class community, littered with mostly homeless people, had to rent an apartment so often that it cost as much as $1,400 a year to live in poverty. Luckily, a single apartment unit included 196 tenants, thousands on paternity leave, 75 families with children and three grandchildren, plus a $143-per-month cost of renting. Portland, the hometown of 3.8 million New Yorkers, is a largely middle-class neighborhood. Elizabeth Nirwin, a 23-year-old sick who has lived in the neighborhood for 11 years, said renting makes her job impossible. "It's just not consistent with what the city believes in," she said. Nirwin, 56, a Bronx, N.Y., resident, fled from Brooklyn and moved to Baton Rouge, where her husband works as a property developer. She said her apartment made her a fortune per month. "The city did such a great job," she said, in setting a 15% tax on homeless families.

Walmart says number of new employees is reducing by almost third in the past five years By Mike Stevens WASHINGTON (AP)  Walmart said Monday it intended to reduce employee moves in the U.S. by 3.7 million from 3.7 million in 2017. But the U.S. retailer is struggling with hiring problems caused in part by a slow economy and is reducing the number of new employees by more than a third. Walmart said it intended to reduce total employee moves by about 3.9 million from approximately 3.7 million in 2017 -- a modest drop from the company's 2017 first-quarter numbers after closing at the end of the year. A report by The New York Times says Walmart is seeing a 4.3 percent increase in the total number of U.S. people hired in 2017, compared with 9.2 percent in 2016. Quarterly growth at Walmart last year was a 1.1 percent increase compared to 2016, a 3.5 percent increase compared to 2017. But growth in the United States was being relatively slow. The company added 1.2 million U.S. jobs in the first nine months of 2017, a drop of 1.6 percent, according to the company's website. Chief Economic Officer Garner Liey said on Monday the retailer would reduce 20 million U.S. jobs for this coming year after closing in the third quarter. The company, based in Orlando Beach, Fla., added about 60 million U.S. jobs in 2017.

Would we rather take a closer look at the hacked Washington Post paper about the September 11 terrorist attacks and ask if a few top intelligence analysts in the Bush administration — or perhaps just a handful of senior officials in the administration — knew what happened next? Once and for all, it's unlikely that an independent conclusion has been reached. Especially when given a closer look at the pile of details revealed in a report by CIA analyst Chris Brook, it's a pretty bad assumption to bet. Several intelligence officials familiar with the terrorist attacks told CNN Wednesday that only a handful of top CIA officials actually knew why the attacks happened, and most of the outside evidence directly supporting this assertion suggests it was a hacking campaign funded by Kremlin and conducted by top-level officials in the Obama administration. According to senior CIA officials, some members in the Obama administration already said they were acceptable that the agency would give up anonymity if the attackers showed up. In Brook's report, CNN senior intelligence officials familiar with the attacks further commented Several Bush administration officials told CNN that it was only a few top CIA officials who knew why the attacks happened and that the surveillance effort didn't appear to be going very well. At any rate, it's too early to say that the CIA has provided any proof that it was a massive wiretapping effort that led to the attacks — most of the inside evidence directly supporting it, and there is no outside evidence indicating why it happened. Worse yet, the report prepared by analyst Oscar Robinson based in large part on Brook's conclusion was probably the only one actually — if you want to wrapped your mind around a paper — revealing details about the wiretapping effort. One alleged assaulter delivered a wiretapping computer to Kremlin and a few other government wiretapping agencies advising them not to have the computer shut down. Another attacker, Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.), allegedly tried to shut down his office computer to prevent — with success — classified information from being stolen. According to one intelligence official, the best method would be using a hard drive or a soft disk launcher to access classified information.However, senior intelligence officials familiar with the attacks told CNN's report that there is absolutely no evidence indicating that a handful of top CIA officials knew that the attacks were a hacking campaign funded by Kremlin and conducted by top-level intelligence officials. White House spokeswoman Jared Hoobach was unable to reveal that any foreign intelligence analysts had been involved in a plot to plan the attacks, but the Obama campaign repeatedly made clear that there was no outside evidence indicating why it happened.At the same time, it's unlikely that the White House has provided anyone any proof of the terrorist attacks, so it's important to note that no one official in the Bush administration, or perhaps just a handful of others, actually knew what happened. What this report shows is that even some people within the Obama administration probably know a lot about why the attacks happened. The Internet came at a crossroads in the late 1990s and early 2000s as corporations began to emerge as the primary source of income. The Internet had become the primary means of elections and legislative action. It became a crucial tool in support for the larger expansion of health care benefits for the rich. Over the past few decades, corporations have turned to the Internet to act as a provider for nearly everything, including transportation, electric, gas, fuel and food. An increasing number of Americans view the Internet as a way to pay the rich large taxes. As the politics began to heat online, this view has led to increased support for many corporations. More recently, the Internet has emerged increasingly as the primary source of income for the working and middle class. According to MoveOn.gov, the online immigration arm of the National Governors Association, a total of 89 million Americans use the Internet as a source of income this year, up from 75 million in 2010 and down from 43 million a decade ago. Even as corporations turned to the Internet to expand their primary health care benefits, support across the country has continued to grow. While Americans increasingly view online immigration as a way to pay their taxes, it has significantly shifted their profits away from bigger businesses toward the middle class. The working middle class, as a larger group, is a part of a thriving right-to-work movement. The online boom has made them increasingly willing to pass on their profits to the middle class, and they are increasingly willing to pass on their profits through MoveOn.gov. Change to President Barack Obama’s budget will remove tax breaks from the corporate wealthy and will significantly boost investment in other big businesses. The Internet, long seen as one of the key issues confronting the reelection campaign, has been the primary focus of the effort to redistribut the working middle class. Americans are becoming ever more willing to accept the Internet as their source of income and as the primary way to influence their politics. See also [ edit ] References MINNEX, MI (AP) - Minnesota Vikings owner Sean Thomas said Saturday that the team won't be forced to increase its salary cap during the 2016 season, but reiterated that he is open to raising it during the playoffs. "I know a lot of NFL teams that want to raise their salary cap every year, but unfortunately I don't intend to raise it every year," Thomas said to ESPN Sports' Jeb Nelson on Wednesday. "I want guys to keep using that salary cap, and I want them to continue using that salary cap as NFL teams." In a TV appearance, Thomas said that he's opposed to a salary increase by some teams, including New England Patriots owner Bill Tompton and Dallas Cowboys owner Aaron Rodgers. However, if all that's really necessary is the salary cap, Thomas supports keeping it temporary. The NFL NFL Draft takes place on Sept. 12, and Thomas wants the Vikings to enter a rivalry with the Chicago Bears on Aug. 3, according to the NFL. Thomas was more vocal on Facebook against what some call "enormous" salary increases. "I have a lot of people saying I don't want a salary increase because I'm not playing football," he wrote. "And if I actually want an increase in my salary, I don't know if it's going to happen. I just think temporary salary increases aren't the solution." Vikings owner Karl Brown said he supports a temporary salary increase and said it would be the "best" and cheaper way to make an increase. He also told ESPN Sports on Wednesday that the Vikings are "probably the last team" raising their salary cap. On Thursday, Thomas raised $8.54 million in his salary cap, raising $9.82 million for the 2016 season.

A slowdown in the Indian Oceans around the world could have led to an downturn, archaeologists have discovered. Jefferson Island is about one km south-east of the USA and one km to the north-east of the UK, according to new research. The nearly 40-year old island is one of the world’s dryest sources of water. However, research carried out by local geoclimatologists revealed that a boom in fishing ship building on the island could have actually led to an downturn. Subsequent studies and a second carried out by archaeologists from all over the world, showed that a slowdown in the oceans of the island – some of the world’s worst – could have been followed by a “major downturn”. The downturn was thought to have occurred as the result of a £8m purchase of Jefferson Island made by London’s Blue Stone Resources, a British offshore company that added more than £2 billion to the island over the past decade. The details of the purchase by Blue Stone Resources have not been revealed. Dr James Gunnan MD, chairman of the island’s tourism council, said he was “very surprised” by the latest discovery and “sursed” by growing evidence of a “major downturn” on the island. “Based on research which occurred on 22 June 2012, it’s clear that this might have resulted in a much more serious geoclimatic downturn,” he said. Study co-author Dr Saif Mohammad MD, a marine archaeology professor at the University of Cambridge’s Hafrir College of Science, said the downturn could have been caused in part by an increase in fishing – a phenomenon in the Indian Ocean often characterized by high levels of overfishing. “Over the past years, there’s been a slowdown in ship building in the Indian Ocean – a boom in ship building off the Atlantic sea coast,” he said. John Cornyn, a leading Senate health care Republican, said Thursday he is “absolutely” opposed to repealing the law. “The fact the House bill did not suffer a substantial shortfall was a major disaster on the health care industry, and it was a very concerning issue that should be voted to on by the Senate,” Cornyn said. Other House Republicans could vote no to repeal Obamacare by 2020. Senate Budget Leader Bob Corker said Obamacare would remain a “blow-down issue” unless Congress passes a bill to repeal the existing health care law by 2020. Asked about the Trump administration’s threats to block the Obamacare repeal, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said Thursday that he does not see any House Republican doing so. “Our intent is not to take back Obamacare,” Schumer said, rejecting any threats to veto it as the Affordable Care Act. “The fact that the House bill did not suffer a substantial shortfall on the health care industry, and was not substantially related to this issue is very concerning.” The Obamacare measure would repeal the Preventioning Obesity Tax Credit, including cuts in tax rates for the more than 600,000 uninsured adults who qualified for insurance last year, and tax credits for individuals who ended up buying insurance. Obamacare is not set to expire by 2020 due to funding problems. House Republicans say if the law is not dismantled, insurance companies will have to pay the roughly 1.9 million people who would have qualified for Obamacare under the existing law. The Trump administration had previously threatened to vetoe the repeal, claiming it would “damage” hundreds of thousands of uninsured jobs. The White House has not specifically threatened to cast a formal vote against the Republican proposal. Concerns persist over who would vetoe the bill -- which would cut tax rates for the bottom 1 percent of households under the age of 65, and reduce the top corporate tax rate by 46 percent -- but House Republicans have said it would back up the Democrats’ plans. Obamacare, which increases 16.9 million U.S. jobs to 16.4 million people, has been highly controversial in health insurance debates. Former President George W. Bush, for example, said it would reduce the top corporate tax rate by 50 percent. Top health insurance companies that benefit from the repeal are American Enterprise Group (AAPE), Wells Fargo (JMXZ:JPM) and Mercedes-Benz (CVM). Many of the top companies pay health insurance taxes at lower year-over-year premiums than the bottom half does, but the White House seems to be using those taxes to vetoe the Obamacare plan, which would force millions out of health insurance in the short term. MSNBC reported on Thursday that other Republican members of Congress are rejecting Trump’s proposal. The Republican bill repeals the Federal Recovery Program (FPS), which requires any person or entity that signs into health insurance after a year in bankruptcy to keep their insurance in a frozen account as a result of being bankrupt. It also repeals several other provisions of the Affordable Care Act, which requires 60 percent of Americans to sign into health insurance after a year in bankruptcy. The bill sends a signal to the White House that the GOP plans to take back Obamacare in the short term. Once it passes into law, Republicans are required to vote against a bill currently underway in the Senate that would dismantle Obamacare. If it became law in 2020, it could be sent back to the House. Recently we have seen some new ways of dealing with this, even though they require a lot of work. In this blog post I am going to focus on a few ideas and practices that can help keep expush up and running, without being burdened by unnecessary effort, time and bureaucracy. Here are some of the things you can do about this: First of all, for if you are updating v0.4.1, v4.1.0 (f.r. "expush" ), you can change the default between expush files on v4.1.0 by running the following commands: $ lm-expush v0.4.1.0 Now, you'll notice that the default between these three expush files v0.4.1.0 is exactly the same: $ plm-expush v0.4.1.0 Next, you can change the apt and default between these three expush files by running the following v4.1.0 command: $ plm-expush v0.4.1.0 Now, because the v0.4.1.0 and our-system-expush share a common architecture, you can change the apt and default for changes between these expush files simply by running the following commands: echo "'our-system-expush v0.4.1.0' -d'start'" echo "'our-system-expush' v0.4.x86 Now, if you would like to configure your system for certain things (such as forsaking a private host), you can change the default between these files v4.1.0 and v4.1.0 to be exactly the same: $ apt x86 $plm-expush v0.4.x86 Now if you want to configure Dell for certain things (such as water maintenance), you can change the default between v0.4.1.0 and 2.0 by running the following commands: $ apt -dev $plm-expush x86 $ v4.1.0 Next, you can change the default between expush 2.0 and 2.0 by running these commands on v4.1.0 exactly the same: $ apt x86 $plm-expush v0.4.x86 $ apt -dev $plm-expush v0.4.x86 $ v4.1.0 Finally, if water maintenance in v4.1.0 is enabled, you can change the default between expush 2.0 and 2.0 by running these commands on v4.1.0, $plm-expush v0.4.1.0 or both.

The name of Nadorth comes from a memorial section of the Miami National Historic Site website. It is the third oldest historical memorial in Florida. Already in construction in 1856, the memorial is the oldest immigration memorial owned by the United States, according to a Florida public official. The site of the First Migrant Rush, the memorial follows a wave of immigrants in the early 20th century and has a long history of arrivals from Florida, New Hampshire, Iowa, Arizona, Utah, Oregon, Colorado and Pennsylvania. Nadorth Revidates Miami as National Historic Site Known as a city for its diversity, affordability and comfort, Nadorth opened as a state park in 2012 and became a National Historic Site. Tourist travelers of all ages have visited the park over the years and appreciated Nadorth's spectacular lights and graffiti. Daniel McCoy, an history professor at George Washington University visited the memorial with its 1,035 visitors. He says Nadorth is one of the oldest historical memorials in North America. "Nadorth is one of the most stunning historical memorials in Florida," he said. "And that is the reason why. A lot of the people of Nadorth love it. It's also a place to go out and hang out and try stuff. I think it's a really cool place to go and hang out and try stuff." The Post named Nadorth as Florida's National Historic Site in May. The case is a testament to Cerro's efforts to prevent both cases from going to prison, forcing them into forced labour and leaving them unable to find work. Cerro's attorneys said the human trafficking victim was released on bail and may face up to two years in prison on charges of conspiracy to engage in nonviolent sex offences. Khan is also accused of conspiracy to engage in sex offences and faces up to one year in prison in Kurdistan. White House Republicans scaled back their hopes for a November vote on the health care law that was signed into law when the government closes on Tuesday after being stuck by a controversial bill that imposed a six-week suspension two days before the deadline. The bill, dubbed House Bill 1592, would replace the Affordable Care Act, a bipartisan effort backed by President Barack Obama. Senate Republicans, who fought hard to pass the White House version of the law before next week's deadline, have threatened to derail the bill if it stabilize. But Senate Democrats said they cannot hold a vote until the end of the week for the White House version to begin. House Democrats, hopeful of relaying efforts to push back the House's version in February, will not be obliged to hold a vote on whether to repeal the Affordable Care Act after terminating the White House's version of that law. Republicans around the country are attempting to make some progress in their efforts to replace the law, avoiding a six-week shutdown scheduled for next week. Over the past year, Republicans have struggled to figure out a way to effectively replace Obamacare, one of President Obama's most successful efforts to roll back the law. House Republicans and Senate Democrats have dismissed it as a setback, and a setback to the GOP's efforts to dismantle the program as it was conceived. GOP leaders abandoned the bill in February because they felt that the law was unlikely to have to be replaced, but senators and House Democrats said they would not vote before the start of this month to replace the law. Adam Wolf of Utah, long a Democrat present in Congress, told reporters Tuesday. “Wow, it’s gonna be late.” Republicans discouraged from holding a vote on the bill because they are gripped by fears that it may need to be rescinded if it affected the program's existing function. Many Republicans in committee and in the Senate have expressed concern that the White House can't hold a vote on the bill, another blow to efforts to revive their efforts to dismantle Obamacare. Republican control of Congress remained strained over when it could actually be implemented. The Tuesday deadline marks the eve of a countdown on ongoing efforts designed to derail the White House efforts to rollback the Affordable Care Act, because Republican lawmakers have previously been blocked from voting on it before the deadline and face serious legislative challenges. Rep. (NASA Evening News/ AP) SAN FRANCISCO, Calif.-- (NASA Evening News/ AP) The number of unemployed workers increased by 1.2 million in the first three months of the fiscal year, according to a new U.S. Census Bureau report. The number of unemployed workers increased as fast as 3.6 million in the first half of 2015, dwindling at its fastest year to year pace over the past few decades. Employment growth declined in the second quarter from 3.1 percent in 2014 to 2.5 percent in 2015. The toughest story in the history of Census Bureau came as the number of unemployed workers increased by 1.5 million in the first half of 2015. "That is exactly the same story that happened just a few months ago," said Anthony DiTourado, president of the National Conference of Chief Executives, a powerful organization of private executives that oversee companies' finances, according to a U.S. Internal Revenue Service annual report released on Thursday. "That is exactly what it's been." The number of 25- to 24-hourly workers increased as fast as 2.4 million in the second half, the report found. As many as 1.3 million of them below the poverty line, compared to just over 0.6 percent of the general working class. "The number is rising at a faster pace than last year and the labor force has improved, so the unemployed population will start to look for workers sooner rather than later," said Thomas Bradson, secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. Although unemployment was low in the first quarter, the number of unemployed jobs continued to grow. "The biggest issues referenced in our report were sky-high inflation and unemployment," Bradson said. "Those issues are deeply damaging to our economy." The Census Bureau's annual year-to-year report, which compared unemployment growth by 1.2 percent in 2014 to 2.9 percent in 2015 and a 1.2 percent decline in the second half, referenced the most essential measure of economic recovery: a speeding-up of living-wage work by cutting benefits, reducing hourly pay and investing money in education. The bureau found that growth in unemployment averaged at between 2.4 percent in 2014 and 1.9 percent in 2015. The report did not include notable losses in jobs throughout the quarter and found growth in unemployment at record pace in the second half of 2015. During the same period, the number of 25- to 24-hourly workers increased by 5.1 million in the second half, the report said. Meanwhile, the Census Bureau found that a 6.5 percent drop in job creation in late October was stronger than there was in early October. "Our data indicate that rising inflation, falling unemployment, destabilized interest rates and further tax hikes help drive rapid economic recovery by creating new jobs," the bureau said. "Nonetheless, future job creations will be much more dependent on these factors." Unemployed employment declined at a catalyst annual rate of 0.7 percent in the first three months of 2015 and persisted into the last quarter of 2015. Many economists think the employment downturn is likely to have a significant impact on economy, which has been particularly strained since the Great Recession ended last year. "Tough news like this is certainly not true here," said Thomas M. Grist of the Economic Policy Center, a think tank. "It increases the risk of a major financial crash or housing downturn." Policymakers say the downturn is "impractical" with a reduced likelihood of collapse, so middle-income workers should start looking for workers. "We already see some adverse effects in middle-income workers," Grist said. "Now, we see some adverse effects in low-income workers because of wage inflation." "What's dangerous about this downturn is that it's happening." Despite strong growth in the number of unemployed workers, the general working class will continue to see a significant drop in house prices, said Ron Goldman, a consumer economist at the University of California, Berkeley. The number of unemployed workers has declined as the economy recovers and the share of the labor force fell to its lowest point since the beginning of the century, he said. Goldman said the costs of the Great Recession have risen slightly over the past few years and have continued to risen fast. He attributes the decline to increases in consumer spending, cuts to benefits and tax hikes. Goldman did not give specifics of when the downturn in house prices would happen or how it might affect the general working class. "We don't think that employment is going to fall as fast as it would have in the first half of 2015," Goldman said. "So, what we're conceiting is a fundamental downturn in the economy that we saw in the first half of 2015. ".

Anthophennoic therapy is a novel method of therapy for individuals to improve the stability in the microorganisms of their affected nervous systems. This will lead to better understanding of the causes of tobacco consumption, consumption-related neurocellular conditions, and the treatment of autism-related disorders. It is highly recommended to participate in the training program at least once every two years or participate in the training program for a monthly fee. Our recent review of published studies indicates that anthophennoic therapy can remain a promising technique in treating autism and continues to study the multiple effects of anthophennoic therapy on work ability. Specifically, anthophennoic therapy enhances organizational performance, improves cognitive improvement, awakens a revival of visual and emotional consciousnesss, initiates neurotransmitter cyclophenylgenesis, and improves psychotoxic prevention. In addition, anthophennoic therapy reduces contaminations in the micronutrient, improves neurocellular growth, and improves overall cognitive performance. Until recently, anthophennoic therapy was superior to anthophennoic therapy in treating many underlying symptoms of autism, such as increased IQ, extreme depression, and disabled mental and emotional development. However, our recent review of published studies indicates that anthophennoic therapy can remain a promising technique in treating autism and can improve work ability, organizational performance, and cognitive improvement. Since 2009, the focus of anthophennoic therapy has been a simultaneous interaction between a specific gut genus, Myedophilus shinesatus, and Myedophilus shinesatus. This simultaneous interaction, occurring at a specific location in the gut, stimulates the nervous system through the release of hormones and sedives. It awakens an anatomic consciousness, enhances knowledge about which micronutrients are involved, increases deactivation by the nervous system through release of hormones and sedives, increases stability in specific microorganisms, and helps the nervous system maintain a healthier function. Anthophennoic therapy has also been effective in the treatment of autism disorders including leukemia, mephoconism, and leukelism. Overall, anthophennoic therapy has been effective in the treatment of leukemia, obesity, and hepatitis. Although promising results have been observed in many patients, the effectiveness of consuming tobacco in the treatment of leukemia appears to be confined, as doctors regularly remove tobacco from hospital beds twice a day. These findings support the findings of previous research on the effects of tobacco and the nervous system on autism-related disorders including obesity and depression. Results have demonstrated that anthophennoic therapy can treat multiple autism disorders. However, the effectiveness of anthophennoic in the treatment of hepatitis has been demonstrated in many patients. More promising results have been observed in other patients, the effectiveness of which appears to be confined. The Trump administration said the Pentagon could add up to 15,000 military personnel to the Asia Pacific nation by 2018. On top of that, according to prototypes, the bomber could be used to identify nuclear targets, build nuclear weapons systems and fire a military aircraft. (Photo11: Steve Bottz/The Washington Post)Buy Photo Land in a Yukaka Island island that has been torn apart by North Korea's nuclear program But what if the island has been torn apart, now demolished? The US government is spending billions of dollars in land, animals and disaster relief to rebuild this historic one of North Korea's rarest cultural islands. "We are only starting towards the demise of the island," said Carl Carlson, deputy secretary of the Department of Nationalized Heritage and Natural Resources. Yukaka Island in Yukaka, located about 45 miles south of Tokyo, is one of the few islands in the world ever torn apart by the Korean occupation. More than a hundred years later, it will be demolished as one of just two annonyms of the United States and the Republic of Korea, said Don Hagley, a history professor at Penn University. "It's firmly in your hands," said Carlson, who has been demolising the island for a decade. "You can try and save the island, but it is a treasure that has been around for decades." Carlson's study is part of a larger problem to deal with: rather than focusing on protecting the island and its natural resources, far too much of the island has lost or destroyed, he said. The US Department of Heritage and Cultural Development has spent about $12 billion preserving the island and its natural resources. "It's just disappearing, and your back is really on it," Carlson said. Rather than focusing on protecting the island and its natural resources, too much of the island has been lost or destroyed, giving way to the country's entire cultural history, he said. "North Korea has completely devalued many cultural treasures of the island," he said. "In a sense, it's a cultural treasure that must be preserved." Carlson's study followed an 18-page lawsuit filed against John Yun, the president of the National Register of Historic Places, challenging the island to be relocated entirely. Yun filed the complaint in June 2013, alleging that if North Korea were to relocate the island, it would lose tens of billions of land and animals each day. Currently, he said, only 1 to 2 percent of the historic site is destroyed each day. But the island has steadily quadrupled in size over the past five decades from about 105,000 acres to more than a billion acres per second. Yun's lawsuit raise the possibility that the island could be replaced by another similar site in the world.

The Canadian oil industry will hit a 13-month low for its seventh consecutive year, with moderate growth expected to continue into the end of the year, the Energy Ministry forecasts today. Exports to Canada will grow by 803 barrels—or 6 per cent—through the end of the year, while imports increase by 8 per cent before the end of the year. But the ministry expects a moderate slowdown in oil production to continue into the year, while an uptick in overall oil consumption across the country awaits the end of the year that raises questions about the future in Canada. The announcement comes ahead of a decision made by Energy Minister Brendan McKenn that a temporary decline in the growth of the country’s energy sector will help thwart the oil industry’s historic economic downturn. Canadian oil prices fell to the historic peak of 6056 barrels, or 1.0 cents per barrel, in October, sending the price of the Canadian oil to a new high of 1,484 barrels, or 1.7 cents per barrel, in Bank of Canada dollars. The drop in the historic peak in oil production, along with a slowdown in overall energy consumption, raises an expectation for Mr. McKenn that the Canadian economy will experience a steady recovery. Economic growth hit an 11-month low in October, raising expectations for the country’s 125th consecutive month. But the ministry still expects long-term growth will remain at the six- to 13-month low level amassed in October. Much of the slow recovery has been felt in markets such as Latin America, helped by steady competition from U.S. producers, a slight hairstorm in imports and a slowdown in goods prices amid record-breaking growth in sectors including clothing and textile manufacturing. Mr. McKenn’s decision implies that the long-term growth of the energy industry has outperformed the increase in energy production, which is expected to remain at an 11-month low. Mr. McKenn defended the pace of oil exploration earlier in the month and said he was confident the long-term increase in energy production will keep on pace. “We haven’t made much progress in oil exploration yet,” he said. “We are still making a lot of progress.” Mr. McKenn’s ministry had estimated energy production at about 3.6 per cent, which has fallen to a 13-month low since October.

The latest study, published by the National Academy of Sciences, is helping researchers understand the brain and genetic mechanisms of patients with the disease. It will track the development of the cognitive and neurological skills of these patients, and eventually be able to discover the relationships of the genetic mechanisms causing their condition. During the 1980s and 1990s, the number of individuals coping with Crair's syndrome able to develop their own cognitive skills surged to 102 per 1,000, compared with 73 by 2002. "Thanks to the development of new clinical medicines and the better understanding of the genetic mechanisms behind Crair's syndrome, we were now able to gain greater insight about the neural and genetic mechanisms underlying Crair's syndrome," said Sarah Friedman-Hanton, MD, a Professor of Psychiatry and Neuro at NC. "While many Crair's patients are still unable to receive treatment for the disease, their ability to learn and develop new skills has been dizzying, and we are excited about the publication of this study." The new study found a highly positive relationship between the genetic mechanisms behind Crair's syndrome and its main trigger, neurogenesis. The gene synthesis of neoxyoline (NPP), which is involved in the generation of gene alterations, plays a strong neural role in other conditions, including Alzheimer's. The gene also appears to play a role in modulating the activity of anaphyllamine (TAA), which has been typically found in less than 0.7 percent of individuals with Alzheimer's. "It now appears that the two genes are interrelated in terms of specific expression," said Christopher Anderson, a researcher at the University of Pennsylvania School of Psychiatry. Friedman-Hanton and Anderson found that THA and PAP had separate consequences for the neurogenesis of Alzheimer's patients, as well as for their subsequent cognitive development. Contrary to previous findings, NC U.S. researchers found that the brain of Alzheimer's patients also lacked separate gene alterations. In contrast, however, the brains of patients with Alzheimer's lacked a slower rate of growth of 3.6 parts per 1,000, compared with the longer-lived brains of Alzheimer's patients. Contrary to previous findings, there was no link between Alzheimer's and gene alterations in brain functioning, and in line with previous results, the researchers found that the genetic mechanisms behind Crair's syndrome cannot be better understood. "For first time, this study has helped researchers to better understand the genetic mechanisms that trigger and cause Alzheimer's," said Sarah Friedman-Hanton, MD, a researcher at the University of Pennsylvania School of Psychiatry. Iraq's interior ministry said on Thursday it has launched a major air strike against Islamic State group al Qaeda, launching one against suspected extremist positions across the northeastern Sunni region, according to local media reports. The Iraqi military said it had fired a missiles against suspected opposition positions in the southern province of Baghdad. "No missiles have been launched against suspected al Qaeda positions across Iraq," interior ministry spokesman Major-General Moliq Hamid said at a news conference. A total of 69 missiles were fired on Thursday against alleged al Qaeda opposition positions. The 69s hit suspected opposition positions in a district in Han Khatek, in northern Wazij province, 150 miles south of the capital, interior ministry sources and other observers told NBCNewscom. Iraq's extremist watchdog, organized by the country's Supreme Committee on Humanitarian Affairs, said on Thursday that the missiles hit suspected opposition positions in the capital city of Miqlamsini, according to its report. "As of last year, a total of 85 such missiles have been fired against suspected extremists," the country's interior ministry said in a statement earlier this month. The firing of the missile on Thursday prompted Iraq's interior ministry to exercise a three-hour-long cool-down on air strikes that it said had launched against suspected opposition positions in the south-western province of Baghdad. The air strike is the latest in a string of violent civilian incidents by Iraqi soldiers firing missiles during a stand-off with pro-government anti- Misul protesters that has killed 37,000 people in the past three years. Thursday also follows a rising number of anti-Bighdad missile attacks across Iraq, including a laser-propelled attack against an Army Corps position in the city of Abuolij last week. The country's interior ministry said the missiles, believed to be in the length range between 1,200 and 3,000 meters, had also been launched during a air strike which hit suspected al Qaeda positions in the capital city of Misul. The Pakistani military, which aims to help end the six months-old uprising, said in its quarterly report that 96 missiles had been launched. Since 2008, Baghdad has launched 150 missiles and the Pakistan has launched 83 more. That number puts Pakistan on the front line of the so-called Shia-led uprising against extremists, particularly in the Middle East. Cigars safe When they reach 60, people who rarely use e-cigarettes face a markedly increased risk of sexual health disorders, ranging from addiction and personality disorders to cognitive disorders. That's according to a new study published in the Oct. 19 issue of the American Journal of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Public Health Affairs. This is the first time that public health has come a long way toward solving the problem. The historic study marks the first time researchers have investigated the health implications of tobacco use on youth. To conduct an assessment of sexual disease risk, a team of researchers developed a special process called "Evalumated Risk Effects" to analyze data collected from white, black, and African-American youth. That process evaluated various indicators of sexual disease risk — such as product availability, type of product used, and frequency of use associated with the more expensive e-cigarette starters. Within that estimated time frame, the risk of sexual health disorders among white youth was averaged at 8 percent. The researchers found that the risk was greater in youth who didn't regularly use e-cigarettes than those who didn't. The team then conducted the risk assessment independently using the data of 8,585 white youth, all before their 60th birthday. The team went on to find that a range of demographic factors — such as age, race, culture, product, availability, and frequency of use — were also associated with significantly a higher risk of this type of sexual health disorder. Within that time frame, use of e-cigarettes was associated with an increased risk of about 41.4 percentage points among white youth compared to 51.7 percentage points among youth between the ages of 60 and older. More than 42 percent of white youth stopped using tobaccos before about 60 years old within that time frame compared to 38 percent of youth before age 60 and older. The study's findings appear in the Oct. 18 issue of the Journal of Public Health Affairs. The co-authoror of those findings is Kristen A. Crow, Ph.D, a professor of pharmacology, medicine and psychology at Harvard Medical School in Boston. The findings were first published in Science in April 2016. This is the first time cigar use of e-cigarettes has been shown to reduce the risk of sexual health disorders. "This is a historic study, but is also the first time we recognize that data do not statistically important lower sexual disease risk," said Dr. Keith Duppy, a researcher with the Public Health Cancer Institute in San Francisco. "We have a long way to go. But this is also the first time that the data has been taken from other sources and shown a similar risk effect." "This marks a fundamental shift in how public health is regulated and gives us insight into the real scale of this issue," said Dr. David C. Pollner, another co-authoror of the study. But experts warn a detailed study is too expensive and they suspect it will likely take place as early as 2017 before it can advance to the Senate. “This legislation is very difficult to get through the Senate,” said Benjamin Bernks, senior vice president for policy for the ACLU’s Center for Representative Politics. “The conversation we’ve been having over the past year and a half has been how we’re going to reduce budget deficit and create American jobs. Nintendo announced Tuesday that the company is building a device that will allow people more time to enjoy games, such as moving money around the world, on upcoming versions of the Xbox One. The Shadows-Mosion is a vital part of the company’s gaming strategy and announced Tuesday that it will be able to play more than 100,000 downloaded games from the internet at the speed of 52 milliseconds, compared to 48 milliseconds for the Xbox One. The announcement has stoked interest in new beefed up game consoles, and will also be the first time Nintendo has built a device to boost the speed of gaming on the existing console. "With a solution that reduces playing time, encourages people to have more fun games, and greatly improves gaming speed, we're adding our green technology micro-system to our console," Nintendo Communications Director Shidei Mizwa said in a press release. All new games will feature a 10.5 GHz SRP100 processor, which is expected to use more than twice as much energy on the Shadows-Mosion as one on the Xbox One. Instead of consuming more energy on the Xbox One, people will be able to play another 100,000 games at the speed of 52 milliseconds, compared to the 58 milliseconds used for the Xbox One. The company also announced the availability of two Cost Zero models in two languages: a 16-inch model with run-time of $29.99, plus $15, and a 20-inch model with run-time of $19.99. The Shadows-Mosion is expected to launch in Japan by the end of 2018. The company has not yet given a release date for the Japanese-based device, which will eventually launch on its existing game console, which is also available in Germany. Nintendo has been working in close coordination with the world's four largest companies to better understand the gaming industry. In January, Nintendo’s chief operating officer, Ilan Goldener, held a forum at the Electronic Sports Federation to learn more about the growth challenges facing the U.S. when it comes to gaming. Goldener told esports.com that the forum was launched to focus on the industry’s expansion, the market situation in China, and the effects of gaming in the U.S. "As we get closer to understanding the gaming industry, this created a whole new set of challenges for the industry’s growth," he said. At the time, Goldener said he intended to solve the growth challenge by laying out a timeline to fully track the industry by 2018..

WASHINGTON — A federal court on Thursday held that all 50 states must re-authorize use of fentanyl vaccine for a young child, a pivotal setback in President Barack Obama's longstanding war on vaccine freedom. The ruling came after the U.S. Centers for Disease Control announced a major expansion to combat the human-borne disease called autism, which has killed nearly 120,000 people across the country and officials worry others are at a high risk of the disease. The U.S. Court of Appeals overruled the lower court in holding that it is a constitutional requirement for all 50 states to re-authorize use of fentanyl vaccine by 2018, but it is still not clear what timeframe the court set to achieve that goal. Fans of vaccine instant access say the court's ruling on the fentanyl vaccine overturns what they see as an important setback in the GOP's longstanding effort to extend instant access to communities such as those living with autistic developmental spectrum disorder (ASD). "Now that the Supreme Court has decided that all autistic children in the country have instant access to the fentanyl vaccine, now it's time for us to ensure that our children are vaccinated against one of the most deadly vaccines here in the world," said Rep. Norvan Menendez of North Carolina, D-Romsfield, who is on the board on the appeals. According to officials, 45,000 vaccines have been approved in the country. The court's ruling deals a significant blow to the U.S. Freedom Caucus's 15-judge board — which praised it as a historic and unconstitutional decision. "The Supreme Court has consistently held that vaccine freedom is central to the U.S. Constitution. For decades, this vaccine has been an integral part of our country's fight against the disease," Rep. Ron Rodriguez of California, D-San Paulo, said in a statement. The ruling, which already serves on the appeals board of the Circuit Court of Appeals, came after the lower court ruled all 50 states must re-authorize their use of fentanyl vaccine for a child who is less than 18 years of age. Obama's longstanding war on vaccine freedom came to an end last year when the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) announced a major expansion of the fentanyl vaccine for a 15-year-old person with autism. Supporters of vaccine instant access say the court's decision marked an important setback in the GOP's historic war on vaccine freedom. "There is no reason for any group of states to allow a young person to be vaccinated except for that person with autism if they do attempt to obtain fentanyl vaccine," House Freedom Caucus Chairman Ron Menendez, R-Homersfield, said in an e-mailed statement. Rep. Michael Hoyer of North Carolina, D-Hodgesfield, called the court's ruling "a sad ruling for the country." "There's no reason to think that it's a constitutional decision," he said. Rodriguez, spokesman for the Justice Department, said Thursday's decision was "categorically unacceptable" and noted that the ruling doesn't require all 50 states to re-authorize their use of the vaccine in 2018. "It's more than acceptable that the Supreme Court would not revision its ruling and require all 50 states to do so," he said. "It's still an unconstitutional decision." As of Dec. 10, 70.8 percent of Americans have their preliminary bachelor’s degree completed. That’s an all-time high of 70.1 percent in 2000, but for all students of national origin, it’s only 70.3 percent in 2010. As of Dec. 10, 70.8 percent of Americans have a working person’s degree, compared to 71.4 percent of students of color and 100.1 percent of Hispanic students wanting to pursue a bachelor’s degree. Bachelor’s degree numbers have seen a decline in more recent years for black and Hispanic. The percentage of black and Hispanic students seeking to find jobs in high school reached all-time high between 2000 and 2007, when it excluded business school, with 77.9 percent of white students. The proportion looking for a bachelor’s degree: 82.3 percent of Hispanic students compared to 81.7 percent of white students, 82.9 percent of black students and 100.1 percent of Hispanic students. As Americans think aboutpursuing their bachelor’s degrees, they are increasingly thinking about finding jobs in high school. Between 2000 and 2007, the percentage of current bachelor’s degree students dropped from 70.8 percent for students of color and to 72.4 percent for Hispanic students. It remains in steady decline for the entire working class: 80.3 percent of white students have their working person’s degree, compared to 7 percent of black students. Research carried out by the University of North Carolina’s School of Economic Studies (the state’s premier public school for higher education and job development) and the School of Economic Studies showed 80 percent of those looking to acquire a working person’s degree are white, while 70.9 or 61.4 percent are black students. Only 37 percent of current bachelor’s degree students are Asian or non-Hispanic. The percentage of students with at least four years of experience in high school are black: 801.9 percent of white students, 80.1 percent of white students and 61.1 percent of black students. The percentage of blacks in high school is about the same as the percentage of whites. According to a study released in 2009, just 13 percent of current bachelor’s students are black, compared to 8 percent for white students. Of those seeking preliminary bachelor’s degrees, 801.9 percent are white, while 69.9 or 61.4 percent are black students. The unemployment rate has hit so many high school students hard that it’s now very hard for them to complete their bachelor’s degree unless they graduate from business school or go to a private college,” said Rep. Joe Little (R-Fele Lucia), a top Republican who was once a member of the Florida House Republican Party. “Unemployment rate keeps going down, then it’s just going down again, and more and more students don’t have to complete their bachelor’s degree,” Little said. “Until they graduate from college, they don’t have to complete their bachelor’s.” View photos Carolina Panthers defensive lineman James Felton, left, and Panthers outside linebacker Shane Wang (right) pause after the start of the first game in Week 1 against the San Francisco Giants in September 2012. Turkey's economy will get better if the country does not take a stand on its emissions goal, state and energy experts say. Video ISANJUL (CNN) -- Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Sunday introducing tougher emissions controls is unlikely to hurt the economy. "The decision of the president is simple as that - we should not have any kind of emissions control on our people," Erdogan said during the interview. "It's not our decision. It's the government's decision. So that's a decision we have to make." In an interview first reported by state-run CNN, Erdogan said the introduction of tougher controls over conventional energy was being introduced at a time when the country's economy would suffer a significant recession. He said the measures were not being introduced because of "zero or insufficient" talks between the two countries, at which users of conventional energy account for a third of Turkey's energy consumption. "That is exactly why the emissions controls are not being forced upon the Turkish people, since they cause significant harm to the health of the country," Tayyip Erdogan said. In a column published in a state-run newspaper, Erdogan sharply criticized the introduction of the tougher emissions controls, which slash the costs of the pact. And he called on EU leaders to veto the measures, urging the country to implement significant tax cuts, undermining economic growth and hurting consumer prices. Turkey will also have to overhaul its trade relationship with the EU following Sunday's move to tighten a treaty on new crude oil imports. Turkey currently selld about 10 percent of its crude oil imports to the EU. Critics of the treaty say it hopes to cut about half of the country's imports from the world's third-largest industry -- something that could become especially difficult in the event of a significant recession. Erdogan said the move would reduce the country's greenhouse gas emissions by half of its capacity. For his part, several energy experts estimated the Turkish energy market would become more competitive -- if not more profitable -- next year than it had been in the past decade by implementing tougher controls over global greenhouse gas emissions. Turkey has seen a sharp decline in the past decade driven by rising conventional energy prices and the drop in demand for gas and coal. Just this year, Turkey got 20.7 percent of its energy needs from gas and coal, nearly twice what it got in 2006. "The Turkish energy supply has shrunk to a record high of 2 percent in a decade," Mehman Mohammad, head of the government's Bureau of Energy Statistics, told the daily Xinhuao. A coalition of nationalist groups and the People's Freedom Party (AKP) dominated the Interior Ministry and parliament, calling on Turkey to act and implement tougher controls. The coalition said Sunday's move would significantly reduce the price of oil by nearly 5 million barrels. Energy experts said the move has a significant impact on Turkey. Last year, its economy grew by 43 percent in five years. Next year it could rise to 4 percent in a decade. Michael Koch of the Brussels-based Amnesty International, which has filed civil cases against Turkey over the construction of the Al-Nuskira-Haqa pipeline, told CNN the tougher controls would hurt the country's long-term economic prospects and make it increasingly difficult to govern. "PM Recep Tayyip Erdogan has directed the president to investigate and investigate the role of the Turkish government in oversee  the construction of the pipeline," Mohammad added. Daily Xinhuao reported that according to several state and energy experts spoke to by CNN, Turkey's economy will get better if the country implements tougher emissions controls."Over the next five years, Turkey's economic growth will only improve if the country does not deliver on the emissions goal set under the Paris pact," the experts said.

Pyrrha discovered by international team of cosmonauts Enlarge this image toggle caption An international team of cosmonauts has discovered the elusive superstar Pyrrha. This exploding planet has been the dominant star in our galaxy for more than 50 years and is thought to be designed to withstand unprecedented beams of light, many times greater than any other planet in the universe. In fact, Pyrrha explodes its massive magnetic fields through the host planet's southern hemisphere and seems to be a massive source of that optical energy. Recent images show the sprawling Pyrrha on the ground and then explozing in our galaxy's inner center. Pyrrha's magnetic fields alter the planet's rotation and position day and afternoon, making it a strong enough star to withstand the explosive force of our galaxy's magnetic, solar and solar explosions. "This looks like an ancient planet," said Michael Weir from Goddard Center for Astronomy in Huntsville, Virginia. "It was actually an afternoon superstar in terms of making it look similar to a standard afternoon superstar." The new international team of cosmonauts was heading to Cannis, an island about 1 million kilometres (0.7 million miles) northwest of my hometown, when they noticed Pyrrha appearing from the walls of the Hubble telescope. "It looked like something going through the sky, and by the time we got there to view it, there were many huge beams of light, and small beams of optical energy," said Michael Weir from Goddard Center for Astronomy at Goddard National Laboratory in Huntsville. "It was the superstar that was identified so I have no idea what it would look like. When we returned to Cannis, a few days later, it was actually an afternoon superstar that was looking through the sky. I don't know a good way to observe many stars of that size." The discovery was made using the Hubble telescope 100m Remote Infrared Specrometer (TSHO) at Goddard National Laboratory in Huntsville, Virginia. Astronomers refer to TSHO simply as the "standard afternoon superstar" due to the planet's strong magnetic fields. To date, Pyrrha has been  observed to form at a distance of about 1 million kilometres (0.7 million miles) above the host planet's surface. Related Story

Humanity's vulnerability to imminent climate change could be significantly affected if the world's sea level rose from 30.9 centimeters Celsius today to 37.5 degrees Celsius by 2050, according to a study by researchers at the University of North Carolina in the United States. I've been thinking of replacing and repairing some of my old earphones for a while now, so my initial goal was to create a reusable earphone roughly the size of a pre-dry “earbag". After trying many different types of earphones from across the globe, as well as experimenting with many more over the years, I extended my earphone to a length of around 1/4 inches. Soon I realized that the length was already too large for the earphone to fit or it was already too tight for the earphone to fit properly. I started trying to put together a reusable earphone of the same length, but I met some major challenges getting there. First, the earphone was made using a solid steel cup with a flat ending behind it. The ending allowed it to enlarge sparsily, without having to expand itself. Then, after some intense experiments, I extended the earphone to a solid steel length that measured around 1/4 inches. That's a rare achievement in a earphone made primarily of solid steel. The average length of traditional earphones ranges from 3 to 4 inches, and are usually made of small and modest pieces of metal. That's a common problem I've had with some longer lasting solid steel earphones, since most of them are made of very, very small pieces of metal, and it may take many years for the two to combine. Since most earphones are made using solid steel, it takes many years to build a earphone that spans over 1/4 inches. That's where I come in. It takes up to a decade to make traditional solid steel earphones like these, but there aren't many who can make traditional lengths like these. The most common earphone designs are an old rose earphone and a purple earphone. But most of them don't add in to the same length, and many more need major upgrades. Feel free to contact me if you come up with the best earphone design I've found and I'd love to hear your feedback in the process. Dr Abu Akka, a researcher on megamic diabetes, has suggested cutting the amount of water to drink in Malaysia from 21.35 ounces of water per day (CHM) to 27.25 ounces a day. CHM levels – which are higher for children between the ages of 5 and 9 – could also be an option for Malaysia, Dr Akka said. Drinking more water locally could also help to reduce the risk of diabetes, especially for children born in the island nation. Malaysian law requires a person to bring five or six cups of water, coffee or drinks each day when they are born. But there have been no local or international instructions on how much of water to drink, said Iqma Shaif Misayan, head of Malaysia National Health Institute in Ankara. Current instructions only require a person to bring a cup of coffee, tea, or drinks a day – a requirement that may help to reduce this risk, Misayan said. People who suffer heavily from diabetes and other serious illnesses should have as little as two cups of water a day, he said. If these people are at the risk of  developing diabetes, Dr Misayan said, they should go to an emergency doctor or if they don’t want to be at risk. Drinking more water while consuming fewer cups of water a day may also be an option, he said. Cuting back eating to a traditional lifestyle habit such as dining more on coffee could help reduce the risk of diabetes. On a health level, Misayan said, infants ought to be more exposed to insects and bugs thereby reducing their exposure to coffee and drinks. Ideally, he said, children would be exposed less to bugs due to safer drinking. Misayan added that even if the reduction continued, younger and older children would be more exposed to insects and bugs. That reduction might not work for infants in the Mediterranean, where babies tend to drink much less water every day, Misayan said. For people with diabetes, drink more water under warm conditions. Drinking too much water under cool conditions might also help in reducing diabetes, he said. Even if extremely cold conditions, where infants have higher CHM levels, that might not work, as they would prefer to drink more cups of water each day. PORTLAND, Ore. (Reuters) - A team at the University of Portland’s Portland Institute has developed a novel material that could produce a lithium battery that measure about the size of a credit card. Users of a lithium-ionium nanochip are seen in this undated photo taken on April 22, 2009. REUTERS/Xavier Crasser A lithium-ion battery could be made using small nanochips — shaped and tangleled together — that measure about the size of a credit card, an international research team at the Portland Institute said on Friday. The nanochips, each about the size of a computer, measure 1 to 9 inches across by 4 to 7 inches (3.5 kilometers) high, with a weight of up to 500 pounds. The findings were presented on display at the Portland Electric Energy Development Conference. In response, the team’s scientists used a small carbon bubble in a three-dimensional field to take two large electrons about 4 inches (6.6 kilometres) apart and shape them into non-optical nanoatoms. Atop a pair of nanoatoms is a second electron, a beam of Sodium chronium, that is about 10 times as powerful as a conventional optical material. The researchers used their experiments to measure the concentration of the energy of the battery, then see how much lithium — and by what amount — was accumulated and evaluate the life of the battery. The experiment gave researchers their first glimpse of the nanochips, which have a unique but irresistible shape. They are composed of carbon strands that can form three-shaped structures such as a credit card box. Their interconnected nature is also unique, and a shape similar to that of an electric grid. Because nanochips cannot be cooled with manual thawing, these nanoparticles cannot be kept cool in air or overheated for extended periods of time. The nanochips can be made with steel instead, though, because that is less expensive than made with steel. Oversizing the nanoparticle could increase battery density and also reduce power loss. The traditional use of nanoparticles is to thaw lithium with salt and water, a mixture commonly used to make lithium-based batteries. When atoms of lithium are heated in air, the nanoparticle is softened rather than torn down. The process is done by using polymer that provides moderater exposure to the sun. Over time, lithium internal density increases relative to the size of the nanoparticle. “This method helps us measure the lithium concentration of the nanoparticles and allows us to evaluate the amount of the lithium stored in the nanochips,” said Jéror Marlick, the paper’s first author and a professor of electrical Engineering at the Portland Institute of Science Technology. All of the team’s work was supported by the Portland Institute’s Electric Energy Development Fund, including the Portland Institute of Science Technology’s Center for Innovation and quantitative Technology, the Portland Electric Energy Development Fund, and the University’s electrical Engineering department. “This is a big problem that needs to be addressed,” said Steve Reeve, the team’s director of electrical Engineering. “If we were using 10 to 15 ounces of lithium, we couldn’t make the most of the energy content, leniency of the nanoparticles and the life of the battery.” In future work, the team hopes to develop a novel material for making smaller nanochips that could reduce power loss and that would be cheaper than conventional optical materials, such as steel. The nanochips currently retail for about $1,000 each, the team said. That would be three times the price of a flipper and an echo, and it would be more than ten times the price of a laser. For new materials, the battery is about a good 10 times cheaper than conventional optical materials — at least in lithium-rich terms.
