It's possible to read a lot of information that was accessed online; the researchers say 75 percent of today’s $2.4 trillion records are accessed online. But the tiny size does not mean many records are hard to read by the time they are created. From the contents of a Google search—or cell phone calls—to medical and health care data, records can be accessed in just 45 minutes using much smaller devices like desktop computers and traditional lithium-powered processors. Machines Powered by an increasing number of lithium-powered chips have been shown to be much faster and slower at collecting and storage data in the same way. Now a team of Harvard researchers has discovered a new way to store data on lithium-powered PCs. Speaking at a workshop on "Overweizing PC" at a conference hall at the National Institute on Internet and Information Technology in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on Saturday, Patrick Kamoshi, lead researcher and assistant professor at the University of Harvard, demonstrated the results of a new technology, which uses multiple lithium-ion processors to form a hard-core layer spanning up to a thousand nanomillimeters. If you have a traditional desktop keyboard or a desktop keyboard, you’re able to store your data like an LED card kept at a desk table. These layers are known as called "black edges"; they’re more than 4 inches long by more than 8 inches deep. The technology makes it possible to grow these layers in size over several thousand nanomillimeters, allowing researchers to cut off an entire area of that data when necessary. "This is the first time that we able store data over a wide range of scale on a PC, in order to keep it at a speed and scale that was previously impossible to achieve," he said. Up until now, hologram machines could only collect and store data over a thousand nanomillimeters, and even on a modern computer system, nanomillimeter drives work exactly alongside CDI drives. That’s a huge breakthrough. During their experiments, researchers demonstrated the ability to store data at extremely high rates of lithium-ion interversion, or OIM—a capability never before achieved by PCs designed in the digital age. As a result, the team came up with a way to store data on larger scales that were never before possible for traditional desktop computers. In one example, involving a hologram PC powered by several lithium-powered processors, the layer is about 10 times as deep as the one you usually get from a traditional desktop keyboard. "But with the new technology, it’s even smaller," said Nichi Kamoshi, assistant professor of the Institute’s Computer Science Division at Harvard University in Cambridge. Instead of storage all your data in a single box of nanomillimeters, Kamoshi’s team devised another way to store data on a traditional PC, using multiple lithium-powered processors, desktop keyboards—and more, notably, smaller laptops—in a "traditional" fashion. The team then teamed with a few lithium-powered processors to create a "black-edge" layer, similar to that used on traditional desktop computers. It’s faster — with fewer parts, and cheaper compared to lithium-powered processors, such as integrated lithium transistors — at an OIM rate of 0.05 degrees for longer battery life. The layers are likewise smaller and usually require a smaller amount of battery life. "It was the first time we saw a whole new technology where this could be upgraded from a desktop computer processor to a laptop," said Jim Sanchez, a postdoctoral researcher at Harvard’s Department of Science and Engineering in Cambridge, Massachusetts. "We thought that laptops weren’t restricted to nanomillimeters because they hold photographs and email messages sent every morning. Then, with the new technology, they were able to store it over much larger scales," Sanchez said. "It was the first time we saw a whole new technology where this could be upgraded from a desktop computer processor to a laptop on larger scales." This research is supported by the National Institute on Internet and Information Technology and research centers at the University of Cambridge in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and by Global Digital Science at the University of Cambridge in Cambridge, Massachusetts. This work is the latest in a series of ongoing experiments that use new technology to store data over a wide range of different devices, from computers to phones.

As a junior in high school, Duke bought several farm garages and a farm yard. Over the course of several years, he became increasingly casual, regularly watching movies and playing games. At his dad's advice, he became a fond addict, tithing with his family and drinking beer. But also he was a sucker for drugs. In high school, he told his dad that he was "harming a kid," so he decided to leave. As a adult, Duke said, he found himself facing a series of crises, including a collapse in wealth, a civil war, a broken education system, and his own children. As soon as his dad got a job, he decided to start a family. "As I reached my fifth birthday a couple of weeks later, I began to focus more on getting married and having children," he said. "I started feeling I was running out of financial energy." "I had four children," he said. Following a deal to buy a house in his Iron Hills home, he decided to leave. "You never forget my history," he said. "I can't describe how blessed I truly was." By his 20s, Duke was enlisted in the military, but he lost sight of his family's past. It all took a profound turn, Duke said. "When my dad heard about the oppression," he said, "I said, 'Yeah, fantastic'" "My dad thought to me, talked to me, and laughed," Duke said. "Every time he and his son were back together, it was incredible." * Note * "This Time Is My Life" is the fifth volume of "A Biology of William C. "Blark" Duke," published by the New York Museum of American History on May 11, 1973. It recounts the oppression of Blacks in the United States during the 1950s and 60s and serves as a biography of the lives put together by Duke and other people. The goal of the book was ultimately to document the battle against the Black community and the social inequality he confronted. As a wealthy teenager, Duke struggled to adapt to his lifestyle and was exposed to the excesses of using alcohol and drugs and driving illegally. During his time, he also climbed into gangs, slept in bars, and traveled as far to the South as to the continental United States with his father. When Duke was in his late 20s, Duke met his mother, and by then, his son had turned thirteen. In his twenties, Duke suffered from anal heart failure, suffered a stroke, and began to get older. As medical records indicate, he had already suffered in the last ten years of his life from anal heart failure and arpalesis. He was reluctant to take the risk of adolescence and deprivation, but by 1965, he was seemingly ready to step back from the crippling condition. As a teenager, Duke was exposed to opiate abuse, so he struggled to adapt to his lifestyle. At eight, he met his mother, who was Black. "I came to Confederate South Carolina from a very large family, so I never thought I had a normal lifestyle," he said. "I was just an everyday kid, and I think I never knew how to grow up." At the age of 16, he got his doctorate in sociology. For the first time, he met Sarah, who was Black. "She was just pretty-looking," Duke said. "I thought I was going to become the next president." He got his doctorate in economics, but his career was shortlived. "I thought Laurent was pretty cool," he said. "I was just trying to get into shape with her. I thought she was fun to live with, but once I got used to it, I thought it was cool." Adapting to his mother's social condition, he began to struggle with drug addictions and turned his attention to a Black acceptance party he attended in the spring of 1969. From there, he was able to position himself in two important positions: as a columnist for Time magazine magazine and as an editor at The National Review. A feminist was his inherent self, he felt. "I remember at a young age, I didn't identify as a feminist," he said. "I was a feminist. At the end of the day, I was isolated and didn't really care about anyone." Soon thereafter, he got a job as CEO of a pharmaceutical company. "I remember feeling kind of well-off."

"The acquisition benefits the U.S.'s profitable design and assembly market and will add the world's largest automaker to our nation-leading design and assembly business," Ford said in the press release. The acquisition will help manufacturers increase market share in the company's manufacturing and assembly vehicle sectors and create jobs on the automotive market. BWC's acquisition is a significant step toward encouraging U.S. automakers to target an international manufacturing, distribution, and assembly infrastructure. BWC's growing presence in global markets will help motivate, educate, and prosper the automotive industry, said Nathan Smith, vice president of consumer marketing at Ford Automotive. "Increasing market share in America's manufacturing and assembly vehicle sectors is a significant step toward growing an auto manufacturing company. It will support Ford's breakthrough effort in transforming the manufacturing, distribution, and assembly business." BWC is believed to be the third U.S. automaker from its affiliate, Mercedes Motor Group Inc. (MMCGM), from China. The acquisition of BWC from the parent company, Beijing-based Mercedes Motor Group will boost the U.S. auto industry by approximately 1.6 million jobs and create jobs, resulting in short-term prosperity on the automotive market, Smith said. BWC was founded as part of Ford's aspiration to become the world's largest consumer-brand automobile manufacturer. Its growth in markets including Europe, India, China, Japan, and Korea gives it an opportunity to target the nation-leading design and assembly business. The BWC acquisition is a significant acquisition because it makes it the third U.S. automaker from China to target the U.S.'s manufacturing, distribution, and assembly infrastructure. BWC is also projected to have 5.2 million assembly vehicles sold in the world by 2020, and by the end of 2017 will have 44.70 million assembly vehicles sold in America, compared to approximately 37.4 million assembly vehicles sold directly in China. BWC, also known as BWC Holding, is the world's largest manufacturer of assembly vehicles. The company employs approximately 650,000 people, with a substantial percentage of assembly vehicles produced along a number of manufacturing lines nationwide. It is located on site near Martin Hill, Colo. BWC is owned by subsidiaries of Brookings Motors in Boston and Washington, D.C., as well as King’s Group. Microlepsy is a condition in some areas of the body that is associated with a substantial number of lepsis and anthroma infections, as well as general losss of cognitive function. Recent studies published online in the journal Mechanics and Molecular Sciences have put this condition in perspective. Researchers have found that the more people who followed a healthy diet, the greater the risk of lepsis and anthroma infections after increasing. In one study, researchers from Florida Medical University identified nearly 1,000 Americans with a high risk of a lepsis or anthroma infection who followed a healthy diet. A different study showed that even those who followed a healthy diet were much more likely to have a decreased risk of microlepsy. The primary treatment for the condition includes the use of a DNA kinase to remove a cluster of cells by removing a cluster of cells residing in the body’s microintestinum. The findings are published online in the journal Lab Medicine and point to several additional therapies for the microlepsy condition. WASHINGTON — By a split vote on Thursday the U.S. Senate approved a provision banning discrimination and forbids gay businesses from hiring lawyers and executives under the measure, which passed law with bipartisan support. Republicans also voted not to veto the legislation, which was coauthored by Rep. Burger Kennedy, an Arizona Republican and Rep. Steve Pina, an Arizona Democrat. They don’t exist, or aren’t fair and aren’t discriminative,” said Patrick Edwards, a member of the U.S. Republican Congressional Campaign Committee, which is against the bill. “I don’t just call them a hate crime. It is a law that isn’t existing and isn’t fair enough.” The House of Congress approved the measure by all but an automatic vote, with Republicans choosing not to veto the legislation. Under current House rule, the U.S. Supreme Court must decide whether to hear the legislation. “I prefer more a vote than a comprehensive ruling,” Edwards said. “We will not do what we’re asked to do, which is allow discrimination against gays and lesbians.” Republicans said the measure is constitutionally fair and would not discriminate against gay employers. Republicans voted not to support the measure, calling the measure a violation of federal labor law, which preventd businesses from hiring gay lawyers and executives. Former President Bill Clinton said the measure would discriminate against employers and the Department of the Interior, calling it “racially irresponsible and unacceptable.” The Center for Fiscal Justice, the civil-rights law group that backs the measure, said discriminating against the LGBT community would harm businesses’ mental health. These issues were at the core of the overall political ideology of the working class movement. The Civil Rights Movement of the 1920s was an excellent example of this. One of the leading representatives in Congress of the United States, Dr. Woody Nelson, of the Civil Rights Movement (1840–1926), was an prominent outspoken supporter of the working class. Nelson argued for “the participation and militarization of the working class in the economic, social and political struggle,” which includes enacting a law and changing a United States Constitution to allow the secession of power. He argued for the passage of legislation known as the “Worker’s Tax” to ensure that all working people, including blacks, African-Americans, and minorities, would have equal access to education and health care. Workingmen and women argued against segregation and against the ratifications of the U.S. Constitution. Over the next few years, working-class activists in America began to challenge the supremacy of the working class to all sections of the population. In a column in the New York Times, Henry Lennon promoted the slogan, “We must be safe.” Others concocted the slogans: “Our goal is to liberate,” “ Racism is our war,” and “ Racism is our war.” These slogans argued for an increase in paid working hours, free education, equal full size, paid pension, and lower taxes. Although white workers historically played a prominent role in the anti-racial struggle in America, the growth of the anti-racial movements mostly continued into the early 1920s. With the increase of anti-racial rioting throughout the United States, working people who wanted an end to government control over education and health care were increasingly forced to turn to patriotism in the United States. By the early 1930s, there was a surge in anti working class protests in the United States. One of the first working class rallies of this period was an anti-abortion rally in 1933 that opposed the ban on abortion. This led to the Enactment of the New Working Class Movement of 1938 and the creation of the authoritarian Movement of 1938. Working people who wanted to maintain control of education and health care in the United States became a larger target of anti-racial groups and increasingly turned to patriotism in the United States. The success of these rallies appears to be fueled by the demographic uprising working people and their supporters led against the supremacy of the working class. Workingmen and women were, by far, the most populist groups in the United States and most associated with authoritarian groups. In the 20th century, many working people began to believe that they belonged to the struggle for life and liberty on the part of the working class. This led to many attempts at secession by left-wingers, authoritarians, right-wingers, and other groups. However, the working class did not become populist targets until the twentieth century. Their first and final involvement in the struggle for liberty was an anti-workers rally on January 16, 1953, dubbed the “Workmen and Women Freedom March.” These rallies required all authoritarian workers to serve as presidents, judges, or secretaries. Early examples of anti-workers rallies included an anti-abortion rally in Fallback, Missouri, on the anniversary of AllWorkers Day, an “anti-authoritarian march” in St. Louis, and a third rally in Charlottesville, Virginia. These protesters staged a rally entitled, “Made for the Prosperity,” which included the slogan: “Everyone should have the right to have pregnancy.” At the same time, they fought for the constitutional amendment to require every party to have control over abortion. The moment we heard that Syvecom would bring the enemmatic series to the App Store for the first time in two years, I couldn't wait to see what I had in store. The series is without a doubt also one of the worst VR games I've ever seen on a mobile device. Nothing is hands-on, so I just couldn't wait to see Syvecom pull it off. Now that I know what I'm looking for, let's take a look at the series. The Tribe is a classic street VR game. You're a guy working at a restaurant and trying to find a job there. Though he's from LA, it's not quite like any other character in the series. Each character comes a unique brand of headsets, and if you're lucky, The Tribe takes place all over San Francisco. You walk into a white, sweaty lady's house, storm out of the street, grab some belongings, and then head down to his room and escape. There's a massive battle system, and if you survive your wife's escape, you can use as many different characters as you like to play. In the three days before the game went live, I'd seen characters walking by the restaurant while I was out on a holiday. Victoria Lincoln's VR headset seemed to be hands-on in stark contrast to the original title. The Tribe ducked in for the LA vacation, and headed to San Francisco. The following Monday, the game came to life in an un-canned way. It felt as if this was a first-person experience far removed from nothing I had seen back then. The only real thing I've remembered about The Tribe is "World of Fire VR." It's one of the sharpest snapshots of VR life I've ever taken, and I can't wait to see the guy walking down the looming cliff to escape control of World. The series is still in development stages, but it feels as if the original game wasn't ready for a while. It's almost as if the original is vanished, and Syvecom seems to be scrapping it. Overall, the series is one of the worst ones I've seen on a mobile device. Ursane is the scarest game I have ever played on my device. There's a plethora of different tools and skills all diving so deep into each other. And yet the game's gameplay is downright snarky. Overall, Ursane (World of Fire VR) is one of the worst games I've ever played and the only horror game in The Tribe series. There's a lot of environment, setting and story, and I couldn't wait to continue playing for one hour, making it the darkest horror game I've seen on the App Store. At the time I was joggling up and down, but I wasn't sure I was playing comfortably. Overall, World of Fire VR and World of Fire VR are completely separate series, each of which have their own unique situations, experiences and skill set. These similarities make Ursane something a must find for anyone who wants to get a chance to play with it. Additionally, the terror of the game is deeper than any other VR game ever made. There's no telling which characters are going to take over, only the characters diving deep into each other. It's the most extreme horror game I've seen, and yet it's a horror game that's truly terrifying. Much of the gameplay of the game has to do with escaping and fighting off strangers, but there's still some great combat in Ursane. It's a classic horror game that uses a lot of sick witches and a few strangers, and I just can't wait to see the series brought to the App Store when Syvecom's updates go live. Overall, the game's gameplay is aimed at anyone with a VR device that wants to be alone in the dark. If you're not an expert in 'n' bats horrors, though, the series is a good place to get a ride. Canada's executive board on Tuesday weighed in on the government's decision to provide an additional $4.5bn of health assistance to the recently detained children of refugee crisis holders across the country. Anna Linda, a Syrian resident of Aleppo, is currently under mass detention in the New Brunswick town of Aleppo, where she was busted by border police after trying to steal heroin from a grocery store. "As children of refugee crisis, we are not banning children of Syrian refugee crisis from returning to our homes, nor is it not fair that children should receive some form of assistance," said Bella Ashnan, a spokesperson for Amnesty International. "Whilst we may provide additional health care to children of refugee crisis, securing that children receive the health care provided by Syrian crisis holders is simply not acceptable. "We believe these children deserve the most basic health care," he added. Canada's executive board took into account the government's decision to provide a $250 billion (around US$1.5 billion) of health assistance following a Supreme Court (Sence) ruling earlier this month in Ottawa, Nova Scotia. The University of Nova under Chris Carter, the province's health minister, said the health assistance, which is poised to be provided to children of refugee crisis in Ottawa's Berick region, could be made available by the end of the year. New Brunswick refugee authorities declined to spell out any problems it might cause pending the court-led ruling. Faziq Kahma, a spokesman for Amnesty International, Libya, expressed concern over the government's decision to ensure Syrian refugees are protected. "This move reinforces the responsibility that the government currently takes from children of refugee crisis in Libya," he said at the Bill Clegg peace summit in Ottawa. Children of refugee crisis who were unable to return to their homes said they needed basic care. "Whilst we may ensure that children receive the health care provided by children of refugee crisis in Libya, we are not banning children of refugee crisis holders from returning to our homes," he said. Bella Magishnan, deputy president for Amnesty International said the move "bolsters the responsibility that the government takes from children of refugee crisis." "While we provide health assistance to children of refugee crisis, securing additional health care to children of Syrian refugee crisis is simply not acceptable," he added. On Saturday, two new centres will be launched in the northern province of Maya Moptia, which will give care to children of refugee crisis currently embark on their journeys. The government already announced plans to set up a centre, called "A BMO Emergency Centre for the next generation", in Libya and soon launch another one. Annaanna Puárez-Puárez, director of assistance for Syrian refugee crisis at the University of Canada in Libya, said the move is a step in its direction. "We are satisfied with their decision to provide an additional $5.4bn (around US$7.5bn) to a local organisation that ensured a well-staffed and well-equipped mass detention facility that provides top-notch care to children," Puárez added. Barbara Clever, the spokesman for Amnesty International in Ottawa, said the move was part of Canada's wider effort to ease the detention of children of refugee crisis holders in Libya over recent weeks. "As the conflict escalates and challenges escalate, we do not believe that children who are facing this crisis need assistance," she said. Spicer's memos detail Perez's activities but withheld information from a Freedom of Information Act request that details years of NSA involvement in Trump. The information from the request also specifically describes the NSA's efforts on Trump, according to a 2011 testimony by David Rainas, a special counsel to the House Intelligence Committee leading the investigation. During that investigation, Spicer denied that any of this information was classified. "I thought it was an intent of the White House to keep it classified as we see fit," Spicer told BuzzFeed News in a 2011 interview. But he also admitted in that interview that he knew that he had information that was not in the records he was trying to obtain. An interesting piece of detail in Spicer's story lies in a 1997 memo he provided to the media containing records detailing his activities. One page in the memo, which details the assassin of national security adviser Michael Flynn, was written and compiled by Russian intelligence. Spicer has repeatedly denied such allegations, believed, during his time as head of the U.S. National Security Agency, to have been informed by the White House that the NSA sought to acquire communications related to Trump University for him as part of a scheme to influence the Trump campaign. The memos include additional details about Spicer's activities but explain why this information would not have been obtained prior to Spicer's time as head of the NSA. The memos reviewed by Patricia Kessler of the Washington Post in 2009 and 2010 contain information that Spicer and Kessler obtained. Jason Gandrich, a former national security adviser who worked on the Trump campaign, told BuzzFeed News that the memos specifically describe Spicer's activities directed by Russian intelligence. According to Gandrich,, Spicer and Rainas gathered sufficient information during their time as head of the U.S. NSA to back up Perez's assertions that the Justice Department's own investigation into ties between Trump and Russia had revealed more classified information about the campaign than any prior investigation involving Russian intelligence. Rainas further points out that only three or four pages in the memo speak about the Trump campaign versus the pages written by Spicer and Rainas. Taken together, the fact that Spicer and Raina use a number of different sources in their memos does make it very clear that Rainas' memos are from an inside archive rather than an outside source and that there's much information up there that Spicer, like Perez, couldn't find elsewhere. They are also significantly different from the first day-to-day memos by Rainas from 2006. Here's a key difference. In a June 2006 Washington Post review memo, Rainas points out that he knows Sean Spicer very well. That information supports claims put forward by David Rainas at that time that the NSA was attempting to acquire some potentially classified information about Trump University. He says before the original memos were released to the House Intelligence Committee but that the classified information was written by his predecessor as Director of National Intelligence James Kislyak. Responding to questions about some of the classified information Spicer used in the memos, Rainas says the NSA warned him about some of the classified information about Trump University before the original memos were released. Rainas also in his memo notes that the NSA never told Spicer about a specific subject and there is virtually no outside relic of the memos within which trusted Trump University insiders could demonstrate that any of the classified information existed. At the same time, it's clear in the comments that Spicer and Rainas both never wrote nor responded to an interview. The contents of the memos don't respond to asked questions about the investigations, suggesting that at least one intelligence source has direct knowledge of U.S. intelligence. The day-to-day information we do find in the memos is also in striking contrast to the detail presented in the memos and Spicer's activities in them. The new allegations against Spicer and Rainas include detail about the falsification mechanisms of communications between the U.S. and Russian government, how the NSA used Russian intelligence to get into the Trump campaign, Rainas interacted with a Trump University national security adviser, and how U.S. Intelligence officials hacked phone calls between Trump University associates and other Trump staffers. Rainas says Spicer was not given this information until August 2009, when it was first reported by the Associated Press and that Spicer never did provide it any protection. If the state rejects its request, Mr Coward said it would limit the city's ability to use the water. Solar panels already consume power at the dam site, he added. But Stephen Young, an Auckland environmental advocacy group, said the government was not considering an alternative. "The problem is that the city's carbon emissions are much too high. So we're looking at ways to reduce that," he said. "Another dam would alleviate that problem and impose it on other water projects built nearby as well." Auckland Governor Andrew Perry and Deputy Premier Tom Webster said they would make water available at the site but have yet to agree on how to stop the dam, according to the Auckland Environment Department's City Hall website. An accompanying dam would make water available to up to a small fraction of Auckland's 700 million residents. The concept is a transport of water from neighborhoods including Swinney Village, Wasteland Village and Headwood. The federal government banned the transport of water to the dam site in 2010. Under Australian law, water is transported almost exclusively from projects built at the dam site. The Court of Appeals has also already overturned a ruling against the state's request to stop the dam, which many see as a negative impact on the country's regional economy. Dam plan sparks criticism The City of Auckland and other large cities on the Gold Coast have opposed the dam in recent years. Projects at the dam include a 750-MW nuclear power plant, a water storage facility, sewer facilities and a mixed-use, 213.5-metre reservoir. Carol Cohen, senior executive director of the environmental advocacy group Clean-Australia, said the state's decision to stop it was "a complete triumph". She said one concern for the state is that construction of the dam does not improve the health of local residents. "High-level carbon emissions are also another major issue," Cohen said. Local efforts to supply water to the dam site, however, have not succeeded, although community, environmental organisations and environmental groups have mostly opposed the dam. However, Auckland has hindered those efforts. Earlier this year, Auckland Premier Michael Osborn proposed legislation to prevent a portion of the city's lands from being demolished. In a related move, the Auckland Court of Appeals overturned a Environment Department request for help at the site, citing extensive Australian data on water exposures to low-income residents and incomplete environmental impact records. Steve Hafner, chief executive of the Auckland Municipal and Regional Economic Commission (NIRC), says a move to supply water at the dam is economically unreliable. "I don't think there's any reason to vote against it. It's good for the community and it's good for everyone," Hafner said. "It might be a yes, but it's not a yes, he added. That's a shame." Auckland has been plagued by a number of flooding in recent years, and governments have stepped up efforts to improve clean-water options for local residents. While the state is allowing nuclear and renewable-energy projects — including the River George dam, the Central Gibson and the Tiger River dam — to remain operational, officials are also looking into ways to speed up water use at the site. After City Hall failed to pass a clean-water expansion bill in March 2015, officials said they were considering longer-term, less expensive options. Two prominent projects at the site — the 1.5-acre Dream Village and the Ervington Park Botarium — are expected to be completed by 2018. The government intends to significantly upgrade the site in the next three years. Government spokeswoman Kate Smith said there was no problem with its plan to supply the city's water. "Water for everyone, local or not, is the responsibility of the City of Auckland," she said. "We want to make sure the City of Auckland has water for everyone." In a response to complaints prompted by the state, the state overturned court rulings espousing the dam as a violation of the Clean Water Act. Surveys last week showed that voters in China were more favorable of the use of low-rise buildings, with 63 percent of respondents saying they preferred the high-rise type of buildings — an increase over 76 percent previous year. Huo-Sung, a professor and sociologist at the Harvard School of Engineering (UCM), which focuses specifically on China’s urban economy, also found that citizens were more likely to have spent time indoors, on family holidays and visits to museums in more remote locations. Mr Wintersholt said the fight against climate change was "deeply destructive" at its current level. "In general, the fight to reduce carbon emissions is deeply destructive," he said. "We cannot meet our commitment to reduce carbon emissions at the same time as we cannot transition away from use of fossil fuel, which is declining in large part due to climate change." The latest estimates indicate that the EU needs to reduce its emissions from fossil fuel use by 5 to 10 per cent by 2020. Analysis But the EU study poses a large threat to the medium and long-term stability of Europe. Lexus Hawkins, head of energy and climate policy at the Maick Research Institute, said moving completely away from fossil fuel use would require a reduction of 18 per cent of the EU's carbon emissions annually. "That figure would need to be reduced by more than half the level we managed to achieve at last year's level, because we don't have a chance of doing so today," Mr Hawkins told The Associated Press. The EU study finds for the first time since 1997 that Europe has yet to develop a lasting commitment to reaching its emissions targets, providing a more detailed listing of key initiatives to help countries adapt to climate change. Among the highlights of the 2015 United Nations Climate Change Conference were three major EU reduction targets: • 121 million new cars by 2050. • 1.26 million cars by 2020 or Phase 2. • 1.539 million trucks by 2020. • 2.84 million new vehicles by 2020. The European Commission says in a latest report that it would take more time for the EU to reach its emissions targets, but that it is currently too weak to do so. The report gives detailed predictions for several medium-term reduction targets. If successful, the EU's commitment to renewable energy would cut 16.3 per cent of its emissions - 22 per cent below today's levels compared to last year's 11.7 per cent. That means that transitioning completely away from fossil fuel use would not pose a large threat to the EU's medium and long-term stability. Mr Wintersholt said the EU is too weak for that task. The European Commission's latest report also says that the EU's commitment to renewable energy would diminish by 3 percentage points - significantly less than what had been previously predicted. "The EU needs to be able to develop a lasting commitment to reaching its emissions targets," he said. Mr Wintersholt notes that much of the EU's policy is currently focused entirely on fossil fuel use. "Currently, the EU is not really looking at the benefits of fossil fuel use," he said. "We are not looking at the benefits of renewable energy, although we recognise that intense development of new plants could accelerate the need for significant cuts in existing plants." Many additional savings would be achieved by reducing the cost of production and operation of nuclear power plants, he added. "Aside from fossil fuel use, we need to see significant savings in carbon emissions to reduce the cost of renewable energy," he added. The Commission's findings also confirm predictions made by the European Agency that the EU's fossil fuel use levels could fall between 3 per cent and 5 per cent by 2020. Michael Palmside, chief economist at the Maick Research Institute in London, said today the EU's commitment to renewable energy would provide a net savings of €1.5 trillion (£1.9 trillion) if it is successful. He expects Europe's energy use to still be below its current level over the next decade. But renewable energy use will probably decrease by 8 per cent and remain below its level over the next decade, he said. It was also predicted that the EU could decrease by 1 per cent of its carbon emissions by 2020. "Given the large disparity between the EU's commitment to renewable energy and its decreased emissions from consumption, renewable energy use is likely to significantly fall in 2020 by 8 per cent," he said. Mr Palmside said it was not possible for renewable energy use to reach a level lower than 70 per cent by 2018. "The EU will seek to meet that commitment as swiftly as humanally possible for renewable energy use in a variety of sources, including fossil fuels, wind turbines and geothermals," he added. After 17 years of selling and tattooing sports, Feldman came up with a hard-edged product. On 10 June, he tattooed a photo of the Philadelphia Eagles beating the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 10 of the 1969 NFC Divisional Championship Playoff. Feldman has been an active force in the sports movement since he grew up. "My grandfather was a sports fanatic and I was still playing football in second grade," Feldman said. "And football was the game I loved to watch. It wasn't until after I was older, when I was going to high school, that I started to get interested in sports." In October 1972, the New England native went to Washington Redskins Academy of Science, Washington, to study football, astronomy and economics. At 16 a year younger, he began playing competitive football. When he was a kid, he wore the San Francisco 49ers jog -- a similar jog he worn during the Redskins' Week 4 loss to the Patriots -- and later a "gate cap." In the early 1970s, partly out of a love of the arts, he joined a group of star artists called the Gary Feldman Group. Feldman sold and tattooed everything he loved, including famous NFL players, NFL game discs, NFL teams and NFL jeans. Most successfully, he also sold and tattooed weapons. He collected a wide variety of beautiful and rare objects -- wood, steel, mosaic, glass -- and passed on them for artistic study. Around 1973, Feldman worked with the artist and anthographer Parky Jamison on his final work -- a flashy yet haunting adaptation of the 1974 film Lights & Dark. "They thought I looked like an amazing artistic talent," Jamison said. "And they knew I could come up with my own artistic concept. So it was a big breakthrough." BUYING NYJS In 1987, Feldman opened up a jersey business in Los Angeles to make some money. His friend, baseball legend A.J. Jones, had taken him to a jersey business in Buffalo. The two had a discussion about opening up the business. The same year, he opened another jersey business in Los Angeles in 1989. "I didn't perform well, but I had a decent budget, and I started selling for perhaps tens of thousands, and I was so happy and made a profit," he said. In the 1990s, he acquired a jersey business near Buffalo and opened a jersey business in 2001. When sales started to trickle up, Feldman couldn't afford to stock up anywhere. He decided to buy jerseys everywhere, and offer them to new buyers. "I paid for a jersey at a exorbitant price," he recalled. "For the next year, I wanted to buy a jersey that I loved all my life. And that was the way to go." In 1992, Feldman began picking up jerseys for the New York Times, and a magazine deal blew out, offering them for $158,000. "I thought they would be pretty cool," Feldman said. In 1993, he acquired a custom-designed jersey hockey jersey in honor of William Peterson, a Los Angeles Chargers fan who wore a jersey hockey jersey on his head. For the next two decades, he held up the Chargers logo, displayed directly to the right of Peterson's statue. "The jersey isn't actually 20 years old," Feldman said. It's just another step in Feldman's artistic journey. He's now a sitting member of the Board of Trustees of the National Football, Baseball and Hockey Association. KTAGAD (Reuters) - More than a dozen American servicemen have died in intense operations in northern Afghanistan, the Afghan military said Friday. U.S. troops discovered the bodies of four servicemen on Wednesday and Thursday evening in the city of Bacha, the first such discovery since the Sept. 11 insurgency between NATO and Taliban-linked militants. The serviceman, 31-year-old Toriq Imoprah, was kidnapped and shot by the insurgency about three weeks ago when he arrived in the city as a guard. Imoprah had been kidnapped by the insurgency for nine months before he was moved to Bacha. Imoprah was shot in a training ground in Bacha, a city where soldiers train mercenaries, officials said. At least five different special operations forces - including the U.S. Guards, the U.S. Air Forces, and the Afghan National Defense Forces - have been carrying out operations in northern Afghanistan. A U.S. military spokeswoman said all five servicemen were in stable and critical condition after their injuries. “We will do everything we can to restore them for special operations service,” she said. U.S. reaction More than 2,000 servicemen entered northern Afghanistan around midnight on Thursday in search of supplies and helping those fleeing the violent insurgency against Taliban-linked militants. U.S. officials said more than 3,600 servicemen were in hiding in the area. The bulk of northern Afghanistan has been involved in intense operations in recent months, which have prompted an increasing number of deaths. Some 1,400 American servicemen arrived in the area on Thursday, and U.S. troops went to Bacha on the southern coast to help in the fight against the Taliban-linked militants. Mohammad Adona[when?][when?] (born November 8, 1960) is an Asian-American professional basketball player and championship hopeful who is based in Mumbai, New Delhi, India. The cause of her death is formally unspecified. According to some reports, Adona underwent a autopsy and was found dead near Darthmouth, Maryland.[1][2] Her family discovered her body in their village of Jajarde, Mumbai on November 8, 1960. The village was located just a few kilometers south of Mumbai, where Adona's younger brother, Mohammad Adona, was found dead on November 8, 1960. Adona died three years later in the grave found in the village.[3] The official date of her death is listed as November 8, 1960.[4] Career [ edit ] Reaching 16 years of age, Adona was a rising star in the sport, winning the Asian Championships, European Finals and National Championships from 1973 to 1979. In 1978, she became the first woman to represent Division I and became the first Indian athlete to win her gold medal. BEIRET (Reuters) - The husband of a 34-year-old woman from Syria was the first person killed in three bombings in the country since April, authorities said. Ali Ypiyeh, 34, the husband of children, told a news conference that she was killed and wounded by a fleet of Iraqi Islamic State (ISIS) fighters. The bombings were carried out in the west coast village of Coyashawa, 100 kilometres (30 miles) from the Turkish border with the Syrian city of Jordan. Two Turkish men were injured in the blasts, resulting in two others being killed and one wounded. A pregnant Turkish woman was hit by a suicide bomber as she was crossing the border and trying to enter a car, Turkey's Foreign Affairs Ministry said on Saturday. Four of her family members were reportedly in critical condition at the scene, the Defence Ministry said. No details have been released on which of them were killed in the attack. The Defence Ministry said the Turkish Revolutionary Protection Forces (YPG) was targeting a fighter from the Iraqi Islamic State (ISIS) fleet in Turkey. The first fighter was in critical condition. Turkish officials said they believed the first fighter was killed in the attack. The Turkish Defence Ministry said it was unclear how the fighter was killed. A foreign ministry spokesman did, however, did not say one Turk was killed in the attack, arguing that the attack violated parts of the country's foreign policy. ISIS fighters have stepped up several recent attacks, including targeting of an industrial plant in Arbaneseen, close to the Turkish border in April, as well as attacks against Turkish troops and linked insurgents in May. Eight Turks were killed and five wounded in separate bombings that hit a village in central Turkey in April. No details have been released. Turkey's Defence Ministry said four Turks and one of a family members were injured. Speculation as to the purpose of the attack is yet to be released. A Turkish citizen believed to have played a key role in the bombings and two foreign citizens were killed in the attack, the Defence Ministry said on Saturday. The Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the bombings were carried out against ISIS fighters as well as on Germans in the country last month. The bombings crashed into a car factory off the eastern coast of Pankar, Turkey on May 7, injuring 36 Turkish people. Among the bombers killed were two people of sub-Saharan origin and one person of Lebanese origin, the Turkish Foreign Affairs Ministry said. Two men were also injured: a man believed to be known only as Haled Raqab in Coyashawa and a man believed to be known only as Khaled William in Bucharest. Authorities say both men are believed to be associated with the ISIS fighters in Syria. No details on either suspect has been released. One foreign citizen was also reported to be killed in the attack. Turkey's Defence Ministry said the bombing, which left 82 Turks severely injured, was intended to fight the finances of Islamic terrorism. Turkey's special ambassador to Syria, Yuri Kusan, said security forces had been stationed to investigate atrocities. "We have no official reports of atrocities, but we have a number of reports of atrocities, and as we know they are under ongoing investigation," he said in a statement. In April, a Turkish woman who died in the village of Ypiyeh was rushed to an Indykar emergency center and is in critical condition. No other details have been released. But that strategy, Trump says, is still not working well at the core of his presidential campaign. Based on poll data, public belief in God has continued to decline in some demographics: in 2008, about 44 percent of Americans said they were non-religious, up from 46 percent in 1980. The share of non-religious views in the Catholic Church was down 10 percent overall, nearly twice what it was in 2008. In Protestant churches, they decreased slightly last year, Trump said. The share of non-religious views in the Catholic Church increased from 23 percent to 37 percent in 2008 — up from 43 percent in 1980. At the same time, he has been trying to shine a light on social issues in the U.S. political arena. Throughout his presidential campaign, he said, his efforts to reinforce public belief in God have taken to a new level. During polling on this issue, 71 percent of Republicans and 66 percent of independents said that they did not believe in God. Non-religious Americans serve longer in the military than conservatives, but more tend to feel okay about issues such as immigration, same-sex marriage, LGBT rights, housing and health care, and their low faith in God, Trump said. For the District of Columbia, the share of non-religious views increased from 44 percent to 37 percent in 2008. In 2008, 41 percent of Americans expressed conservative views, up from 46 percent in 1980. For the first time, non-religious people had to make informed decisions based on their age, ethnicity, and sexual orientation — while not believing in God, Trump said. He described his efforts as part of a strategy to make life easier for everyone. "The proportion of non-religious Americans under the age 65 has gradually declined following the election of then-serving President George W. Bush in 2002. JIM SALLER: Well, I think it would be okay for the Republican Party to stop spending on tax breaks and put more money into addressing global warming. (Photo11: Dave Janzansky, Associated Press) WASHINGTON (JPAN) — The global economy is on the long-term path of stagnating for the 12th time in at least a decade, a U.S. Federal Reserve report concluded Thursday, pointing to record-breaking job losses, unprecedented population growth and declines in investment. Short-term annual gains in jobs, accompanied by rising oil prices and increases in consumer spending, may have a significant impact on the employment outlook. The findings, published in The Wall Street Journal, add fuel to concerns that the economy is on the verge of stagnating over the next decade. Despite the decade-long slowdown, the economy has grown by 63 percent this year and the job market has declined by 27 percent, according to the new Fed data. The current levels of relative uncertainty indicate that the economy will remain depressed for the foreseeable future, economists said. Some have suggested the economy may rebalance in the relatively short term, though such a scenario appears unlikely. After one of its most deadly economic accidents, the Great Recession (GSI), and a series of other slowdowns in the late 1950s and 1960, the economy remains at greater risk of stagnating in the long term, said Kurt Weddle, a professor at the University of Chicago Business School and a co-author of the report. "If you were seeing a near-term consolidation and a severe recession probably you're going to see the slowdown is taking place," Weddle said, "but it's unlikely you'll actually see it happening." In a second sign in recent months that the job market is at its highest level in decades, economists said that happens sooner than expected. With the labor market deteriorating and consumer costs halving, employment in the U.S. grew 75 percent during the second half of this year compared with the previous quarter, according to the American Association of Economic Professionals. This is the 14th consecutive month of the Fed data, making the gains in jobs and record-breaking growth highly unlikely to economists. The official forecast shows a 63 percent slowdown over the next 14 years, according to Jim Edwards, senior economist at the Center for Fiscal Studies, a conservative think tank. "It was never going to be easy," he said. The U.S. economy is projected to reach its lowest level in 20 years, Edwards said, but expects population growth to become more sustained in the next decade or two. "We're on track to reach the levels seen during the 1940s and the '60s," Edwards said. Related Story: Everything You Need to Know About Japan Is Still Falling on the Bold The economy's slowdown is partly caused by rapid growth in the infrastructure and investments around the world, authors of the report said. But countries that experienced a similar slowdown during the 2000s may have been unable to cope with the stress of the recession. The Lions required the first four points of the game with less than 30 minutes to play. Monday's loss marks the sixth time in the history of the NFL that a team has taken less than 30 minutes in its game against a NFL opponent. Since 1970, the Lions have lost 10 games without 30 minutes. In the loss, the Lions averaged 56.0 percent on the road and 43.9 percent on the ground. It is still the lowest 30-minute rushing average for any team in the NFL, but the Lions are looking to take on another team that dipped 14-of-14 in the 46:46 span of time. With 14 minutes to play in the fourth and final quarter of the game, the Lions racked up 87 rushing yards. That was tied for the most in Lions history with a rushing performance in the 50-yard line. The Lions closed a huge deficit for the Patriots with 29 points to build a 10-14 lead on Monday by beating the Denver Broncos with 14 minutes left to play. The Lions tied Broncos' franchise record in rushing with 41.39 seconds remaining. The Broncos looked primed to strengthen that record Monday night with a 26-point win over the Giants. Their deficit fell to 53.89 seconds remaining at the start of the second quarter, and the Broncos continued to fall just short of the record. With 14 minutes to play over the final 50 yards of the game, the Lions should build a similar 10-14 lead over the Broncos as they did on Monday night against the Indianapolis Colts. A recent study on women at the college level found their prospects for college admission were diminishing, while men are still searching for college admission. The results show the share of women with a college degree has decreased. Women ages 25 to 34 expressed less desire to graduate from either high school or private school. In addition, women ages 25 to 34 expressed less appetite for a degree than women ages 40 to 49. Women aged 25 to 34 are less likely than men to graduate from high school or at the private sector than women aged 40 to 49 as their prospects for college admission decreased based on age, gender, and ethnicity, the study found. One of the main reasons for women's decreased prospects for college admission was an increase in the share of older women who are looking for college admission, the researchers wrote. " Men aged 25 to 34 were less likely than men older to hold majors in computer science courses than men and women aged 40 to 49," the researchers wrote. "Similarly, the proportion of women with a college degree has doubled over the past 10 years, from 4.4 among women aged 25 to 34, 4.6 among women aged 25 to 34 in 2015 and 4.8 among women aged 40 to 49." Similarly, from 1989 to 2015, the share of women who have a college degree swelled from 8.4 percent in 1989 to 8.4 percent in 2015 while the proportion of women looking for a bachelor's degree has more than doubled for women ages 25 to 34 seeking to graduate from high school or at the private sector. By 2015, the proportion of women with a college degree diminished from a high of 8.6 percent in 1989 to a low of 8.4 percent in 2015. Additionally, "from 1989 to 2015, the college admission rate for men with a college degree decreased by 27 percent, compared to 27 percent for women over 25," the researchers wrote. The college admission rate towered from 36.0 for women aged 25 to 34 to 4 for women aged 40 to 49 per year. From 1989 to 2015, the proportion of women with a college degree had further increased for women in high-income households — an increase of 8.6 percent for women in lower-income households. "On the long term, increased college admission rate might be related to retirements for women from less-educated sectors of the U.S. workforce," the researchers wrote. "On the medium end, the increase in college admission might stem from retirements for women from the less-educated sectors of the workforce." The share of women looking for college admission has decreased increasing the line between high-educated and lower-educated jobs, the researchers wrote. "The increase in the proportion of women with a college degree looking into high-educated jobs but in less-educated fields might also be related to the retirements of college-aging men currently in the workforce," the researchers wrote. As the share of women looking for college admission has decreased, the proportion of women with a college degree looking into computer science and IT jobs decreased by 8.6 percent for women who have a college degree in 2015 compared to 8.4 percent for women with a college degree in 2015. * * *

WASHINGTON (WFMA) — U.S. lawmakers on Sunday voiced dismay that President Donald Trump decided to fire acting assistant FBI Director James Comey, apparently because he hadn't disclosed enough details about terrorist attacks he was accused of planning during his presidency. The Wall Street Journal said the decision to fire Comey came just days after a Jan. 6 report that Trump fired a Russian government lawyer who pledged to become a criminal prosecutor on speech defamation charges to the federal Justice Department in the case of Jared Flynn, the Trump national security adviser who reportedly was under intense surveillance by a Russian government lawyer. Comey stated in his letter last week that those actions were planned. Shortly after the Sept. 11 bombings, a House Oversight Committee Chairman Jeff Sessions (R-TX) remanded Comey as an FBI director over multiple allegations that he engaged in a collusion between the United States and Russia, as well as hacking into the 2016 presidential election, according to the Washington Post's report. With Sessions's resignation and now Trump is expected to step down as FBI's director, Comey was bolstered by former House Intelligence Chairman Clapper to serve as an assistant attorney general. Clapper has yet to make a selection to be an FBI director, prompting Comey to be sacked. Comey told lawmakers last month that he would defend the actions of the FBI and the House Intelligence Committee against any claims he hacked into the 2016 election. Comey also has stated in on-screen filings that he planned the Sept. 11 attacks without revealing any details, according to the Washington Post. Sessions's resignation comes days after the U.S. Attorney General's Office denied that he obtained or disclosed confidential information including phone numbers, emails and home addresses, despite efforts to back down on any claims that he obtained such classified information. Comey's firing news comes because the Attorney General's Office has just finished finalizing the FBI's probe into his involvement. Follow Evan @WFMAViel INDIANAPOLIS, Va. (WFMA) — It's been a week since volunteers staged closed-entry doors to help provide affordable housing to the homeless community in many parts of the city. Late-night meetings haven't been scheduled, so Charitarians stayed late to take in free parking and drinks. Openings kick off at 5 p.m. Sunday, Jan. 3 at 1140 Chattano Dr. in Pearl Park, the first-time year-round event at a homeless person's home. The cost of the event will be $10 per person, and lots of people are expected to take in parking. Organisers for the event say they already had a door-to-door meeting with as many as four people. "We've been homeless for over 10 years and had a great community on the way, and it's been a busy week," said Robert Morrison, president of Imprency 41, a non-profit organization that is working to help provide affordable housing to the homeless in many parts of the city. "We have been unemployed homeless persons for over 10 years, and we have had some great communities on the way," Morrison said. Organisers for the event say they already had at least two or three meetings with the homeless community, so they're hoping there are dozens more. Openings kick off at 5 p.m. Sunday, Jan. 4 at St. Thomas GRAEATY, 9900 Woodside Blvd. in Indianapolis, the first-time year-round event for the homeless public. The cost of the event will be $10 per person, but attendees must be 18 years of age or older. Adults, grownups and anyone with a family member are welcomed to take in free parking. Door opening from 6:30 a.m.-9 p.m. are available from homeless.org at (91)976-3559. Charitarians and other volunteers in the area staged closed doors at approximately 10 a.m. local time. Openings will take place from 7 p.m. to 8 a.m. Sunday. "I was exciting to see all the food and drinks together," said Robert Morrison, chief communications officer for the event. "To see all the food and drinks put together, it's really exciting, but it's a little bit of fun to just go to the bar and drink some drinks during a year-round event," he said. "It was a bit of a shock to drive down the street and see lots of other people driving past during a year-round event," Morrison said.

(CNN) Apple updated its revenue outlook Thursday, adding that it expected more competition from e-commerce giant Amazon. The update comes after Amazon confirmed that its shares of its flagship Apple iPad dropped by about 10 percent in the fourth quarter. "I think our revenue outlook is pretty good," Amazon said in a blog post Thursday. "I think that's why it's not the end game." The net operating profit for the iPad started at $94 million in the fourth quarter before hitting $89 million in the third quarter. The net total operating profit for the iPad dropped by about $551 million in the fourth quarter before slipping to $635 million in the third quarter. Apple reached a deal with Amazon over selling its iPad in August last year, but the tablet's share price hasn't changed since its introduction. While Amazon's shares are down about 15 percent from the last, there are Amazon expectations of more competition on tablets. The news comes just four months after Apple shut down its iPad after a nine-month span that included shooting down an Apple Watch, a computer the company hadn't used since it first launched. Around the same time, Apple unveiled a six-year software update for the iPad. In a blog post on Sept. 24, Amazon increased its operating profit for the iPad by about $180 million ($800 billion) in the fourth quarter from about $170 million ($2.784 billion), and by about $114 million ($2.72 billion) from about $104 million ($2.795 billion). The net total operating profit for the iPad dropped by about $553 million in the fourth quarter before plunging to $635 million ($593 billion) from about $550 million in the third quarter. In a blog post that day, the company announced that it has sold 569 tablets since it first launched, bringing that total to 557 by the end of 2016. At the time, the company had only unveiled 411 tablets, of that total. Apple now sold 583 tablets in its fourth quarter, down 29 percent from 574 tablets the year before..

It was not immediately clear whether the missile was at the site or had been a suicide attempt. Iran's Arahman news agency said the strike had occurred during "an important moment in the relations between Israel and the United States and its partners in the disputed east, west and central regions." "Iran made no attempt to show its courage and courage in its battle with ISIS in those regions," an Israeli military statement said. "Israel forces launched a cruise missile at a base of a group fighting ISIS in those regions on Monday. No further launches are immediately planned," Israeli Prime Minister Isaac Hammond said in a statement. "Iran was not a suicide attempt, but showed its courage and courage in its battle with ISIS." More newsletter By Aaron Freeman, Columbia University, New York At about 11:30pm, the hot heat sent me on a desperate quest to find another place to sleep. After getting stuck for an hour, I rushed into the tent, trying to stay as high as I could. But, strangely, I couldn’t figure out who was sleeping or what I wanted to do. The fact is, it was 9:30pm on a beautiful day and I wasn’t allowed to stay up outside or look out the window of the tent. Nor did I come up with any ideas for how high I sat. That being said, it was a truly unprecedented and joyful night, better than anything else I’d experienced in my entire life. In many ways, at least, it just didn’t turn out the way it should have. For the remainder of three nights I slept on hot, dry bed and uncooled legs. I couldn’t walk or talk and felt numb for so long. Unfortunately, it’d taken three, four or five nights to get back into sleep on my own. However, I’ve followed Final Fantasy on a regular basis over a decade, following few games that have such a strong fan base like the Pink’s Toy series. Final Fantasy XIII is, quite frankly, the least attended game of the franchise, so let’s take Hulk: Winter Wars as a prime example. In 2011, when Winter Wars reached a gruesome end with Pink’s Toy Story: Children, it created a total App Store sales of an astonishing $40 billion. Well, I’d admit it myself. That same year, the series managed to beat Final Fantasy XIV by nearly $185 million. By saying it was the best game I ever watched, I was absolutely wrong. That being said, I never watched Hulk: Winter Wars in any manner whatsoever, not even for a week. In fact, as far as I knew, I’d never seen the game again. And without a doubt, the footage I watched instantly became one of my favorite features of Final Fantasy XIII. By the time it was announced, Final Fantasy: Winter Wars had been watched more than 900,861 times on the App Store, prompting overwhelming reviews, ratings, likes, teases, and criticizations. Since then, in a matter of months, since the game was officially announced on November 19, I’ve seen videos watched by more than 900,859 times on the app. Today, whenever I watch Hulk: Winter Wars, I’m almost in a state of shock. As you can imagine, I watch only about 15 million videos on YouTube, minus Netflix, these days. As I grow more familiar with the game, it felt natural for me. It was probably my biggest excitement, likely the biggest joy of my life, because of all the hard work I’ve put in so far. It’s an annoying feeling when you have something that has endangered you and you can’t fix it. It’s also one of the reasons I’m so focused on grappling with the pressures of being a Final Fantasy player. With Final Fantasy XIII, getting to grips with the crew, cast, writers, and producers of the team was, without a doubt, a huge experience. ::

On December 13, unemployment stood at 398,000, up 14 percent from the month before, according to data from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (NOHMS). That number is down from the 398,000 as seen the month before, or even as the month before, when 25 percent of full-time unemployed workers were unemployed and 27 percent of full-time unemployed workers. At the same time, Denver's job market has surged markedly, with more than 427,000 full-time workers now working full time. That's up from the 396,000 part-time workers seen the month before. "It's a shaky market, with no things falling off," said Ronald Edston, chief economic statistics officer for NOHMS. The proportion of workers transitioning from full-time to part-time hasn't changed much since January, but NOHMS believes other reasons, including lack of new hiring, sluggish economic growth and inability to find new employers, are likely to be contributing to reductions in unemployment. About 427,000 Denverans now hold either full-time or part-time jobs. During the past 12 months, there's seen more than 427,000 switch from full-time to part-time jobs, up from 365,000 earlier, as the city faces a marked drop in unemployment. Clearly it's a tight economy. "A lot of big cities are helping to slow the economy down," said Doug Scengell here with NOHMS. "Bigger cities are a way of encouraging more people to find work, and it's also driving up unemployment." But Denver's tight housing economy is making life difficult and forcing people to look for work or to find a job, Scengell said, adding that many people may find themselves unemployed or unemployed, or may find themselves unable to find a job in their or their home town. "That's exactly what's happening here," said Sarah Coltossed, chief economic officer for NOHMS. "Even as the proportion of workers transitioning goes down, an already-tight economy is coming to a standstill." A robust economic recovery in the past 12 months has slowed job growth in Denver. About 137,000 have found work in the past 12 months, but NOHMS officials see little indication of an increase in those numbers. The city's unemployment rate has jumped to levels at or above 7 percent since January, and officials say some of those numbers are bad news. About 36 percent of Denverans are unable to find a job, up from about 9 percent in the month before. They say those numbers are a sign of progress in the months ahead. "That's not an indication of things cooling down," Edston said..

More than one quarter of the planet”i‘s population could become the world’s third-largest emitter of carbon dioxide by 2050, say studies published today. The ocean — which holds at least 40,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide each year — could also hold more than 1% of the planet’s population, according to the new study. The findings come in response to a growing call to reduce the ratio of emissions scrapped from the atmosphere by 2050. The research by the U.S. State Department’s Center for Atmospheric Research (OCI), and funded by the University of California, San Diego, found that between 2020 and 2050 roughly 80% of the world’s carbon dioxide emissions would be extinguished as a result of either agriculture, coal mining or climate change. OCI proposes a population of at least 20,000 metric tons a year, which would represent more than 1% of the planet’s population by scrapping carbon from the atmosphere for industries such as skiing and fishering. The ocean’s population would reach 39,000 metric tons by 2050, and that number would be 7 times that of the Atlantic Ocean, the study authors note. Meanwhile, the ocean is generally assumed to be home to about half of the planet’s population, or about four and a half metric tons. The ocean — which holds more than 100,000 metric tons — is the world’s third largest emitter of carbon dioxide. The ocean’s population holds considerably less carbon dioxide than the atmosphere, though it would lose about 65% of its emissions from climate change, OCI says. There would still be concerns about health effects associated with scrapping of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere for industries such as skiing and fishering, the researchers note. But the world could also suffer the health effects of many types of industries, including agriculture — which increases the rate of global warming — thanks to the removal of many metric tons of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, the researchers note. The new study by the University of North Carolina’s OCI Center and the revised findings of the study, can be found in the Journal of Atmospheric Research. The findings are backed by growing calls for tougher taxes on emissions, as well as proposals for faster encroachment of U.S. presidential nominee Barack Obama’s Cleanr Power Plan, which would see the United States remove about 7 million metric tons from the atmosphere by 2010. Under Obama’s plan, the United States could lose about 100,000 metric tons, and by 2010, the world could lose 100,000 metric tons. Reduceing the ratio of emissions to the effects of climate change would eliminate thousands of jobs, mostly in productive industries. The reduction of the emissions could in large part slow the growth of productive industries, such as coal mining, and hit slower-growing industries such as fish and meat production, which release almost 40 million metric tons of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere each year. Today’s animals emit almost one million metric tons of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere every 38 seconds. By 2025, emissions from fish and meat are projected to average almost 3 parts per cubic meter. Environmentalists say that the loss of carbon dioxide is marginally caused by extreme weather conditions such as heat and drought. Carbon dioxide reductions would slow the growth of fish and meat production, but they would also put a strain on the world’s economy, according to the researchers supported by the National Science Foundation. But a study conducted by Arctic scientists at the University of Calgary suggests much of that is also being lost in the Great Plains. To find a solution, researchers gathered data comparing the land wealth, culture, ethnic group and political situation of six Arctic nations, which are a major producer of freshwater. They found that four of our wealthiest nations — across Southeast Asia, Africa, the Caribbean and parts of North America — have become so poor they are losing a portion of their freshwater supply. “We found that Alaska is by far the largest producer of freshwater in the Great Plains,” said Donald Mattata, from the University School of Economics and author of the latest study. Alaska is estimated to lose an additional $256 million gallons’ worth of freshwater within a decade, he said. The Great Plains derives an estimated 224 gallons of natural freshwater a year from Iran, a major source for two-thirds of global freshwater imports. Much of that freshwater comes from agriculture and fresh-water storage, which are being shutted down because of climate change. But although all of that freshwater is consumed by one-third of the Great Plains’ residents, a bigger bulk of that comes from agriculture and natural water storage. “Iran and Tunisia are the third-largest importers of freshwater,” said Malmat Yousefzah, a biologist with the Department of the Atmospheric and Atmospheric at the University of Calgary, who led the study. “Our Arctic nations are particularly poor because of the effects of global warming. There’s a lot of freshwater here, too.” The Great Plains are heavily polluted by marine and plant animals, which consume millions of pounds of freshwater. Coral, fish, whales and particularly aprians make up the bulk of the freshwater used each year in the Great Plains, according to WHO. But about one-third of our natural freshwater supply is being cut off. Global warming has reduced demands for freshwater in the Great Plains but has led to a slew of freshwater shortages that could be disastrous for both nations, said Mattata. Scientists have lowered freshwater demands by nearly 70 percent over the past 20 years — not by halting climate change but by adapt to extreme temperatures, as the latest study on that topic suggests. WASHTON (CNN) -- President Donald Trump's decision to repeal the Affordable Care Act, which would replace Obamacare with Social Security and Medicare, is "incredibly unacceptable and a disgrace," according to a release from Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Jeff Sessions (R-Calif.) of the bill on Wednesday. "I firmly support repealing Obamacare," Sessions said in a statement announcing his decision at a news conference at the American Family Institute in Washington, D.C. "I would like to recognize back the incredible, heroic work I have accomplished in fighting to the utmost to shut down the Affordable Care Act, and I look forward to leading a campaign to revoke the Affordable Care Act," Sessions added. "This President uses my leadership and long-standing experience to help restore the health of this nation and defeat the Affordable Healthcare Act." Sen. Chuck Grass (D-Nev.), the ranking Democrat on the committee, said the battle over the healthcare bill was a "stab to the head" and called the president's decision an "disgrace." "It is overwhelming and remorse to see such an important bill taking such power to the utmost - which is exactly what it is," Grass said. Sen. Chuck Grasham (D-Calif.) and Sen. Bob Booker (D-Conn.) also called on Trump to repeal the Affordable Healthcare Act. Sessions said the president's failure to do so was "irreversible." The move came just a day after Trump publicly threatened to reverse a section of his healthcare bill that would have allowed older patients for better access to medical care. But in a series of subsequent missteps, Sessions said the date to repeal Obamacare would move to Aug. 21, despite a warning from GOP leaders who said the date to repeal Obamacare had remained fairly unchanged. The Senate version, released Wednesday sets the effective date of repealing Obamacare Aug. 21, 2018. Related

The reservoir could serve as a reservoir for fermentation and storage, because trillion liters of water would need to seep into it. The extraplanetary landing, reported Nov. 8, took place at 1336C over "a relatively low altitude that is less than a quarter of the altitude on all planets," NASA's website states.
