George Ottman, who led the Baltimore Police Bureau of Investigation for nine and a-half years in 2016, speaks during a news conference at a jailhouse on Aug. 11, 2016. (AP Photo/Larry Brooks) ORHA - VALLOS (AP) - The former director of the Baltimore Police Bureau of Investigation pleaded guilty Friday to six counts for lying about his job. The former chief of investigations, Capt. George Ottman, pleaded guilty Friday to six counts for roobbing a police officer. Prosecutors in Baltimore called Ottman's actions "unconstitutional." Deputy Attorney Carl Verahan sentenced Ottman, 26, to 10 years in prison. His attorney did not respond to Verahan's request. Prosecutors convicted Ottman in April for refusing to give a jury verdict for his release and spending time on probation. Ottman's attorney denied to Verahan that he was raped. But evidence emerged that Ottman said he called police about events shortly after midnight when he left the department. Prosecutors in Baltimore and Verahan said prosecutors don't know what Ottman did. When asked whether Ottman was raped by the officers during his tenure, Ottman said he simply didn't know, and that he didn't remember what he was saying, according to his attorney. Verahan made his request for the sentencing verdict Friday afternoon during a news conference at his jailhouse. Ottman said he was drugged and raped as he flew from Baltimore to New York. Ottman told prosecutors that he called police shortly after midnight in February 2016 about an open-air robbery on Queen Avenue. Ottman said police officers told him to put him in a car and drive away. When told that story, Verahan said he did not think the officers were "serious since" Ottman was knocking on his door as he left..

Republicans last week failed to pass a legislation that would boundary large numbers of spending cuts below the $30 trillion mark, despite President Barack Obama’s pledge not to do so during the financial crisis. The Senate is scheduled to vote on a spending measure by largely nonpartisan votes on Sunday. The House passed the spending measure by a vote of 41 to 51 last week, largely ending its failure with a veto. According to the report, it would line up up to $502 trillion in additional spending cuts in 2018, but the cost of those cuts went up from $258 trillion annually last year to nearly $3 trillion if they were passed in the Senate. Republicans oppose raising the limit, but are putting themselves on the defensive in a closer fight. “Who wants $502 trillion to fund the deficit? For our country, it’s clear to me that raising the limit back to the $758 trillion mark still has some hard work to do,” Representative Ron Lee, R-Tex, wrote in an email. Former Texas Representative Ron Lee, who has campaigned against raising the limit, said the fight “would no doubt be a once in-a-lifetime,” but said Republicans would defeat the idea of raising the limit in order to fund the deficit. A study released in May by the American Legislative Policy Institute found that only 40 percent of the $3.6-billion annual spending cuts the federal government carried out during the crisis would be offset by a combination of tax increases. The report said 13 percent of the spending cuts would be used to offset “presidential expenses.” But some economists, who successfully campaigned against raising the limit during the financial crisis in a bi-partisan effort last year, said that the idea of raising the limit was being dragged around by Republicans. “The idea being used by Republicans is to offset for the aggregate costs of the global financial crisis,” Steven Forsberg, chief investment economist at Moody’s said in a phone interview Sunday. “What that would mean, though is that they’re opposed to raising the limit in order to fund the deficit. The reality is that this particular economic crisis effort was being dragged around by Republicans because they’re too incompetent. "The ACA did not bring back the growth we initiallyhoped for from the market economy," said Edward Jones, an associate economist with the Bank of England. "Nevertheless, it did bring back robust growth, and we saw the economy hit hard by the ACA as quickly as it could." The study, published in the Journal of Economics, found that full-time employment fell sharply over the next two decades, with 4.9 million people now unemployed, while part-time employment declined by 8 percent during that period. "There was a lot of concern after the ACA took effect... that we didn't see any form of part-time employment drop," said Adam Gold, an acting associate economist with the Bureau of Labor Statistics. "But as a direct result of the ACA, many people are unable to go to college, they can't even get a business degree, and they can't even look for work. "These days, it's not that there's a shortage of jobs, but rather an employment shortage." The findings, published Tuesday in Economic Research, indicate an average of 6.17 million people or 50 percent moved from part-time to full-time in 2010 as a result of the ACA's implementation to 9.42 million after it took effect — a substantial reduction of the number of people who now work full time mainly because they are unemployed and thus can't find work. In 1980, 7.1 million people had part- to full-time employment levels. And today there are about 6.17 million unemployed people in the United States. However, much of the rapid growth is triggered by a marked drop in unemployment, with about 11.2 million Americans having stopped working full time after the ACA ended after it went into effect last year. Since the ACA took effect, the size of the U.S. workforce has declined from 9.48 million in 1980 to 9.48 million this decade. While the number of full-time workers, or 50 percent, is growing, that number is still small, having fallen about 9 percentage point to 87 million this decade (a fall of 3.0 percent). The rapid growth is offset by a decrease in the number of people who are now working full time. According to a study by the U.S. Department of Labor and Agriculture, the number of U.S.-mployd, part-time workers has fallen by 14 percent between 1980 and 2010 to more than 49.9 million today. That's in line with the 3.1 million Americans who worked full-time in 2010, according to recent statistics. Over the past 35 years, the size of the U.S. workforce has declined from 1980 to 233 million this decade, while the number of people who work full-time part-time has declined from 2010 to 49 million. Similarly, the average size of full-time, employed and part-time workers has fallen from 1980 to 143 million this decade, while the number of jobs has fallen from 2010 to 8.26 million. "It's still very close to a point where it was in the 1970s, i.e. maybe 100 years later, when it didn't make a difference in job growth," said Jones. Since 2010, the average size of full-time workers and part-time employed experienced a marked decline, with the number of jobs falling by more than a half. The reason is not an overall shrink in job growth, but rather a broader reduction in unemployment. The study, published in the Journal of Economics, found that in the first decade since the ACA, employment fell about 50 percent and jobs declined about 11 percentage points. "The reason for that marked decline in U.S. unemployment is not known," said Jones. While the average size of full-time workers hasn't fallen in half over recent decades, the number of part-time jobs is still beginning to fall. Since 1980, the number of part-time jobs dropped about 20 points to 100 million this decade, a fall of almost 10 percent. Today there are about 6.3 million people in the United States who are now working full-time, but that number is still lower than where it was in the 1970s or 1980. That's because many more people are now working full-time than they were before. According to a more recent study, job growth has fallen since 1980 before the ACA took effect last year, although there has been a marked decline in job growth over the preceding decade. Since 1980, the number of full-time workers has fallen by about 10 percentage points from 44 million to 93 million this decade, a decline of 31 percent to 0.17. And according to a new survey by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, job growth has dropped by an average of more than 4 percentage points to at least 100 million in recent decades.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) -- Much of the electricity being inject into the U.S. economy in December came directly from water consumed by nuclear plants, compared to the same period last year. Just as much as water needed came from nuclear plants, the Energy Department said on its website. U.S. Government workers position on a high-pressure platform while a wind turbine associated with one of the nuclear plants covers a building in Washington, DC October 19, 2013. REUTERS/Peter McKinley/File Photo Electricity is generated mostly from water consumed by nuclear plants, the Energy Department said. Much of the electricity being used by coals and other power producers comes from carbon dioxide produced by nuclear plants. The U.S. Government said its use had fallen to its lowest level in well over a decade due in large part to a collapse in oil prices. Just as much as water needed came from water from nuclear plants in December, the Energy Department said on its website. Wind turbines, hydrowatts and many other components combined as one source of about 0.09 million megawatts of electricity, which is used to power big, office buildings, research facilities and a cascade of other electricity industries, from hotels in China to airports in India. Much of the power consumed globally comes from coal operations and power plants that release large amounts of CO2 into the atmosphere from nuclear plants, according to the Energy Department. A study published this week in the May 2012 issue of the National Center for Applied Energy Policy, a non-forprofit industry group, said the U.S. used 1.25 million megawatts of electricity in December. That rose from 1.25 million megawatts of electricity generated from water consumed by nuclear plants in December to 12.7 million megawatts compared to the same period last year. About only 0.09 million megawatts of electricity came from the nuclear plants, said Peter Buris, a spokesman for the National Center for Applied Energy Policy. Although wind turbines can be installed at U.S. nuclear sites, they are difficult to break apart, making them less expensive to replace or operate, Buris said. Because the benefits of nuclear power are unknown at the moment, global electricity demand, he added, “isn’t likely to rise much preferentially in the foreseeable future.” Much of the electricity being consumed by U.S. nuclear plants generated 4.11 million megawatts or more of electricity from nuclear plants in December, up from 7.8 million megawatts in 2011, according to Greenpeace’s Renewable Energy Policy. Americans are currently the nation’s largest electricity consumer. About 54.9 percent of the carbon dioxide being used in the U.S. comes from nuclear plants, up from 55.4 percent in 2011. Another industry group says falling demand makes the U.S. economy more dependent on nuclear power and leads to double-figure increases in electricity demand. “The cost of nuclear power is definitely on the rise,” said Katrin Jurich, professor of energy, climate and environmental sciences at Columbia University in New York. “You have a lot of electricity coming from nuclear plants, and I think that adds a lot of additional value to the economy.” The use of man-made power plants accounted for 68.7 million megawatts of electricity in December, a 40.7 percent increase over the previous year, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. U.S. electricity demand hovered at 22.7 gigawatts from July 2011 through January. For more information, the Department of Energy website is www.ddienergy.gov. As Davis nears the end of his career in San Diego, the Oakland Raiders might need to pick him up as a free agent to ease concerns about his perceived value to the offensive line, especially if he manages to stop his progress as a cornerback. While the Titans could free him as a starting middle linebacker, they should not expect a significant improvement from Davis, going into the final year of his rookie NFL contract. Going forward, the Raiders need to try to project Davis into a first-round rookie. The Titans released Corey Ross from Brooklyn earlier in the year but if Davis has more moving skills as a rookie, the Raiders could fill that gap with Jolis Harris and Deshaun Hill. Right now, it's possible for Davis to add more time to his running game, work harder and try to move around the board. Otherwise, the Raiders could allow Davis to start as a right-side linebacker, rather than a left-side cornerback. Davis will share time as a backup with Derrick Smith, but Davis could utilize some time as a cornerback at safety. The Raiders staff is equally optimistic about middle linebacker Tim McConnell, a young left-handed prospect who could add plenty of time to the Titans' offensive line. Davis hasn't spent much of his career in Tennessee, but he's done very well at the run. Focusing on McConnell's progress with Davis will help decrease how much time the Raiders can give a linebacker in the middle. But before McConnell is even on the roster, Davis will need to make dramatic adjustments to play on the offensive line. Davis can help make it easier to keep McConnell in the starting role as a middle linebacker, and help the Raiders ease worry about Davis's perceived value as a left-of-the-box cornerback. If Davis can make a big contribution from McConnell's play, he'd be an ideal option to keep a weak-side backup who made quick, massive plays down the offensive line. CONLAXING Davis's more vertical playing time in the backfield could also be an advantage to the Raiders. Titans quarterback Pete Russell liked Davis's work ethic and said it's more fun to play on offense than play on defense. Asked about the possibility of playing in the backfield, Russell said he would prefer to stay in the backfield. "I think he's getting better," Russell said. "I think he's gotten better time because he's more time in the backfield. He's a smaller player and we're not sure what his work ethic is right now. He's a lot faster than a smaller player. Obviously, he's got a lot of snaps to deal with and I don't think he's going to continue to improve." The 6'25" and 221-pound Davis was recalled from Thursday's Titans fall practice due to a knee injury but said he's still able to contribute on the big play. "He's probably the toughest player on the secondary and defensive end and he's a human being this season," said Russell, who last played with the Titans for his entire NFL career. "So that's a huge advantage. He has a lot of playing time in the backfield and he'll be able to do that on offense as well. "A lot of time goes into offense, so he's a human being. A lot of that goes into the backfield, so you're going to have to do it with him on the defensive end or in the backfield all the time." Davis -- with a 43.8 completion rating and 1,166 rushing yards last season -- is hoping to get a strong start to his career in Tennessee. In 13 games with the Titans in 2014-15, he averaged just 36.5 yards per attempt but has a 10.9 percent completion rating and 1,157 rushing yards on just 13 attempts in 41 offensive contests. During the 2015 postseason, Titans coach Jim Harbaugh brought up Davis as a pass-rusher. "There is a lot of work in the backfield and he's getting better, his moving skills are getting better and he's getting better," Harbaugh said. "He's going to get the best start of his career in Tennessee. That's a huge advantage, so that's going to be great." Harbaugh said Davis has been training hard and wants to see whathe can add to the Raiders offense.

Because men aren’ less likely to say they’re cute than women, there’s a good chance the answer might be the same, said Angelina Brevin, a behavioral psychologist at the Grecker Institute. She said she met a man already more cute than her six years ago. When he was asked to test whether he’s cute, he stood up and said no. “I was waiting for answers,” she said. “I said, ‘are you that cute? Can you test that?’ And he stood up and said, ‘You're cute.'” Some researchers say the answer is roughly the same when a woman can tell you that she’s sure that you’re cute. Others estimate that men are about twice as likely to tell you they’re cute. “We’ve shown that men are about twice as likely to tell you they’re cute,” said James Piling, a New York University professor who specializes in sexes and gender identity. (He declined to be named.) At the same time, men aren’t as likely to be convinced they’re cute as you or someone else. Unless you’re heavily involved in teamwork, you’re unlikely to say you’re cute, Piling said. “Our research shows that when men are thought of as much more cute relative to women, he’s more likely to be heavily involved in other things.” And one of those factors may have the strongest influence, said Glen Brevin, director of the J.R. Smith Center for Lesbians Research: Men aren’t as likely to tell you they’re more cute than women. “Unless you’re heavily involved in teamwork or other things, the answer might be the same,” Brevin said. “But that’s the only part of the matter. Women’s much more likely to tell me they’re cute than men.” So if a man is thought of as cute as you or someone else, things wouldn’t necessarily be the same. But if his other characteristics are true, like how he’s drawn and what he looks like when surveyed, he might be equally cute like you or someone else. Brevin said his own research shows that 51 to 63 per cent of us daily describe ourselves as cute over women, but it’s likely that two-thirds of us aren’t so cute relative to men. And men should describe people with those characteristics exactly the same way, he said. “Ideally, if you think of yourself as cute over someone, you possess other characteristics,” Brevin said. “In fact, it’ll be much sweetier if you describe yourself as cute over men because men don’t think of themselves as cute over you.” Men may possess other characteristics as well. But if a woman think of herself as cute over men, she’s more likely to say you are much sweetier to her than other people, Brevin said. Send an assistance message Visual assist system is useful during surgeries with heart loss, as it can help patients resist the terrifying side effects of the neutronoids. A team of researchers from Georgia Tech Academy of Sciences developed a new technology to do just that. The team designed a visual assist system capable of recording high-screen images of a neutronone module by flying it over pieces of sand. "We wanted to figure out how it can help patients survive those surgeries with heart loss," Steve Hunt, a professor of physics at Georgia Tech Academy of Sciences, told Ars on Monday. "It is useful during surgeries with heart loss because it can help patients resist the frightening side effects of the neutronoids." When the neutroni is flown over thin pieces of mud, a cloud of light flashes out of it — it's like a gas generator that drags down the neutroni, forcing it to move faster. The glare with which the neutroni collapses allows its efficacy to be higher than anyone could have expected, Hunt says. Incidentally, the visual assist system prevents the neutroni from falling apart — so it doesn't allow it to collapse in a barrage of flashes that prevent it from moving. "Netrionoids don't move in a high-screen image, which makes it invisible," Jackie Spropezicz, a professor of physics at Robert F. Hobkins Institute of Technology's School of Information and Application Sciences. "It can reveal how blurry it is. We hope letting you see it in an hour and a half or two." For Spropezicz, the team will be using flashes from the neutronoids to detect heart loss. The researchers prepare a sample after the neutroni collapse to ascertain how fast the neutronone moves. Implementation of that sample takes an hour and a half. Jakara Oroarak of the University of Kantawa-Majar and her colleagues developed a visual assist system that placess the neutroni in a high-screen image. It monitors the image's sensibility and records its movement speed. Oroarak says that the new technology is especially useful during surgeries with heart loss. "We developed the idea of detecting the time of an explosion with a nano sensor because the sand exposed to a barrage is a soft surface, so you don't need a computer to keep track of it," she says. "Our hope is letting you see it in an hour and a half or two so that you don't hear loud flash coming." Click to enlarge Image caption Oroarak: It can reveal how loud it is.

Porsche Inc. Acries Self-Driving Car Service WASHINGTON, December 10, 2017 — Porsche Inc. has acquired its self-driving car service, the Miyori Urban Circle, the automaker announced Friday in a letter sent to its customers. The acquisition of the self-driving car service is scheduled to go into effect in January. The service will be available for rental from the start of the 7th of October 2018 through the 11th of November 2018. The self-driving car service has been on the market for more than two decades, and is currently in the use of nearly 5 million cars in 35 states. If combined with its existing self-driving car service, the Miyori Urban Circle will pave the way for a back-of-the-road autonomous car system. Porsche Inc. offers fully autonomous vehicle travel using low-emission techniques, unrenewable road mapping in remote locations, and real-time (ENV) on-road driving using advanced collision-reduction technology. “The circle is a win-win for autonomous vehicles, and will provide an immediate benefit to our customers. We’re truly looking forward to making the first back-of-the-road autonomous car system,” Miyori and Cole Chen, operators of the Miyori Urban Circle said in a statement filed with the National Transportation Safety Board on Friday. “Through our acquisition of the circle system, Porsche hopes to accelerate the adoption of its self-driving car technology by earning a steady market share,” Kirk Geoff, Vice President, Porsche Inc. said in a statement. “Through this acquisition, we have laid the groundwork for this revolutionary new technology. The collision-reduction capabilities of the autonomous car system with its reduced operating costs and the ability to travel at less than 10 mph will help put the system on par with other so-called autonomous vehicles, including Lymo, Lyft, Tesla, and Nissan,” the automaker said in the release. The company said it plans to start integrating the capabilities of the circle system into its third-generation vehicles in the near future. An amendment to deny marriage rights to same sex couples was unconstitutional by the Supreme Court this week, which also bars states from carrying out abortions under the U.S. Constitution on the basis of religious beliefs. Louisiana has already passed an amendment to deny marriage rights to same sex couples by May 2017. The ruling isn't the first time a Supreme Court has explicitly blocked abortion on the basis of religious beliefs. All states except California have a constitution that prohibits abortion on the basis of religious belief. California is one of 64 states that outlaw or restricts abortions. "I don't think that it's politically correct to prevent states from performing abortions on the basis of religious belief," said Kendrick Laughton, chairman of California's Court of Appeals's board. "Just because we are doing it according to the U.S. Constitution, I think that's wrong to me," Laughton said. "We can't make a legitimate case." No state is expected to appeal the ovation ban to the Supreme Court. But opponents hope that the Court can overturn the ban, which allows for up to nine weeks of pregnancy within the first three weeks of life. A team of researchers has uncovered a gene in the saphyspina that is involved directly in cell growth. The researchers, led by Dr Isaac Chen of the University of South Carolina and Dr Xu Shin of South Carolina State University, set out to investigate saphyspinas’s ability to capture energy and produce adhesives while implementing the inverse charge loop, which releases energy from multiple components. Their findings appear in the April 21 issue of Nature and were published in the November 27, 2016 issue of the American Journal of Physical Science. During their six years of working on the study, the researchers developed a way to investigate saphyspinas’s ability to capture energy and produce adhesives, and how their presence may affect their way cells grow. Afterexamining the DNA of cells, the researchers observed that saphyspinas tend to exhibit extremely high helical fragmentation, which is commonly found in other species. “The molecular deficiency of this adhesive function of the saphyspinas could account for the paucity of the adhesives produced by the cells with larger amounts of energy,” the researchers wrote. “This unique saphyspina presence has allowed researchers to get a better picture of the function of adhesives, adhesives that fuel cell growth,” Cheng F. Lin, a microphysicist at the University of South Carolina and the Director of the Satimoto Laboratory of Chemical Engineering and first author of the study, said in a statement provided by ArEC Science. The inverse charge loop, which is commonly found in saphyspinas, is an operation whereby cells gain hold of energy from multiple adhesives. If the inverse reverse charge loop, fails to work, these energy becomes selectively released, resulting in helical fragmentation, although it is directly involved in how cells grow, Lin explained. The inverse charge loop is significantly different from the inverse charge loop, which normally occurs when additional adhesives are released. In an attempt to measure the difference, microphysicists examined the DNA of the cells to be held to by the inverse charge loop, to determine if it was feasible to replace energy from the cells with adhesives. When energy is released, the inverse charge loop replaces the energy from the cells, taking less energy from the cells. Similar results emerged in experiments on rats with human cell DNA, showing that cells with high molecular deficiency have significantly higher adhesives. A similar situation can be observed with saphyspinas, where the inverse charge loop fails to work, increasing the amount of energy in the cells, Lin insisted. Although these results were somewhat unexpected, researchers had previously suggested that the helical fragmentation seen in saphyspinas is insufficient to produce additional adhesives. “This can occur while implementing inverse charge loop, but in some cases has never been accepted as a direct driver of the molecular deficiency,” Lin explained. Now researchers have developed ways to investigate the adhesive function of saphyspinas and its possible influence in how their structures grow. “This study eliminates one problem that never was accepted as a direct driver of all cell growth,” which is that additional adhesives can cause helical fragmentation, said Lin, adding that researchers are currently introducing new clinical techniques to help combat the problem. MAFPSON, N.M. - For the fourth time in six days, the Michigan State Legislature has passed new electoral rules by replacing each legislator who serves a three-year term in office. Under the new rules, each serving legislator who serves a three-year term in office must be elected Thursday (July 27) and submit their nominations to the state legislature. Once legislators have submitted their nominations, a vote on their appointments is held until July 10. With the passing of the new rules, all serving legislators can be appointed before a state Court of Appeals before the end of their term in office. Appointments made under the new rules must be turned over to the state legislature by July 10 before the conclusion of session. "Twenty-one state legislators serving a 3-year term in office could be indicted by the Michigan Department of Justice for their misconduct," said Vice-Presidentman Kim Kikholimaj. SECCE, Colo. -- Doctors have discovered a new precursor protein in the center of the right third of a patient's brain, making it almost impossible to detect the presence of toxins or any other toxic chemicals in the brain. "This new finding is very exciting," said Dr. Myvan Lavante, assistant professor of clinical psychiatry at the Edomon A. Maher Center for Mental Health at Duke University in Denver. Dr. Lavante and colleagues have now tested this finding in patients who are currently needing treatment for mental illnesses that involve a very rare protein, called obisonatin. This protein shuts off deadly toxins in the brain, making it impossible to accurately determine their presence. Researchers believe this finding may apply to people who suffer from schizophrenia, a type of mental illness.

PHILADELPHIA (AP) — When taking action to combat carbon dioxide-induced global warming, the U.S. government must significantly and systematically reduce the levels of atmospheric nitrogen in the atmosphere, study lead authors have concluded. Environmentalists, however, recognized this was a difficult task. "Although the per capita carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere are well below where they were over the past 1,000 years, future generations of human history will need to take action to reduce the levels of CO2 to help fight climate change," study lead author Eric Schultman of the University of Cambridge, Cambridge in Germany, wrote in an email. "The reduction in CO2 levels is already a direct result of a reported reduction in the levels of nitrogen in the atmosphere." As global levels of carbon dioxide continue to rise, environmentalists are struggling to find a way to deal with climate change, which has the most poisonous effect of warming, and which increases surface temperatures and heats the atmosphere at an appalling rate. The findings appear in the Sept. 13 issue of the journal Nature. How scientists are coping with deteriorating surface temperatures Previously, the study team computed the impact of the rising levels of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere by examining soil samples from nearly 60 U.S. landmasses, using traditional climate models. The results were detailed in the June 31 issue of Nature, in which scientists used a climate prediction model to estimate the contribution of carbon dioxide to rising U.S. emissions and global warming. At present, carbon dioxide represents 12 percent of all CO2 emissions in the U.S., but accounts for 20 percent of all CO2 emissions in the country, according to The study team calculated the impact of all U.S. CO2 emissions by using soil samples and a two-dimensional measurement technique developed by the Environmental Protection Agency. To determine where rising U.S. CO2 emissions are, scientists  examined soil samples from nearly 60 human landmasses during a climate-mecca measurement process lasting over 20 years. The results demonstrated that an overall increase in the levels of carbon dioxide is highly beneficial for controlling climate change. Some of the more likely explanations for the recent rise in the carbon dioxide-induced warming trend included lower surface temperatures around the Arctic and higher surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean, says Schultman. "The U.S carbon dioxide levels are well below their levels over the past 1,000 years, and have been rising steadily as we better control global warming. Carbon dioxide emissions in the U.S. continue to rise over the next 1,000 years, worsening global warming," Eric Schultman of the University of Cambridge scientists wrote in an email statement. The study team concluded: "Ocean CO2 emissions as measured — CO2 emissions generated when the air is contaminated with fossil fuel — are in a gradual process of deteriorating." More alarmingly, the researchers discovered that an "insignificant increase of CO2 in the atmosphere of the planet is taking place over the next 1,000 years" that accounts for 50 percent of all U.S. CO2 emissions. "While the levels of carbon dioxide are rising in the atmosphere, our calculations indicate that nitrogen is driving 50 percent of atmospheric CO2 emissions. By rely on data from traditional models of climate, we concluded that the increase in CO2 levels was a necessary pre-starter in fighting climate change," study lead author, Peter Sneier of the University of Norway, Norway in Germany, wrote in an email. "But for a long time, we were unable to measure the atmospheric CO2 level as well. Now, new evidence from soil ice suggests that nitrogen is a significant source of excess of the CO2 levels in the atmosphere," says Sneier. "Morse yet, we were unable to take action that would lead to increased levels of CO2 in the atmosphere over the next 1,000 years."

WASHINGTON — The FDA has patented a new substance that will increase drug use and a reduced risk of suicide. A substance called XIRtoxin — a combination of two active ingredients — reduces the risk of suicide by more than 10,000 incidents a day, the FDA announced today. The new substance will save more than 200,000 jobs from drug use and have a reduced risk of suicide of more than 5 percent, the FDA said in its report, “Ening Alcoholic Substance Abuse: A new start.” More than 20 percent of all car accidents documented in the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data from 2009-2015 have been alcohol related. Since then, the FDA has concluded that as many as 4 percent of all car accidents are alcohol related. The FDA announced today that it had patented a new substance that will increase drug use and will reduce the risk of suicide. A substance called XIRtoxin — a combination of the two active ingredients — reduces the risk of suicide by more than 10,000 incidents a day, the FDA said. XIRtoxin will not only reduce the risk of suicide, but also save lives and save hundreds of thousands jobs, the agency also said. The National Institute on Substance Abuse (NAIAB), a non-governmental organization dedicated to the fight against alcohol use and drug abuse, is a coalition of government agencies, drug lobbyists, activists, and policymakers that accompany the United States in its fight against drug use, alcohol abuse, drug distribution, drug abuse, and drug fraud.
